findings.claim: Gabaix's main result: if units in the upper tail follow proportional random growth with a common mean and common variance (Gibrat's law), and normalized sizes (size divided by the total or mean) reach a steady state, the upper tail converges to Zipf's law with zeta = 1. The paper adds that the explanation is robust to new cities and to several means and variances.
findings.citation: Gabaix, X. (1999). Zipf's law for cities: an explanation. Quarterly Journal of Economics 114(3), 739-767. doi:10.1162/003355399556133
findings.relevance: This is the canonical prior statement of the working hypothesis. 'Nature doesn't care about concentration' is operationally Gibrat's law, and 'conservation' is Gabaix's normalization by the total. A paper presenting orthopolity as a dynamical law has to start from this result.
findings.formula_or_number: P(S > s) ∝ s^-zeta with zeta = 1 under Gibrat's law plus a stationary normalized distribution

findings.claim: In Gabaix's reflecting-barrier version, normalized size follows a geometric Brownian motion with negative drift mu < 0 and a lower barrier S_min. The stationary exponent is zeta = 1/(1 - S_min/Sbar), where Sbar is the mean normalized size. zeta is strictly greater than 1 and tends to 1 only as S_min/Sbar -> 0, which Gabaix describes as needing only an infinitesimally small barrier. His 2009 review adds that with large frictions (a reflecting barrier, or the Kesten version in his 1999 Appendix 1) a power law arises but Zipf's law does not hold exactly, and zeta > 1.
findings.citation: Gabaix (1999) QJE 114(3):739-767, reflecting-barrier section (text quoted in a search-result summary of the paper; I did not read the paper directly). Gabaix, X. (2009). Power laws in economics and finance. Annual Review of Economics 1, 255-294.
findings.relevance: This is an exact deviation formula, and its friction parameter S_min/Sbar is measurable. It shows that zeta = 1 is a limit approached as friction vanishes, not a fixed point that holds at finite friction.

findings.claim: My own derivation, checked by Monte Carlo: for dS = mu S dt + sigma S dB with a reflecting floor, the zero-flux stationary density gives zeta = 1 - 2mu/sigma^2. Keeping the normalized mean fixed forces the drift loss to equal the resource re-injected at the floor, so -mu = phi, the injected share per unit time. Hence zeta = 1 + 2phi/sigma^2. For a pure Pareto tail this is the same as Gabaix's 1/(1 - S_min/Sbar). Monte Carlo: S_min = 0.2 predicts 1.250, Hill estimate 1.244; S_min = 0.1 predicts 1.111, Hill estimate 1.128.
findings.citation: Own derivation and numpy Monte Carlo in the session scratchpad (mc.py). Builds on Gabaix (1999).
findings.relevance: It rewrites the deviation in terms of a dimensionless injection-to-volatility ratio 2phi/sigma^2. Both quantities can be estimated from panel data, which turns 'deviations are imposed by constraints' into a quantitative prediction.
findings.formula_or_number: zeta - 1 = 2 phi / sigma^2 (exact for the reflected GBM with mean conservation)

findings.claim: In a Kesten process S_{t+1} = gamma_t S_t + epsilon_t (with E ln gamma < 0 and an additive term), the tail exponent is the positive root of E[gamma^zeta] = 1. zeta = 1 exactly when E[gamma] = 1, that is, when the multiplicative part conserves the mean. Normalizing by the total makes E[gamma] = 1 for the multiplicative factor. If an additive term carries a share phi of the total each step, stationarity of the mean forces E[gamma] = 1 - phi < 1, and convexity then gives zeta > 1.
findings.citation: Kesten, H. (1973). Acta Mathematica 131, 207-248 (cited from memory). The condition <b^alpha> = 1 and the normalization argument E[gamma] = 1 are confirmed in secondary sources (MIT 14.13 lecture notes reconstructing Gabaix; arXiv:1511.09449). The phi-dependence is my own derivation.
findings.relevance: It identifies the ingredient that pins zeta to 1: the multiplicative channel must conserve the mean, so all aggregate change is proportional. Once a finite share enters additively, the exponent becomes a free parameter.

findings.claim: For a lognormal multiplier ln(gamma) ~ N(m, v) with additive injection share phi, so that E[gamma] = 1 - phi, the exact Kesten exponent is zeta = 1 - 2 ln(1 - phi)/v, approximately 1 + 2phi/v. Monte Carlo with 400,000 units: phi = 0.01, v = 0.04 predicts 1.503, Hill estimate 1.49; phi = 0.05, v = 0.2 predicts 1.513, Hill estimate 1.51-1.54; phi = 0.02, v = 0.04 predicts 2.01, Hill estimate 1.90-1.97.
findings.citation: Own derivation and Monte Carlo (session scratchpad mc.py)
findings.relevance: It confirms that the deviation from zeta = 1 is set by the ratio of injected share to log-growth variance, not by either quantity alone.

findings.claim: Levy & Solomon argued that multiplicative random processes in systems with many degrees of freedom produce Boltzmann distributions in the logarithm of the normalized variables, which appear as power laws in the raw variable. They state that the mechanism links the system's constraints, the power-law exponent, and the dispersion of the fluctuations. A 1999 review attributes to this line of work the formula alpha = 1/(1 - c), where c is the lower bound on wealth as a fraction of the mean. A model without a floor gives alpha = 1.
findings.citation: Levy, M. & Solomon, S. (1996). Power laws are logarithmic Boltzmann laws. International Journal of Modern Physics C 7(4), 595-601. arXiv:adap-org/9607001. The alpha = 1/(1-c) attribution comes from the review arXiv:adap-org/9912002.
findings.relevance: This is physics prior art (1996) for the same mechanism and the same exponent formula as Gabaix. It also supplies the 'Boltzmann law in log variable' framing a physics paper on orthopolity would naturally use.

findings.claim: In the Malcai-Biham-Solomon model (random multiplicative updates with a lower bound c times the momentary average), the exponent alpha(c, N) is insensitive to the noise distribution but non-universal, and it increases monotonically with c. alpha(0, N) = 0 for any finite N, while alpha(c, infinity) >= 1 for any c > 0, so the limits N -> infinity and c -> 0 do not commute.
findings.citation: Malcai, O., Biham, O. & Solomon, S. (1999). Power-law distributions and Lévy-stable intermittent fluctuations in stochastic systems of many autocatalytic elements. Physical Review E 60(2), 1299-1303. arXiv:cond-mat/9907320
findings.relevance: zeta = 1 exactly is a singular limit whose value depends on the order of limits. A law stating zeta = 1 must specify finite-N corrections and the order of limits, or it is ill-posed.

findings.claim: Bouchaud-Mézard model (exchange coupling J plus multiplicative speculative noise): the mean-field wealth distribution is Pareto with an exponent always greater than 1, tending to mu = 1 + J/sigma^2 as sigma -> 0. The paper describes a phase transition between an economy dominated by a few individuals (condensation) and one where wealth is more evenly spread. A later summary places condensation, defined by divergence of the variance of x_i/<x>, at J <= sigma^2.
findings.citation: Bouchaud, J.-P. & Mézard, M. (2000). Wealth condensation in a simple model of economy. Physica A 282(3-4), 536-545. doi:10.1016/S0378-4371(00)00205-3. arXiv:cond-mat/0002374
findings.relevance: Here zeta = 1 is the zero-redistribution limit, and the deviation is set by redistribution rate over volatility. The model uses noise variance 2sigma^2 per unit time, so J/sigma^2 matches my 2phi/(variance rate). It is prior art for the deviation formula and for framing zeta = 1 as a phase boundary.

findings.claim: Simon (1955) model: with probability alpha the next increment founds a new unit; otherwise it goes to an existing unit in proportion to its size. The stationary Yule-Simon distribution has shape rho = 1/(1 - alpha), so the density tail is s^-(1+rho) and zeta = rho. Zipf (zeta = 1) is reached only as alpha -> 0, and the model cannot produce zeta < 1.
findings.citation: Simon, H. A. (1955). On a class of skew distribution functions. Biometrika 42(3-4), 425-440. Formula confirmed via the Wikipedia Yule-Simon entry and arXiv:physics/0601192.
findings.relevance: This is the oldest version of the same deviation law: alpha is exactly the share of resource increments injected at the bottom. It reproduces zeta - 1 ≈ alpha for small alpha.

findings.claim: Malevergne, Saichev & Sornette show that Gibrat's rule at all firm sizes, combined with firm births and deaths, gives Zipf's law under a balance condition. The condition equates the effective growth rate of incumbents (including their possible demise) with the growth rate of investment in entrants. They interpret Zipf's law as the signature of the long-term optimal allocation of resources that ensures the maximum sustainable growth rate of an economy. A seminar draft gives the long-run growth as max{mu - h, d + c0} and the balance as mu = h (for d = c0 = 0). Here mu is incumbent growth, h the death hazard, d the growth rate of birth intensity, and c0 the growth rate of entrant size.
findings.citation: Malevergne, Y., Saichev, A. & Sornette, D. (2013). Zipf's law and maximum sustainable growth. Journal of Economic Dynamics and Control 37(6), 1195-1212. doi:10.1016/j.jedc.2013.02.004. arXiv:1012.0199. Seminar draft: 'Zipf's law for firms: relevance of birth and death processes' (ETH CER seminar, 2010).
findings.relevance: This is the closest prior art. It already frames zeta = 1 as a resource-allocation principle and states the condition that selects it. An orthopolity paper presented as a new law of resource allocation would be anticipated by it.
findings.formula_or_number: Balance: mu - h = d + c0 (Zipf); long-run growth = max{mu - h, d + c0}

findings.claim: My reconstruction of the general exponent equation in the MSS framework (geometric Brownian motion growth mu, sigma; death hazard h; birth intensity growing at d; entrant size growing at c0): (sigma^2/2) m^2 + (mu - c0 - sigma^2/2) m - (d + h) = 0. Hence m = 1 iff mu - h = d + c0. Writing g = mu - c0 and phi = (d + h) - g for the entrants' share of resource growth in normalized units, this is exactly (m - 1)(g + sigma^2 m/2) = phi, checked numerically for random parameters. phi > 0 gives m > 1, and phi < 0 gives m < 1. With d = c0 = 0, an independent search-assistant derivation for Zhang & Sornette's setting gave the same quadratic.
findings.citation: Own derivation (session scratchpad mc.py). Consistent with the MSS balance condition (2013) and with Saichev, Malevergne & Sornette (2010), Theory of Zipf's Law and Beyond, Lecture Notes in Economics and Mathematical Systems 632, Springer, doi:10.1007/978-3-642-02946-2. The exact equation as printed in MSS was not seen.
findings.relevance: This single identity contains Gabaix (g = -phi gives zeta = 1 + 2phi/sigma^2), Bouchaud-Mézard, Kesten (small phi) and Simon as special cases. It gives a measurable, parameter-free prediction of the deviation and a sign rule: Gibrat-class stationary conserved stocks with injection at the bottom should have zeta >= 1.

findings.claim: The arXiv summary of Saichev, Malevergne & Sornette's book says that, although they use firm-asset terminology, the relations they derive, especially the link between Zipf's and Gibrat's laws, underlie Zipf's law in diverse scientific areas, and the same models apply to other domains. The core result is Gibrat at all levels plus birth and death processes, giving Zipf's law under a balance between firm growth and death rate.
findings.citation: Saichev, A., Malevergne, Y. & Sornette, D. (2008). Theory of Zipf's law and of general power law distributions with Gibrat's law of proportional growth. arXiv:0808.1828. Book: Saichev, Malevergne & Sornette (2010), LNEMS 632, Springer.
findings.relevance: This is an explicit cross-domain generality claim for the Gibrat-plus-balance mechanism of zeta = 1.

findings.claim: Zhang & Sornette measured mean growth r, its standard deviation sigma and the death rate h of Amazee social-network groups. Without adjustable parameters they predicted the exponent mu = 0.75 ± 0.05, in excellent agreement with maximum-likelihood fits. The authors attribute mu < 1 to the average growth rate exceeding the death rate.
findings.citation: Zhang, Q. & Sornette, D. (2011). Empirical test of the origin of Zipf's law in growing social networks. Physica A 390(23), 4124-4130. arXiv:1007.2650 ('Predicted and verified deviation from Zipf's law in growing social networks').
findings.relevance: This is a real conserved-resource system (members) with zeta clearly below 1, and the same Gibrat framework predicts it quantitatively. It counts against zeta = 1 as a law. It supports calculable deviations, and it is prior art for the test design an orthopolity paper would need.

findings.claim: Hisano, Sornette & Mizuno estimated the average growth rate of product market shares, its standard deviation, birth rates and hazard ('death') rates directly. They report that temporal variations and product differences in the observed power-law exponents are fully captured by the theory without adjustable parameters.
findings.citation: Hisano, R., Sornette, D. & Mizuno, T. (2011). Predicted and verified deviations from Zipf's law in ecology of competing products. Physical Review E 84, 026117. arXiv:1101.5888
findings.relevance: The program of predicting deviations of zeta from 1 using measured growth, birth and death parameters has already been carried out and published in a physics journal.

findings.claim: Marsili & Zhang (1998): with a fixed number of individuals, a non-interacting linear model gives an exponential rank-size relation. Pairwise interaction makes the weight scale as w ~ m^2, giving q_m ~ 1/m^2 for m << m* ≈ 1/p and hence R(m) ~ 1/m, which is Zipf with exponent 1.
findings.citation: Marsili, M. & Zhang, Y.-C. (1998). Interacting individuals leading to Zipf's law. Physical Review Letters 80, 2741. arXiv:cond-mat/9801289
findings.relevance: Here zeta = 1 comes from a specific interaction order (pairwise), not from conservation by itself: the non-interacting conserved case gives an exponential. It is prior art for a 'law' of city formation with exponent 1, and a reminder that conservation alone does not select zeta = 1.

findings.claim: Drăgulescu & Yakovenko: in a closed economy where money is conserved and exchanged in random additive amounts, the equilibrium distribution is exponential (Boltzmann-Gibbs), P(m) = C exp(-m/T), with T the mean money per agent. They generalize that any conserved quantity in a large statistical system should be exponentially distributed in equilibrium.
findings.citation: Drăgulescu, A. & Yakovenko, V. M. (2000). Statistical mechanics of money. European Physical Journal B 17, 723-729. arXiv:cond-mat/0001432
findings.relevance: This is a direct counterexample to 'conservation plus indifference to holdings gives zeta = 1'. Indifference in additive (absolute) terms gives an exponential distribution. A power law with zeta = 1 needs multiplicative (scale-invariant) indifference, which is Gibrat's law. The paper must say which kind of indifference it means.

findings.claim: Stationary source-driven Smoluchowski coagulation with kernel K ∝ (m1 m2)^{nu/2} (homogeneity nu) has a Kolmogorov constant-mass-flux solution c(m) ∝ m^-(3+nu)/2, carrying mass from small to large sizes. My arithmetic: the count survival exponent in mass is zeta = (1+nu)/2, and mass per log bin scales as m^{(1-nu)/2}, so O_log holds only for nu = 1. A constant kernel (nu = 0) gives zeta = 1/2.
findings.citation: Connaughton, C., Rajesh, R. & Zaboronski, O. (2004). Stationary Kolmogorov solutions of the Smoluchowski aggregation equation with a source term. Physical Review E 69, 061114. arXiv:cond-mat/0310063. The zeta and log-bin arithmetic is mine.
findings.relevance: A conserved resource carried by a constant-flux cascade does not generically sit at zeta = 1; kernel homogeneity sets the exponent. Orthopolity must either exclude cascade-class systems or accept them as falsifiers.

findings.claim: In Dohnanyi's self-similar collisional cascade (mass flows from large to small bodies), the steady state is dN ∝ m^-11/6 dm (equivalently D^-7/2 dD), so the survival exponent in mass is zeta_m = 5/6 < 1 (top-heavy in mass). Reviews citing Tanaka et al. (1996) say the exponent is set only by the mass dependence of the collisional rate, and that size-dependent strength or velocities move it (to q up to 4 in size).
findings.citation: Dohnanyi, J. S. (1969). Collisional model of asteroids and their debris. Journal of Geophysical Research 74(10), 2531-2554 (volume and pages from memory; the 11/6 value is confirmed via a Bellcomm/NTRS version and reviews). Tanaka, H., Inaba, S. & Nakazawa, K. (1996), Icarus 123, 450 (from memory; content confirmed only via a review). Pan & Schlichting (2012).
findings.relevance: This is a mass-conserving natural system with zeta ≠ 1 and a calculable exponent. Its direction (top injection, bottom removal) suggests that the sign of zeta - 1 follows the flux topology, which an orthopolity paper could test.

findings.claim: Eeckhout: using all US Census 2000 places (no truncation), the city-size distribution is lognormal, consistent with Gibrat's proportional growth without a stabilizing friction. Levy's comment: for the top 0.6% of cities, which hold more than 23% of the population, the distribution departs sharply from lognormal and follows a power law. Eeckhout's reply maintains a lognormal upper tail.
findings.citation: Eeckhout, J. (2004). Gibrat's law for (all) cities. American Economic Review 94(5), 1429-1451. Levy, M. (2009). Gibrat's law for (all) cities: comment. AER 99(4), 1672-1675. Eeckhout (2009). Reply. AER 99(4), 1676-1683.
findings.relevance: Gibrat's law alone gives a lognormal, not zeta = 1. The zeta = 1 tail needs the extra stabilizing ingredient, so 'nature doesn't care' is not sufficient. Any orthopolity claim must be limited to the upper tail and state its stationarity mechanism.

findings.claim: Using the uniformly most powerful unbiased test of Pareto against lognormal on US places, the roughly 1,000 largest cities (more than half the US population) are Pareto, but with tail exponent zeta = 1.4 ± 0.1, which excludes zeta = 1. Smaller cities are better fit by a lognormal. A separate study of 2000 Census places finds a lognormal-to-Pareto switch near population 60,290 with Pareto exponent 1.25.
findings.citation: Malevergne, Y., Pisarenko, V. & Sornette, D. (2011). Testing the Pareto against the lognormal distributions with the uniformly most powerful unbiased test applied to the distribution of cities. Physical Review E 83, 036111. Preprint arXiv:0909.1281 ('Gibrat's law for cities: uniformly most powerful unbiased test of the Pareto against the lognormal'). The PRE citation is from memory; content confirmed from the preprint.
findings.relevance: Under administrative city definitions, the flagship domain for zeta = 1 shows a significantly larger exponent. That direction (zeta > 1) is consistent with the injection sign rule.

findings.claim: Across 73 countries, Zipf's law is rejected for 53 countries using OLS and 30 using the Hill estimator, far more often than chance would give. Under OLS, the Pareto exponent is significantly greater than 1 for 39 countries and significantly less than 1 for 14. Political-economy variables explain the variation better than economic-geography variables.
findings.citation: Soo, K. T. (2005). Zipf's law for cities: a cross-country investigation. Regional Science and Urban Economics 35(3), 239-263. Counts from the CEP DP 641 abstract; 39/14 split from Princeton lecture notes on the paper.
findings.relevance: There is a broad cross-country spread with deviations on both sides of 1. The deviations correlate with institutional constraints, which fits 'constraints cause deviations' but contradicts zeta = 1 as an observed regularity.

findings.claim: When cities are defined bottom-up by clustering populated cells (City Clustering Algorithm) instead of legal boundaries, Zipf's law (exponent close to 1) holds for population down to about 12,000 inhabitants in the USA and about 5,000 in Great Britain. City areas are also close to Zipf.
findings.citation: Rozenfeld, H. D., Rybski, D., Gabaix, X. & Makse, H. A. (2011). The area and population of cities: new insights from a different perspective on cities. American Economic Review 101(5), 2205-2225. arXiv:1001.5289
findings.relevance: This is the best support for zeta ≈ 1 in cities. It also shows that the exponent depends on how the unit is defined, so the reference measure and unit definition must be fixed in advance.

findings.claim: Cristelli, Batty & Pietronero argue that Zipf's law needs a property they call 'coherence' of the sample. It roughly holds within individual European countries but fails completely for the aggregated EU. US national city sizes are near-Zipf, while single-state subsets are not.
findings.citation: Cristelli, M., Batty, M. & Pietronero, L. (2012). There is more than a power law in Zipf. Scientific Reports 2, 812. doi:10.1038/srep00812
findings.relevance: zeta = 1 is not additive across subsystems, so it only applies to an interacting, normalized whole. That matches the role of the normalization/conservation constraint, but it means arbitrary samples (catalog windows, regional subsets) should not be expected to show it.

findings.claim: De Marzo et al. treat Zipf behavior dynamically, with the number of elements as a time-like variable. Genuine Zipf needs a coherence constraint tying the distribution's parameters to the number of elements. They state that earthquakes evolve incoherently and so show Zipf's law only spuriously, that US cities are coherent while world cities are not, and that Zipfian dynamics are not additive.
findings.citation: De Marzo, G., Gabrielli, A., Zaccaria, A. & Pietronero, L. (2021). Dynamical approach to Zipf's law. Physical Review Research 3, 013084. arXiv:1911.04844
findings.relevance: This is a direct challenge to using earthquake catalogs as evidence for zeta = 1 in a conserved resource. It is also prior art for a physics treatment of when zeta = 1 is genuine.

findings.claim: Corominas-Murtra & Solé claim that Zipf's law is an inevitable outcome of a very general class of stochastic systems, derived with algorithmic information theory from a few mild assumptions. The key assumption is that the complexity of the observation sequence is that of a system evolving to a stable state between order and disorder.
findings.citation: Corominas-Murtra, B. & Solé, R. V. (2010). Universality of Zipf's law. Physical Review E 82, 011102. arXiv:1001.2733
findings.relevance: This is an existing high-profile universality claim for the exponent 1 by a route unrelated to resource conservation. A general-law orthopolity paper has to place itself relative to it.

findings.claim: In sample-space-reducing (history-dependent) processes, rank distributions of visits are exact power laws with exponent -1 (Zipf), without multiplicative, preferential or self-organized-critical mechanisms. Adding noise gives frequency exponents from alpha = 2 to infinity, tied simply to the noise level.
findings.citation: Corominas-Murtra, B., Hanel, R. & Thurner, S. (2015). Understanding scaling through history-dependent processes with collapsing sample space. PNAS 112(17), 5348-5353. doi:10.1073/pnas.1420946112
findings.relevance: Observing zeta = 1 does not imply resource conservation with Gibrat dynamics; another generic mechanism produces it. Orthopolity cannot be inferred from exponents alone, and the paper needs mechanism-specific tests such as measured phi and sigma^2.

findings.claim: Kawamura & Hatano present a simple generic model that reproduces Zipf's law (exponent -1). They explain it as a random walk on a logarithmic scale and state that the explanation applies to various natural and social phenomena.
findings.citation: Kawamura, K. & Hatano, N. (2002). Universality of Zipf's law. Journal of the Physical Society of Japan 71(5), 1211-1213. arXiv:cond-mat/0203455
findings.relevance: This is an earlier physics paper claiming cross-domain universality of zeta = 1 via log-scale random growth, the same mechanism family as orthopolity's dynamical reading.

findings.claim: Mora & Bialek show that Zipf's law in a large system is equivalent to entropy being an exactly linear function of energy with slope 1. That makes k_B T = 1 a very special critical point: the system freezes below it, and thermodynamic quantities diverge above it if the law holds exactly. Schwab, Nemenman & Mehta (2014) show Zipf behavior can arise in multivariate data without fine-tuning, through latent variables. Aitchison et al. (2016) make a similar point.
findings.citation: Mora, T. & Bialek, W. (2011). Are biological systems poised at criticality? Journal of Statistical Physics 144(2), 268-302. arXiv:1012.2242. Schwab, D. J., Nemenman, I. & Mehta, P. (2014). Zipf's law and criticality in multivariate data without fine-tuning. Physical Review Letters 113, 068102 (PRL citation from memory; title confirmed). Aitchison, L., Corradi, N. & Latham, P. E. (2016), PLoS Computational Biology 12, e1005110.
findings.relevance: This is prior art for the physicist's framing of zeta = 1 as a marginal or critical balance point, the analogue of orthopolity's 'marginal between bottom-heavy and top-heavy'. It also shows zeta ≈ 1 can arise from hidden-variable mixtures without any conservation law.

findings.claim: Hernando, Puigdomènech, Villuendas, Vesperinas & Plastino derive Zipf's law from a Fisher-information variational principle under scale invariance. In a companion paper they interpret Zipf's law as a special equilibrium state of a 'scale-free ideal gas', with other exponents corresponding to other equilibrium or non-equilibrium states.
findings.citation: Hernando, A. et al. (2009/2010). Zipf's law from a Fisher variational-principle. Physics Letters A (arXiv:0908.0501). Fisher-based thermodynamics for scale-invariant systems: Zipf's law as an equilibrium state of a scale-free ideal gas (arXiv:0902.2738). Journal volume and pages not confirmed.
findings.relevance: This is existing physics work presenting zeta = 1 as an equilibrium or extremum principle, the 'natural law' framing the authors want.

findings.claim: Visser shows that maximizing Shannon entropy subject to a fixed mean of log(observable) gives power laws with exponent z > 1 (needed for convergence). Exact Zipf (z = 1) is never reproduced this way, only approached arbitrarily closely.
findings.citation: Visser, M. (2013). Zipf's law, power laws and maximum entropy. New Journal of Physics 15, 043021. arXiv:1212.5567
findings.relevance: Maximum entropy with a log constraint does not select zeta = 1. The exponent is set by the constraint value, and 1 is only a boundary or limit. This counts against the hypothesis that O_log is 'the maximum-entropy state'.
findings.formula_or_number: z > 1 required; z = 1 only as a limit

findings.claim: Local Zipf exponent under size-dependent growth (Gabaix 1999; used nonparametrically by Ioannides & Overman 2003 on US metro areas 1900-1990): zeta(S) = 1 - 2mu(S)/sigma^2(S) + d ln sigma^2(S)/d ln S. Here mu(S) is the size-specific mean growth relative to the aggregate. I re-derived the + sign on the variance-slope term from the zero-flux Fokker-Planck condition. Ioannides & Overman conclude that deviations from Zipf are explained by deviations from Gibrat.
findings.citation: Gabaix (1999) QJE. Ioannides, Y. M. & Overman, H. G. (2003). Zipf's law for cities: an empirical examination. Regional Science and Urban Economics 33(2), 127-137. The exact printed form was not seen; sign re-derived by me.
findings.relevance: This turns 'deviations are imposed by constraints' into a local formula with measurable growth moments. It is the natural test equation for the authors' thesis.

findings.claim: The firm growth-rate standard deviation falls with size as sigma ∝ S^-beta, with beta = 0.20 ± 0.03 (sales) and 0.18 ± 0.03 (employees), over seven orders of magnitude, so Gibrat's law fails in the variance. US firm sizes (about 5.5 million firms, 1997 Census) are Zipf-distributed, with exponent reported as 1.059 (secondary source). My implication: in the local formula, the variance term alone shifts zeta(S) by -2beta ≈ -0.4, so the observed zeta ≈ 1.06 needs a compensating size-dependent drift or a non-stationary explanation.
findings.citation: Stanley, M. H. R. et al. (1996). Scaling behaviour in the growth of companies. Nature 379, 804-806. Amaral, L. A. N. et al. (1997). J. Phys. I France 7, 621 (beta values). Axtell, R. L. (2001). Zipf distribution of U.S. firm sizes. Science 293(5536), 1818-1820. The 1.059 value is from arXiv:cond-mat/0401053.
findings.relevance: Firms are cited as a flagship zeta ≈ 1 case, yet 'indifference to size' (Gibrat) measurably fails for them. Matching zeta ≈ 1 therefore needs compensation the simple theory does not supply. The -2beta implication is my own inference.

findings.claim: In ecology, the abundance-size exponent is predicted to fall from -0.75 (all organisms on one resource) to exactly -1.0 in multi-trophic food webs with trophic transfer efficiency TTE = 10% and predator-prey mass ratio PPMR = 10^4. In four freshwater food webs, measured TTE was 1.0-3.6% (mean 1.85%) and normalized biomass size-spectrum (NBSS) slopes were significantly steeper than -1 (-1.14 to -1.19). My arithmetic for the implied slope of biomass per log-mass bin is 1/4 + ln(TE)/ln(PPMR). The 1.85% mean gives about -1.18 NBSS, inside the observed range.
findings.citation: Mehner, T. et al. (2018). Empirical correspondence between trophic transfer efficiency in freshwater food webs and the slope of their size spectra. Ecology 99(6), 1463-1472 (bibliographic details from memory; content confirmed from the abstract in the publisso repository). Brown, J. H. et al. (2004). Ecology 85, 1771-1789. Trebilco, R., Baum, J. K., Salomon, A. K. & Dulvy, N. K. (2013). Ecosystem ecology: size-based constraints on the pyramids of life. Trends in Ecology & Evolution 28, 423-431.
findings.relevance: Deviations are quantitatively calculable from measurable constraints (TE, PPMR), which fits the authors' view. But in this theory O_log is not an attractor: it needs the coincidence TE = PPMR^-1/4, and real lakes miss it by a predictable amount.
findings.formula_or_number: NBSS slope = -1 + ln(TE)/ln(PPMR) + 1/4; TTE 1.85% -> slopes -1.14 to -1.19

findings.claim: Mechanistic size-spectrum theory gives a community spectrum N(m) ∝ m^-lambda with lambda = 2 + q - n ≈ 2, where q is the search-volume exponent and n the consumption exponent, so biomass is close to constant in log-spaced bins. Andersen & Beyer (2006) derived lambda ≈ 2.05 from individual-level processes, independent of the predator/prey size ratio.
findings.citation: Hartvig, M., Andersen, K. H. & Beyer, J. E. (2011). Food web framework for size-structured populations. Journal of Theoretical Biology 272, 113-122 (journal details from memory). arXiv:1004.4138. Andersen, K. H. & Beyer, J. E. (2006). Asymptotic size determines species abundance in the marine size spectrum. American Naturalist 168, 54-61. doi:10.1086/504849
findings.relevance: Near-O_log in the ocean follows from physiological exponents nearly cancelling (q ≈ n), and the deviation is lambda - 2 = q - n. That is a constraint-calculable deviation, but O_log is again a parameter coincidence rather than a conservation-selected fixed point.

findings.claim: Global ocean size spectrum (upper 200 m, bacteria to whales): abundance per log-mass bin has exponent -1.04 (95% CI -1.05 to -1.02), roughly equal biomass per log bin. Human impacts have truncated the upper third of the spectrum, and today's slope is significantly steeper than the pre-1800 slope.
findings.citation: Hatton, I. A., Heneghan, R. F., Bar-On, Y. M. & Galbraith, E. D. (2021). The global ocean size spectrum from bacteria to whales. Science Advances 7(46), eabh3732 (citation details from memory; numbers confirmed from the PMC/bioRxiv text).
findings.relevance: This is the strongest single support for O_log in a biomass stock. The deviation is small and on the zeta > 1 side (bottom-heavy), the direction the injection sign rule predicts.

findings.claim: Aki (1981) proposed D = 3b/c with c = 1.5, i.e. D = 2b, linking the Gutenberg-Richter b-value to the fractal dimension of faulting (Turcotte: b = D/2). With N(>r) ∝ r^-D and A ∝ r^2, this means N(>A) ∝ A^-b, so rupture-area zeta_A = b. Empirical tests are mixed: Hirata (1989) found D = 2.3 - 0.73b in Tohoku, while D ≈ 2b held on the locked Parkfield segment.
findings.citation: Aki, K. (1981). A probabilistic synthesis of precursory phenomena. In Earthquake Prediction, Maurice Ewing Series 4, AGU (details from memory; relation confirmed via Hirata 1989, JGR 94(B6), 7507-7514). Turcotte (1986).
findings.relevance: The repository's re-expression (O_log holds for rupture area because zeta_A = b ≈ 1) is anticipated by the long-known D = 2b / N(>A) ∝ A^-1 relation. Its empirical status is contested.

findings.claim: The b-value decreases linearly with differential stress: b ≈ 1.23 - 0.0012(sigma1 - sigma3) with stress in MPa (intercept uncertainty ±0.06, slope ±0.0003), calibrated across tectonic regions and depths. By faulting style, b is highest for normal, intermediate for strike-slip and lowest for thrust (Schorlemmer et al. 2005). Italian zones give reverse 0.75-0.81, normal 1.09 and strike-slip 0.90-0.92 (Gulia & Wiemer 2010). My arithmetic: b = 1, and hence zeta_A = 1, corresponds to a differential stress of about 190 MPa, not to any dynamical fixed point.
findings.citation: Scholz, C. H. (2015). On the stress dependence of the earthquake b value. Geophysical Research Letters 42, 1399-1402. Schorlemmer, D., Wiemer, S. & Wyss, M. (2005). Variations in earthquake-size distribution across different stress regimes. Nature 437, 539-542. Gulia, L. & Wiemer, S. (2010). GRL 37.
findings.relevance: The deviation is calculable from a measurable constraint (stress), as the authors' view suggests. But the reference value b = 1 is not privileged: the global b ≈ 1 reflects the mix of stress regimes in the catalog rather than a conservation-pinned O_log.

findings.claim: Mean-field fault and elastic-interface (depinning) models give avalanche-size exponent tau = 3/2. Hence b = (3/2)(tau - 1) = 3/4 and moment exponent beta = 1/2, which matches strike-slip b ≈ 0.75. Global Harvard CMT depth ≤ 50 km gives b ≈ 0.75 (strike-slip), 0.85 (thrust) and 1.05 (normal), per a secondary source. Under self-similar A ∝ M0^{2/3}, mean-field theory implies zeta_A = 3/4, not 1 (my arithmetic).
findings.citation: Fisher, D. S., Dahmen, K., Ramanathan, S. & Ben-Zion, Y. (1997). Statistics of earthquakes in simple models of heterogeneous faults. Physical Review Letters 78, 4885-4888. Dahmen, K., Ertaş, D. & Ben-Zion, Y. (1998). PRE 58, 1494. Review: arXiv:1312.7156. Kagan (2010), 'Earthquake size distribution: power-law with exponent beta = 1/2?', arXiv:0908.1207.
findings.relevance: For event catalogs, the standard physical theory does not predict O_log in rupture area. Earthquakes are not Gibrat-class stocks, so the Gabaix-type mechanism does not apply, and they need a separate argument or should be treated as weak evidence.

findings.claim: Gabaix, Lasry, Lions & Moll show that standard random-growth (Gibrat/Kesten) models produce transition dynamics an order of magnitude too slow compared with the data, and that tail transitions are even slower than the average speed suggests. Their remedy is scale or type dependence, i.e. deviations from Gibrat.
findings.citation: Gabaix, X., Lasry, J.-M., Lions, P.-L. & Moll, B. (2016). The dynamics of inequality. Econometrica 84(6), 2071-2111. NBER WP 21363.
findings.relevance: The zeta = 1 stationary state may not be reached in finite-age systems. Observed exponents can reflect transients rather than constraints, which a 'law' claim must handle (for example, with relaxation-time estimates per domain).

findings.claim: Gabaix (1999) treats Simon's model for cities, where the number of cities grows at rate nu and total population at rate gamma, giving zeta = 1/(1 - nu/gamma). Zipf requires nu/gamma -> 0, and convergence to zeta near 1 becomes very slow (a criticism also attributed to Krugman 1996).
findings.citation: Gabaix (1999) QJE, Simon-model section; Krugman, P. (1996), The Self-Organizing Economy. From memory; not confirmed in this session.
findings.relevance: This is a further special case of zeta = 1/(1 - injection share), and it raises the slow-convergence issue near zeta = 1.

res.novelty_assessment:
The novelty threat is high for the dynamical core of the claim and moderate-to-low for a carefully scoped, cross-domain test.

The mechanism is old. "Nature doesn't care about concentration" means proportional, size-independent growth (Gibrat's law). Combined with conservation (normalization by the total, E[gamma] = 1) and a vanishing stabilizing friction, it gives zeta = 1 in the resource variable. That is Gabaix (1999, QJE), anticipated in physics by Levy & Solomon (1996, IJMPC) and Malcai, Biham & Solomon (1999, PRE), with alpha = 1/(1 - c). Bouchaud & Mézard (2000) have zeta = 1 + J/sigma^2. Simon (1955) has zeta = 1/(1 - alpha). The exact deviation law in terms of growth, birth and death rates is in Saichev, Malevergne & Sornette (2010, LNEMS 632) and Malevergne, Saichev & Sornette (2013, JEDC). MSS already frame zeta = 1 as "the signature of the long-term optimal allocation of resources", and the book summary claims relevance to "diverse scientific areas".

Parameter-free tests of predicted deviations already exist: Zhang & Sornette (2011, Physica A) and Hisano, Sornette & Mizuno (2011, PRE). Cross-domain universality claims for zeta = 1 already exist through other mechanisms: Kawamura & Hatano (2002), Corominas-Murtra & Solé (2010, PRE), Hernando et al. (Fisher information), Mora & Bialek (criticality), sample-space-reducing processes (Corominas-Murtra, Hanel & Thurner 2015, PNAS), and the coherence papers (Cristelli et al. 2012; De Marzo et al. 2021).

The domain pieces are also known:
- **Ecology:** Sheldon's equal biomass per log class, with deviation theory via TE/PPMR (Brown 2004; Trebilco 2013; Mehner 2018) and q - n (Hartvig, Andersen & Beyer 2011).
- **Seismology:** zeta_A = b via D = 2b (Aki 1981), with stress-dependent b (Scholz 2015).

So a paper claiming "orthopolity is a general law because Gibrat plus conservation selects zeta = 1, with constraint-caused deviations" would be read as a rediscovery.

What I could not find in the literature (searches only, not exhaustive):
1. One explicit criterion, the resource variable plus a reference measure (resource-weighted log-uniformity), applied to both stocks and event catalogs.
2. A single deviation identity, (zeta - 1)(g + sigma^2 zeta/2) = phi, which I derived from the MSS-type master equation. It unifies Gabaix, Kesten, Bouchaud-Mézard and Simon, and I have not seen it tested across several domains with independently measured phi, g and sigma^2.
3. A sign rule tested as a prediction: Gibrat-class stationary conserved stocks with bottom injection must have zeta >= 1, while top-injected cascades such as Dohnanyi (5/6) can have zeta < 1.
4. An explicit split into universality classes (Gibrat stocks, coagulation/fragmentation cascades with zeta = (1+nu)/2, avalanche/depinning events with zeta_A = 3/4 in mean field), stating where O_log is and is not predicted.

These are where a contribution could still be new. The strong "natural law" claim is contradicted by verified counterexamples:
- Amazee social groups, zeta = 0.75, predicted by the same theory.
- US places, zeta = 1.4 ± 0.1.
- Soo's 73-country spread (39 significantly above 1, 14 below).
- Cascades: 5/6 and (1+nu)/2.
- b-values linear in stress.
- Additive conserved exchange gives an exponential, not a power law (Drăgulescu & Yakovenko).
- Maximum entropy does not select 1 (Visser).
- Non-commuting limits (Malcai et al.).
res.implications:
How to make the paper strong rather than rediscovered:

**(1) Reframe the claim as a theorem plus a falsifiable deviation law, not an empirical universal.**
- **Theorem:** within the class of scale-invariant (Gibrat) dynamics of an additive resource, with a stationary normalized total and a stabilizing channel carrying a resource share phi, the stationary upper tail is Pareto with (zeta - 1)(g + sigma^2 zeta/2) = phi. O_log (zeta = 1) is the phi/sigma^2 -> 0 limit. It is also the boundary between the non-condensed phase (zeta > 1, finite mean) and the condensed phase (zeta < 1, where the largest units hold a finite share). Cite Gabaix, Levy-Solomon, Malcai et al., Bouchaud-Mézard, Simon and Saichev-Malevergne-Sornette as special cases. This is the precise version of "nature doesn't care about concentration": it is multiplicative indifference. Additive indifference with conservation gives the exponential (Drăgulescu-Yakovenko), and the paper should say so explicitly.
- **Corrections:** state the finite-N correction and the order of limits.

**(2) Make the empirical core a preregistered, out-of-sample test of the deviation law.**
- In each domain with panel data, measure phi (entrant or floor share of resource flow), g (normalized incumbent drift), sigma^2 (log-growth variance rate), and the death rate h with the birth-intensity growth d, then predict zeta with no free parameters.
- Compare with an MLE zeta (Clauset-Shalizi-Newman with likelihood-ratio tests against the lognormal).
- Candidate domains: CCA-defined cities, Census firms, product market shares, and forest or plankton biomass with turnover data.
- This extends Zhang-Sornette and Hisano et al. across domains. A successful multi-domain zero-parameter prediction would be a real contribution.

**(3) Test the sign rule as a meta-analytic prediction.** Gibrat-class conserved stocks should show zeta >= 1 when injection is at the bottom. Verified data so far mostly agree: US places 1.4, Axtell firms about 1.06, Hatton ocean about 1.04, GLOSSAQUA about 1.015, lake food webs 1.14-1.19, Soo's majority above 1. Known exceptions need explanation: Soo's 14 countries below 1, and Amazee groups at 0.75, where growth exceeds death, i.e. a non-stationary normalized total.

**(4) Separate universality classes.**
- **Cascades:** coagulation with source gives zeta = (1+nu)/2, and Dohnanyi fragmentation gives 5/6. O_log is expected only for special kernels, and exponents are set by rate homogeneity.
- **Avalanche/event catalogs:** mean-field depinning gives tau = 3/2, b = 3/4, zeta_A = 3/4. Self-similar area zeta_A = b is the old D = 2b relation. b follows stress as b ≈ 1.23 - 0.0012 Δσ, and De Marzo et al. call earthquake Zipf spurious.

Earthquakes and flares should therefore be presented as a separate, weaker class needing their own mechanism, or as tests of whether O_log extends beyond Gibrat stocks. They should not be pooled as confirmations.

**(5) Ecology.** Present O_log as near-cancellation of physiological and trophic exponents. The NBSS slope is -1 + ln(TE)/ln(PPMR) + 1/4, and lambda - 2 = q - n. Ask whether any mechanism tunes TE toward PPMR^-1/4; if not, O_log there is a coincidence rather than a law.

**(6) Address the standard objections head-on:**
- Gibrat alone gives a lognormal (Eeckhout), so restrict the claim to the upper tail.
- The exponent depends on unit definition (Rozenfeld et al.), so fix units by a stated algorithm.
- Coherence (Cristelli et al.): only interacting, normalized wholes qualify.
- Slow convergence (Gabaix-Lasry-Lions-Moll): give relaxation-time estimates.
- Alternative routes to zeta = 1 without conservation (sample-space-reducing processes, latent variables, criticality): seeing zeta ≈ 1 does not identify the mechanism, so require measured phi and sigma^2.

Calling it a "mathematical property" is defensible only in sense (1), as a limit theorem within a stated dynamical class. As an unconditional natural law, the verified counterexamples falsify it.

findings.claim: Aki's relation links the fractal dimension D of fault planes to the b-value as D = 3b/c with c = 1.5, which gives D = 2b (b = D/2). Turcotte (1986) wrote it as b = D/2, and Turcotte's book (pp. 178-179) writes N ∝ r^(-2b) = A^(-b) for rupture length r = sqrt(A). The evidence is mixed. Hirata (1989, JGR 94(B6):7507-7514) found a NEGATIVE correlation, D = 2.3 - 0.73b, using the epicentral correlation dimension (a different D from Aki's capacity dimension). Chen et al. (2006, Chi-Chi) and Wu et al. (2017, Wenchuan) found positive D ≈ 2b for single aftershock sequences.
findings.citation: Aki, K. (1981) A probabilistic synthesis of precursory phenomena. In: Earthquake Prediction: An International Review, Maurice Ewing Ser. 4, AGU, pp. 566-574; Turcotte, D.L. (1986) Tectonophysics; Turcotte (1997) Fractals and Chaos in Geology and Geophysics, 2nd ed.; Hirata, T. (1989) JGR 94(B6), 7507-7514
findings.relevance: b = 1 corresponds to D = 2, a space-filling planar rupture set, which is exactly zeta_A = 1. This is the closest geophysical precedent for 'O_log in rupture area as a geometric property'. The b-D link is empirically contested, so it cannot by itself serve as an established law. Verified via secondary summaries; Aki's derivation of c = 1.5 not seen in primary text.

findings.claim: Kanamori & Anderson (1975) found log S vs log M0 'remarkably linear (slope ~2/3)', which implies constant stress drop (~30 bar interplate, ~100 bar intraplate, ~60 bar average). They found M_S ~ (2/3) log M0 ~ 2 log L except for very large events, where it saturates. They state that 'a simple geometrical argument explains the magnitude-frequency relation log N ~ -M_S'.
findings.citation: Kanamori, H. & Anderson, D.L. (1975) Theoretical basis of some empirical relations in seismology. Bull. Seismol. Soc. Am. 65(5), 1073-1095
findings.formula_or_number: M0 = C·Δσ·S^(3/2); log S ∝ (2/3) log M0; log N ~ -M_S
findings.relevance: Primary source of M0 ∝ A^(3/2). The abstract-level claim that b = 1 follows from a 'simple geometrical argument' is prior art for O_log in rupture area (equal total rupture area per magnitude class). I could NOT verify the exact content of that argument (e.g. 'faults of each size class fill the same area'); check the full text before citing it as such.

findings.claim: The scatter around self-similar scaling is large but roughly size-independent for moderate events. Allmann & Shearer (2009): about 2,000 events with mb ≥ 5.5 (1990-2007); single-event stress drops span ~0.3-50 MPa; median ~4 MPa, independent of moment over Mw 5.2-8.3. Strike-slip events have 3-5× higher stress drops than other mechanisms, and intraplate events ~2× higher than interplate. Wells & Coppersmith (1994): M = 4.07 + 0.98 log A (A in km²; all slip types), with SD 0.25-0.35 magnitude units.
findings.citation: Allmann, B.P. & Shearer, P.M. (2009) Global variations of stress drop for moderate to large earthquakes. JGR 114, B01310, doi:10.1029/2008JB005821; Wells, D.L. & Coppersmith, K.J. (1994) BSSA 84(4), 974-1002
findings.relevance: Supports zeta_A ≈ b for moderate events: independent multiplicative (lognormal) scatter in M0|A leaves the power-law tail exponent unchanged. Mechanism-dependent stress drop mixes populations, though, so per-mechanism b and zeta_A can differ by roughly the stress-drop offset.

findings.claim: Self-similarity breaks down for large continental (strike-slip) earthquakes. Hanks & Bakun (2002) give a bilinear fit: M = log A + 3.98 for A ≤ 537 km², and M = (4/3) log A + 3.07 above that (L-model, slip ∝ length, width saturated by seismogenic thickness). The fit was revalidated in 2008 with 7 new M > 7 events. Whether this reflects width saturation or slip extending below the seismogenic layer is still debated.
findings.citation: Hanks, T.C. & Bakun, W.H. (2002) A bilinear source-scaling model for M-log A observations of continental earthquakes. BSSA 92(5), 1841-1846; Hanks & Bakun (2008) BSSA 98(1), 490-494
findings.relevance: This is a quantitative, measurable constraint (finite seismogenic thickness) that predicts a deviation from zeta_A = 1. The prediction is falsifiable: zeta_A should rise from ≈ b to ≈ 4b/3 at a measurable area. It is the kind of 'constraint → calculable deviation' the paper needs. Testable directly on finite-fault rupture-area catalogs rather than inferred from b.

findings.claim: Kagan (2002), Harvard CMT catalogue: the moment-frequency exponent β looks universal (β = 0.60-0.65) for moderate earthquakes. The corner moment is ~10^21 N·m (m_c ≈ 8.0) globally and in subduction zones, and ~5.8 at spreading ridges. An upper bound (corner moment) is required for finite moment flux. Bird & Kagan (2004): best-fit β ranges 0.53-0.92 across 7 tectonic settings, but all 95% CIs are consistent with a common β = 0.61-0.66.
findings.citation: Kagan, Y.Y. (2002) Seismic moment distribution revisited: I. Statistical results. Geophys. J. Int. 148(3), 520-541; Kagan (2002) II. Moment conservation principle. GJI 149(3), 731-754; Bird, P. & Kagan, Y.Y. (2004) BSSA 94(6), 2380-2399, doi:10.1785/0120030107
findings.relevance: Seismic moment is the quantity with an actual budget (tectonic moment rate, via Kagan's 'moment conservation principle'). Its zeta ≈ 0.63 is strongly TOP-HEAVY, not 1: total moment is dominated by the largest events and is finite only because of the corner moment. This contradicts 'zeta = 1 in the conserved extensive resource' for earthquakes. zeta ≈ 1 holds only for rupture AREA, which is not conserved. The repo's b = 0.998 [0.973, 1.024] gives zeta_M0 = 0.665, consistent.

findings.claim: Kagan (2010) argues that the Gutenberg-Richter law follows mathematically from the critical branching nature of earthquake occurrence, with theoretical β = 1/2. After correcting for magnitude errors and aftershock handling, he suggests the empirical β ≈ 0.63 could fall to ~0.52-0.56.
findings.citation: Kagan, Y.Y. (2010) Earthquake size distribution: power-law with exponent β = 1/2? Tectonophysics 490(1-2), 103-114, doi:10.1016/j.tecto.2010.04.034
findings.relevance: A leading statistical-physics theory of earthquake size (branching/mean-field) predicts zeta_A = 3/4, not 1. Mean-field depinning models (Fisher et al. 1997 PRL 78:4885) are commonly quoted with τ = 3/2 for moment, which also gives β = 1/2 (the τ value is from memory, not verified here). b ≈ 1 is therefore not the first-principles value in these theories.

findings.claim: Schorlemmer, Wiemer & Wyss (2005) report that b depends on faulting style: normal events highest, thrust lowest, strike-slip intermediate. They interpret b as a stress meter, inversely dependent on differential stress, and argue against b ≈ 1 being universal. The specific values (~1.1 / ~1.0 / ~0.7) could NOT be verified from accessible text. Gulia & Wiemer (2010, GRL), Italy: reverse 0.75-0.81, strike-slip 0.90-0.92, normal 1.09.
findings.citation: Schorlemmer, D., Wiemer, S. & Wyss, M. (2005) Nature 437, 539-542, doi:10.1038/nature04094; Gulia, L. & Wiemer, S. (2010) GRL 37, L10305
findings.relevance: Shows zeta_A varies systematically, roughly 0.75-1.1, with a measurable state variable. That fits 'deviations from constraints', but b ≈ 1 sits in the middle of a continuum rather than at an unconstrained endpoint. The numbers attributed in the task (1.1 / 1.0 / 0.7) remain unverified.

findings.claim: Scholz (2015) combined a frictional-strength model of lithospheric stress with b-values by depth across many tectonic regions and calibrated b = 1.23 ± 0.06 - (0.0012 ± 0.0003)(σ1 - σ3), with stress in MPa. In subduction zones, b correlates linearly with slab pull and with the net reduction of interface normal force. The relation is an empirical calibration motivated by lab acoustic-emission results (Scholz 1968), not a first-principles derivation.
findings.citation: Scholz, C.H. (2015) On the stress dependence of the earthquake b value. Geophys. Res. Lett. 42(5), 1399-1402, doi:10.1002/2014GL062863
findings.formula_or_number: b = 1.23 - 0.0012·Δσ[MPa]; b = 1 at Δσ ≈ 190 MPa; zero-stress limit b ≈ 1.23
findings.relevance: This is the best available 'constraint → deviation' law for earthquakes. In it, b = 1 (zeta_A = 1) is NOT a privileged or unconstrained state: the low-stress limit is ~1.23 and b = 1 is just one point on a continuum. That undermines 'zeta = 1 is natural, constraints cause deviations', though it supports 'zeta is predictable from measurable stress'. No accepted theory predicts the slope 0.0012/MPa from first principles.

findings.claim: Varotsos, Sarlis, Skordas & Tanaka (2004) claim a first-principles explanation of why b sits near 1 and varies little between regions, using natural-time analysis and a maximum-entropy principle with no tuned parameters. They cite the equivalence N(>A) ∝ A^(-D/2), b = D/2.
findings.citation: Varotsos, P.A., Sarlis, N.V., Skordas, E.S. & Tanaka, H.K. (2004) A plausible explanation of the b-value in the Gutenberg-Richter law from first principles. Proc. Japan Acad. Ser. B 80, 429-434
findings.relevance: This is a prior maximum-entropy-style derivation of b ≈ 1 (zeta_A ≈ 1), directly relevant to the working hypothesis that O_log is a max-entropy state. It must be cited and contrasted. Its derivation and reception were not checked here (abstract-level only).

findings.claim: Zou & Fialko (2024): fault maps spanning lab-sample to tectonic scales give a cumulative fault-length distribution with exponent close to -2. They state this matches b = 1, at least for faults shorter than the seismogenic thickness, and conclude faulting is self-similar. Scholz published a comment disputing the method (area normalization); Zou & Fialko's 2025 reply maintains ~2. Pan et al. (2026 preprint) report 2D outcrop trace exponents of 1.5-3.0, peaking near 2.0.
findings.citation: Zou, X. & Fialko, Y. (2024) Can large strains be accommodated by small faults: 'Brittle flow of rocks' revised. Earth and Space Science, doi:10.1029/2024EA003824; Pan, W., Zhang, Z., Lund, B. & Lei, Q. (2026) arXiv:2603.06892
findings.formula_or_number: N(>L) ∝ L^(-2) => N(>A) ∝ A^(-1) for A ∝ L², i.e. zeta_A(fault area) ≈ 1
findings.relevance: This is independent geometric (non-catalog) evidence for zeta ≈ 1 in fault AREA, the same resource for which the repo's earthquake O_log holds. It is valid below the seismogenic-thickness cutoff, a measurable constraint. The method is disputed, and 2D trace exponents scatter widely (1.5-3).

findings.claim: Hudson's (1991) criterion: for dN/dE ∝ E^(-α), α < 2 means large flares dominate total energy, and α > 2 is needed for small events (nanoflares) to dominate coronal heating. Hudson noted observed α ~ 1.8 against total energy, too shallow for microflare heating. Critics (e.g. Feldman et al. 1997) argue that the peak-flux-to-energy conversions assumed to map exponents one-to-one are flawed.
findings.citation: Hudson, H.S. (1991) Solar flares, microflares, nanoflares, and coronal heating. Solar Physics 133, 357-369, doi:10.1007/BF00149894
findings.relevance: The α = 2 / zeta = 1 marginal case in energy (O_log in energy) has been standard in solar physics for 35 years. The orthopolity paper must present it as an instance of a known criterion, not a new one. Verified via citing papers; Hudson's primary text not read.

findings.claim: GOES soft X-ray exponents. Veronig et al. (2002), ~50,000 flares 1976-2000: peak flux α = 2.11 ± 0.13, fluence α = 2.03 ± 0.09, duration α = 2.93 ± 0.12, with no notable cycle dependence of slope. Yashiro et al. (2006) reanalysis: peak 2.16 ± 0.03, fluence 2.01 ± 0.03. Aschwanden & Freeland (2012), >300,000 events 1975-2011: background-subtracted peak flux α_F = 1.98 ± 0.11, constant over 3 cycles. Earlier: Drake (1971) peak 1.75, fluence 1.44; Lee et al. (1995) peak 1.86.
findings.citation: Veronig, A., Temmer, M., Hanslmeier, A., Otruba, W. & Messerotti, M. (2002) A&A 382, 1070-1080, doi:10.1051/0004-6361:20011694; Aschwanden, M.J. & Freeland, S.L. (2012) ApJ 754, 112 (arXiv:1205.6712); Yashiro et al. (2006) ApJ 650, L143 (arXiv:astro-ph/0609197)
findings.relevance: Independently corroborates the repo's GOES end-fluence result (α ≈ 2.00-2.22). Caveats: SXR 1-8 Å fluence is a temperature-weighted radiated fraction, not total flare energy; and exponents depend on background subtraction and fitting range (Drake's 1.44 vs Veronig's 2.03).

findings.claim: Flare ENERGY exponents are mostly below 2. Nonthermal electron energies: α_E = 1.53 ± 0.02 (Crosby et al. 1993, as quoted by Aschwanden). AIA thermal energies, 155 flares: α = 1.66 ± 0.13. Global Energetics II, 391 flares: thermal energy 1.8 ± 0.2, length 3.3 ± 0.3, volume 1.7 ± 0.2. Global Energetics I, 172 M/X flares: dissipated magnetic energy 2.0 ± 0.2. Refined magnetic modelling (Paper IX): 1.6-1.8. Kepler superflares: ~1.5-1.8.

(2015) ApJ 802, 53 (GE II, arXiv:1502.05941); Aschwanden et al. (2013) arXiv:1308.5198; Aschwanden et al. (2019) GE IX arXiv:1909.08672; Shibayama et al. (2013) ApJS 209, 5
findings.relevance: In the physically conserved resource (energy), flares are mostly top-heavy (zeta_E < 1). This is the long-standing nanoflare-heating problem. The near-2 value holds for an observational proxy (SXR fluence), not energy. Using α_L = 3.3, the resource that is log-flat scales as L^2.3 (area-like), as for earthquakes. Journal volume/page details for GE I/II and Shibayama are partly from memory.

findings.claim: Aschwanden's 'scale-free probability conjecture', exact statement: the probability density of avalanche size L in a SOC system of Euclidean dimension d is N(L) dL ∝ L^(-d) dL for L ≤ L_max. It is justified by treating the number density as 'reciprocal to the volume V = L^d of avalanches with size L', by analogy to dice enumeration / maximum likelihood when breaking up a finite volume. With A ∝ L² and V ∝ L^d, α_A = (1+d)/2 (= 2 for d = 3) and α_V = 2 - 1/d (= 5/3 for d = 3).
findings.citation: Aschwanden, M.J. (2012) A statistical fractal-diffusive avalanche model of a slowly-driven self-organized criticality system. A&A 539, A2 (arXiv:1112.4859); Aschwanden, M.J. (2014) A macroscopic description of a generalized self-organized criticality system: astrophysical applications. ApJ 782, 54 (arXiv:1310.4191); Aschwanden et al. (2016) 25 Years of Self-Organized Criticality: Solar and Astrophysics. Space Sci. Rev. 198, 47-166, doi:10.1007/s11214-014-0054-6
findings.relevance: This is the closest existing cross-domain 'law' to orthopolity and must be engaged directly. The variable is linear size L with d the embedding Euclidean dimension. The A&A volume/article number (539, A2) was not confirmed in search results.

findings.claim: Algebra (my derivation, using the repo's definitions; not from a source). For resource q ∝ L^d, O_lin = q·dN/dL = L^d·L^(-d) = const, so Aschwanden's conjecture is exactly LINEAR orthopolity in Euclidean volume. Under the log measure, O_log(V) = L^d·L·L^(-d) = L, so volume per log-L interval grows ∝ L: top-heavy, zeta_V = (d-1)/d = 2/3. O_log is flat for q ∝ L^(d-1) (area in 3D): zeta_A = 1, α_A = 2. In general, any density dN/dL ∝ L^(-α_L) is log-orthopolic for q ∝ L^(α_L - 1) and linear-orthopolic for q ∝ L^(α_L). The alternative 'per-logarithmic-scale' reading of Aschwanden's box-counting heuristic (dN/dlnL ∝ L^(-d)) would give O_log in volume: α_L = d+1 = 4, zeta_V = 1, α_V = 2, b = 1.5 for earthquakes.
findings.citation: Derived from Aschwanden (2014) ApJ 782, 54 and docs/concept.md §2 of the repo
findings.formula_or_number: Aschwanden = O_lin(V) ≡ O_log(L^(d-1)); zeta_V = (d-1)/d; d* (log-flat resource dimension) = α_L - 1
findings.relevance: Shows that 'orthopolity holds for some resource' is vacuous for any power law: content exists only if the resource is fixed in advance on physical grounds. The data discriminate between the two readings. Earthquakes (b ≈ 1, β ≈ 0.63) and flares (α_L ≈ 3.3, α_V ≈ 1.7, α_E ≈ 1.66-1.8) match Aschwanden's linear-in-volume reading (zeta_V ≈ 2/3) and reject O_log in volume/energy/moment (which needs b = 1.5, α_E = 2). The algebra is exact; 'verified' is false only because it is my derivation.

findings.claim: How the conjecture was tested, and how its predictions moved. In 2012, cellular automata in 1-3D matched the predicted fractal dimensions and distributions within ~10%, and predicted α_E ranged 1.40-1.67. In 2014 it correctly predicted size distributions for 8 of 12 astrophysical phenomena. Aschwanden & Scholkmann (2025): 25 phenomena and 64 size distributions, 80% 'nearly consistent' with α_s = 1.99 ± 0.30; solar flares, earthquakes and forest fires called consistent, others inconclusive. The FD-SOC predictions shifted from flux α_F = 2.0 (2012) to α_F = 9/5 and α_E = 5/3 (2024). The 2012 model also uses an assumed mean fractal dimension D_S ≈ (1+S)/2, while later reviews use D_V = d - 1/2.
findings.citation: Aschwanden (2012) arXiv:1112.4859; Aschwanden (2014) ApJ 782, 54; Aschwanden, M.J. (2024/2025) Universal constants and energy integral in SOC systems, arXiv:2412.03481; Aschwanden, M.J. & Scholkmann, F. (2025) Power laws associated with SOC: a comparison of empirical data with model predictions, arXiv:2505.00748
findings.formula_or_number: α_s = 1.99 ± 0.30 over 64 distributions; FD-SOC (2024): α_F = 9/5, α_E = 5/3, α_T = 2
findings.relevance: Prior art making a cross-domain 'slopes near 2' claim. Its weaknesses are the ones a stronger orthopolity paper must avoid: a tolerance (±0.30) wider than the gaps between competing predictions, post-hoc explanations for misfits, and predictions that changed over time. Also, α_s ≈ 2 is pooled across DIFFERENT variable types (flux, duration, area), so it does not support zeta = 1 in a single declared resource.

findings.claim: Criticisms of FD-SOC and the conjecture. The argument is statistical, not dynamical: the authors concede the model does not explicitly enforce the balance between energy input and avalanche output (unlike conservative cellular automata). Exponents depend on assumed fractal-dimension averaging and on classical diffusion (β = 1). Broader SOC critiques: Watkins et al. (2016) note SOC usage in solar physics has drifted from the original definition; Frigg (2003) argues SOC's universality claims cannot be maintained. No published comment specifically refuting the scale-free probability conjecture was found.
findings.citation: Watkins, N.W., Pruessner, G., Chapman, S.C., Crosby, N.B. & Jensen, H.J. (2016) 25 Years of Self-Organized Criticality: Concepts and Controversies. Space Sci. Rev. 198, 3-44 (arXiv:1504.04991); Frigg, R. (2003) Self-organised criticality—what it is and what it isn't. Stud. Hist. Phil. Sci. 34, 613-632
findings.relevance: If orthopolity is framed via a geometric counting argument like Aschwanden's, it inherits the same objection: counting conjectures do not fix the measure (per dL vs per dlnL), and that choice decides zeta. Bibliographic details for Watkins (pages) and Frigg (volume/pages) are partly from memory.

findings.claim: Dohnanyi (1969): a steady-state collisional cascade gives a power-law mass distribution with exponent ≈ 1.837 (for 5 km/s rms speed), usually quoted as 11/6, i.e. dN/dD ∝ D^(-3.5) in diameter. The exponent is insensitive to the fragment size distribution and to collision physics, provided strength is size-independent. Tanaka, Inaba & Nakazawa (1996) generalized this to any self-similar collision cascade.
findings.citation: Dohnanyi, J.S. (1969) Collisional model of asteroids and their debris. JGR 74(10), 2531-2554; Tanaka, H., Inaba, S. & Nakazawa, K. (1996) Steady-state size distribution for the self-similar collision cascade. Icarus 123, 450-455
findings.formula_or_number: dN/dm ∝ m^(-11/6) => zeta_m = 5/6; mass per log m ∝ m^(1/6)
findings.relevance: This is a first-principles, resource-conserving cascade (constant MASS FLUX through scales) whose standing-stock exponent is zeta_m = 5/6, not 1. Conservation plus scale invariance therefore does not select zeta = 1: the exponent is set by the kinetics (collision rate ∝ cross-section ∝ m^(2/3)). It cleanly separates 'constant flux' from 'constant stock per log scale'. The Tanaka et al. Icarus volume/pages are from memory, not verified.

findings.claim: O'Brien & Greenberg (2003): with dispersal threshold Q_D* ∝ D^s, the steady-state cumulative diameter slope is b_p = 5/(2 + s/3), and the differential index is p = (7 + s/3)/(2 + s/3). Strength and gravity regimes produce separate slopes and a 'wavy' distribution near the transition. Benz & Asphaug (1999), basalt at 5 km/s, give s ≈ -0.36 to -0.45 (strength regime) and +1.19 to +1.36 (gravity regime), depending on fit.
findings.citation: O'Brien, D.P. & Greenberg, R. (2003) Steady-state size distributions for collisional populations: analytical solution with size-dependent strength. Icarus 164(2), 334-345 (arXiv:1407.3307); Benz, W. & Asphaug, E. (1999) Catastrophic disruptions revisited. Icarus 142, 5-20
findings.formula_or_number: zeta_m = b_p/3 = 5/(6+s); s = -0.4 => zeta_m ≈ 0.89; s = +1.3 => zeta_m ≈ 0.68; zeta_m = 1 requires s = -1
findings.relevance: This is the best example of a measurable constraint (material strength scaling, measured in the lab or by SPH) quantitatively predicting zeta. But it predicts zeta ≠ 1 in both regimes. zeta = 1 would need the special value s = -1, so zeta = 1 is not the attractor of this physics. The zeta_m = 5/(6+s) conversion is my algebra from the verified b_p formula.

findings.claim: Cael & Seekell (2016), as corrected by the 2017 corrigendum (a subset of the census had been used): lake areas ≥ 0.46 km² are power-law distributed with tail exponent τ = 2.14 (originally reported as 1.97 above 8.5 km²) and shoreline fractal dimension 1.4. These are compared with percolation-theory predictions of 2.05 (= 187/91) and 4/3. Lakes < 0.46 km² are not power-law. Cael, Biggs & Seekell (2022): the lower limit of power-law behavior is highly variable (0.001-1 km²).
findings.citation: Cael, B.B. & Seekell, D.A. (2016) The size-distribution of Earth's lakes. Sci. Rep. 6, 29633, doi:10.1038/srep29633; Corrigendum (2017) Sci. Rep. 7, 42039; Cael, B.B., Biggs, J. & Seekell, D.A. (2022) Front. Environ. Sci. 10, 888735
findings.relevance: A first-principles (critical percolation) theory predicts zeta_A close to, but distinct from, 1 (slightly bottom-heavy); the observed value 1.14 lies further from 1. Do not cite the uncorrected 1.97 / 8.5 km² values. The 2017 corrigendum article number is from memory.

findings.claim: Downing et al. (2006) used a Pareto model to estimate ~304 million natural lakes covering 4.2 million km², with most area in water bodies < 1 km². I could not verify the fitted Pareto exponent (often recalled as c ≈ 1). McDonald et al. (2012) argue that extrapolating the Pareto law to small sizes overestimates small-lake numbers. Winslow et al. (USGS, 2014/2015) give the Pareto slopes at which total perimeter, area and volume would be evenly distributed across lake size classes: 0.63, 1, and 1.12.
findings.citation: Downing, J.A. et al. (2006) Limnol. Oceanogr. 51(5), 2388-2397, doi:10.4319/lo.2006.51.5.2388; McDonald, C.P. et al. (2012) Limnol. Oceanogr. 57(2), 597-606; Winslow, L.A. et al. Does lake size matter? Combining morphology and process modeling to examine the contribution of lake classes to population-scale processes (USGS pub 70136277)
findings.formula_or_number: equal-share Pareto thresholds: perimeter 0.63, area 1, volume 1.12
findings.relevance: Winslow et al. explicitly frame 'evenly distributed across size classes' thresholds for several extensive resources: the O_log idea, with resource-dependent thresholds, already exists in limnology. The Downing c = 1 value, and the McDonald and Winslow journal details, are unverified.

findings.claim: Wildfires. Malamud, Morein & Turcotte (1998): burned areas in US and Australian records (including paleo-fire) follow power-law frequency-area statistics with exponent ~1.3-1.5 (frequency-density convention, inferred). Malamud, Millington & Perry (2005), 88,916 USFS fires 1970-2000 across 18 ecoregions: exponents ~1.3-1.75, with a systematic east-west change; Zinck et al. (2011) quote -1.9 to -1.3. Hantson et al. (2016), satellite data: only 2 regions are compatible with truncated power laws (β = 1.0, 1.3); several are lognormal. Drossel-Schwabl model: τ ≈ 1.19 (Hergarten & Krenn 2011).
findings.citation: Malamud, B.D., Morein, G. & Turcotte, D.L. (1998) Science 281, 1840-1842, doi:10.1126/science.281.5384.1840; Malamud, B.D., Millington, J.D.A. & Perry, G.L.W. (2005) PNAS 102(13), 4694-4699; Hantson, S., Pueyo, S. & Chuvieco, E. (2016) Global Ecol. Biogeogr.; Corral, Á. & González, Á. (2019) Earth Space Sci. 6(5), 673-697; Hergarten, S. & Krenn, R. (2011) Nonlin. Processes Geophys. 18, 381
findings.formula_or_number: density α_A ≈ 1.3-1.9 => zeta_A ≈ 0.3-0.9 (strongly top-heavy); DS model zeta ≈ 0.19
findings.relevance: Burned area, a geometric extensive resource, is far from zeta = 1 and dominated by the largest fires. Exponents vary regionally (ignition source, landscape), and the power-law form itself is contested. No first-principles theory predicts the observed values (the DS model mismatches). This is a clear counterexample to generality. The exponent convention (density vs cumulative) is inferred, not confirmed from the 1998 text.

findings.claim: Landslides. Malamud et al. (2004): landslide areas from three events (Italy, Guatemala, USA) with different triggers fit one three-parameter inverse-gamma distribution: power-law tail with exponent 2.40 for medium and large areas, rollover at small areas. Brunetti et al. (2009), 19 volume datasets: density exponents 1.0-1.9, mean ≈ 1.3; rockfalls 1.1-1.4, slides 1.5-1.9. Larsen et al. (2010): V ∝ A^γ with γ = 1.1-1.3 (soil) and 1.3-1.6 (bedrock).
findings.citation: Malamud, B.D., Turcotte, D.L., Guzzetti, F. & Reichenbach, P. (2004) Earth Surf. Process. Landforms 29(6), 687-711, doi:10.1002/esp.1064; Brunetti, M.T., Guzzetti, F. & Rossi, M. (2009) Nonlin. Processes Geophys. 16, 179-188, doi:10.5194/npg-16-179-2009; Larsen, I.J., Montgomery, D.R. & Korup, O. (2010) Nature Geosci. 3, 247-251, doi:10.1038/ngeo776
findings.formula_or_number: zeta_A = 1.40 (bottom-heavy tail); zeta_V ≈ 0.0-0.9 (mean ≈ 0.3); implied from area: zeta_V = 1.4/γ ≈ 0.88-1.27
findings.relevance: Area and volume give mutually inconsistent zetas (mixed landslide types). Neither sits at 1 robustly, and area is bottom-heavy above the rollover. Jeandet et al. (2019, GRL 46:4258) model the distribution from Mohr-Coulomb strength (cohesion 10-35 kPa, friction 20-45°) and hillslope geometry. This is a constraint-based theory, but I found no closed-form exponent prediction.

findings.claim: Stellar IMF. Salpeter (1955): dN/dm ∝ m^(-2.35) (Γ = 1.35 per log mass). Kroupa (2001): α = 0.3 (0.01-0.08 M_sun), 1.3 ± 0.5 (0.08-0.5), 2.3 ± 0.3 (> 0.5). Turbulent fragmentation (Padoan & Nordlund 2002): dN/dlogM ∝ M^(-3/(4-β)), with β the velocity power-spectrum index; β = 1.74 gives 1.33. Bondi-Hoyle accretion (Zinnecker 1982, ṁ ∝ m²) gives dN/dm ∝ m^(-2) exactly. Bonnell et al. (2001): γ ≈ -3/2 in the gas-dominated regime, -2 to -2.5 in the stellar-dominated regime.
findings.citation: Salpeter, E.E. (1955) ApJ 121, 161-167; Kroupa, P. (2001) MNRAS 322, 231-246; Padoan, P. & Nordlund, Å. (2002) ApJ 576, 870-879; Zinnecker, H. (1982) Ann. N.Y. Acad. Sci. 395, 226; Bonnell, I.A., Clarke, C.J., Bate, M.R. & Pringle, J.E. (2001) MNRAS 324, 573
findings.formula_or_number: zeta_m: Salpeter 1.35; Kroupa 0.3 (0.08-0.5) and 1.3 (> 0.5); turbulent theory zeta = 3/(4-β) ≈ 1.33; Bondi-Hoyle zeta = 1
findings.relevance: Mass, a conserved extensive resource, is bottom-heavy above ~0.5 M_sun and top-heavy below. Stellar mass per log m therefore peaks near ~0.5 M_sun: there is a characteristic scale, not zeta = 1. A mechanism that predicts exactly zeta = 1 (Bondi-Hoyle accretion) exists but is NOT what the field IMF shows. The turbulent theory gives zeta from a measurable index, and zeta = 1 would need β = 1. Zinnecker's venue and the exact page ranges are from memory.

findings.claim: Galaxy stellar mass function (GAMA, z < 0.06, 5,210 galaxies): double Schechter with M* = 10^10.66 M_sun, α1 = -0.35, α2 = -1.47 (faint end). The later GAMA analysis (Wright et al. 2017, z < 0.1) gives faint-end α ≈ -1.50.
findings.citation: Baldry, I.K. et al. (2012) Galaxy And Mass Assembly (GAMA): the galaxy stellar mass function at z < 0.06. MNRAS 421, 621-634 (arXiv:1111.5707); Wright, A.H. et al. (2017) MNRAS 470, 283 (arXiv:1705.04074)
findings.formula_or_number: dN/dM ∝ M^(-1.47) at the faint end => zeta_M* ≈ 0.47-0.50
findings.relevance: Stellar mass in galaxies is strongly top-heavy, with the cosmic stellar mass density dominated near M*. It is much farther from zeta = 1 than the underlying dark-matter halos, because of feedback and reionization acting through the stellar-to-halo mass relation. That relation is a measurable constraint that converts the halo zeta (≈ 0.9) into the stellar zeta (≈ 0.5): if M* ∝ M_h^γ then zeta_* = zeta_h/γ (my algebra).

findings.claim: Press-Schechter halo mass function: for σ(M) ∝ M^(-(n+3)/6), the low-mass branch is dn/dM ∝ M^(-2 + (n+3)/6). Since the effective index n → -3 on small scales in CDM, the slope tends to -2. Simulations show PS over-predicts low-mass halos; Sheth-Tormen-type fits are flatter, with parameters that depend on n.
findings.citation: Press, W.H. & Schechter, P. (1974) ApJ 187, 425; Sheth, R.K. & Tormen, G. (1999) MNRAS 308, 119; review 'Is there a universal mass function?' (arXiv:0705.1599); Yahagi, Nagashima & Yoshii (2004) arXiv:astro-ph/0401097
findings.formula_or_number: zeta_M(halo) = 1 - (n_eff+3)/6 (PS); zeta → 1 as n_eff → -3; n_eff = -2.5 gives zeta ≈ 0.92
findings.relevance: This is the cleanest first-principles case where zeta = 1 in a conserved resource (mass in halos, with ∫M n dM = ρ̄ in PS) is the asymptotic limit, and the deviation is calculable from a measurable quantity (the local slope of the primordial power spectrum). Note that zeta = 1 here is tied to σ(M) being scale-independent (n = -3). It is a special scale-free initial condition, not a generic attractor, and simulations deviate from PS at low mass. The PS/ST bibliographic details are from memory.

findings.claim: Under the repo's power-cost mapping, earthquake moment-frequency follows b = 1.5β, so N(>M0) ∝ M0^(-2b/3). With M0 ∝ A^(3/2), N(>A) ∝ A^(-b) (zeta_A = b). With M0 ∝ L³, N(>L) ∝ L^(-2b), so for b = 1, dN/dL ∝ L^(-3), which is Aschwanden's d = 3 law. b = 1.5 is the equal-moment-per-magnitude-unit point (O_log in moment), analogous to Hudson's α = 2. Applied to the repo's USGS result (b = 0.998, CI 0.973-1.024; Mw ≥ 5.5, 2010-2024, n = 6,639): zeta_A ≈ 1.00 and zeta_M0 ≈ 0.665.
findings.citation: Repo results/results.json (usgs/cases); conversion standard (Kagan 2002; Kanamori & Anderson 1975)
findings.relevance: For earthquakes, O_log holds for area (a non-conserved geometric measure) and fails for moment (the budgeted quantity). The paper should state this asymmetry explicitly rather than calling earthquakes a confirmation of 'resource' orthopolity.

findings.claim: Synthesis across geophysical and astrophysical systems. Resource with zeta ≈ 1: earthquake rupture area (b ≈ 0.9-1.0), fault area (Zou & Fialko), GOES SXR fluence (2.03), lake area (1.14; theory 1.055), dark-matter halos (asymptotically). Resource clearly ≠ 1: seismic moment (≈ 0.63), flare energy (≈ 0.5-0.8), collisional-cascade mass (5/6, 0.68-0.9), wildfire area (0.3-0.9), landslide area (1.4) and volume (≈ 0.3), stellar IMF mass (1.35 / 0.3), galaxy stellar mass (0.47).
findings.citation: Compiled from the sources above
findings.relevance: zeta ≈ 1 recurs mainly for AREA-like (L²) measures of 3D-embedded, self-similar rupture/avalanche systems, where α_L ≈ 3. In the conserved, budgeted quantity (moment, energy, mass), zeta is usually < 1 and finite only because of an upper cutoff. Where first-principles theories exist, they reach zeta = 1 only at special parameter values (n_eff = -3, s = -1, β_turb = 1, Bondi-Hoyle ṁ ∝ m²). The tabulation is my synthesis.

res.novelty_assessment:
The idea that zeta = 1 (α = 2, equal resource per log-size class) is the marginal case between bottom-heavy and top-heavy has well-established precedents in several domains, so it is not new as a concept:
- Hudson's (1991) α = 2 nanoflare-heating criterion for flare energy.
- The b = 1.5 equal-moment point and b = 1 equal-rupture-area point in seismology. Kanamori & Anderson (1975) explicitly attribute log N ~ -M_S to 'a simple geometrical argument'. Aki (1981), King (1983) and Turcotte (1986) give b = D/2, with N(>A) ∝ A^(-D/2).
- Varotsos et al. (2004), a maximum-entropy/natural-time 'first-principles' account of b ≈ 1.
- Winslow et al.'s lake thresholds: Pareto slopes 0.63 / 1 / 1.12 for equal perimeter / area / volume per size class.
- Sheldon-type biomass spectra.
- The Press-Schechter M^-2 limit and Bondi-Hoyle m^-2 accretion.
- Most directly, Aschwanden's 'scale-free probability conjecture' (2012, 2014; Aschwanden & Scholkmann 2025). It already claims a cross-domain geometric law, N(L) dL ∝ L^-d dL, tested on 25 phenomena (80% of 64 distributions 'consistent' with α ≈ 1.99 ± 0.30). Algebraically it is LINEAR orthopolity in Euclidean volume, equivalently LOG orthopolity in L^(d-1) (area for d = 3).

An orthopolity paper is therefore at high risk of being read as a re-labelling of Aschwanden's conjecture, Hudson's criterion and Sheldon's spectrum, unless it adds two things:
- (a) a rule that fixes the resource and measure BEFORE looking at data;
- (b) quantitative, out-of-sample predictions of deviations from measured constraints.

Genuine novelty could come from:
- showing that the per-dL vs per-dlnL choice in counting arguments is exactly what decides zeta, and that the data discriminate between the two. For volume, energy and moment, the data favour Aschwanden's linear reading (zeta_V ≈ 2/3) and reject log-orthopolity;
- a unified 'deviation calculus' (zeta_A → 4b/3 above seismogenic width saturation; zeta_m = 5/(6+s) for collisional cascades; zeta = 1 - (n_eff+3)/6 for halos; zeta = 3/(4-β) for turbulent fragmentation; percolation 96/91 for lakes), tested on held-out systems.

As currently framed ('zeta = 1 in a conserved extensive resource is the natural law'), the claim is contradicted by the best-measured conserved quantities in this domain: seismic moment (zeta ≈ 0.63), flare energy (≈ 0.5-0.8), cascade mass (5/6), IMF mass (1.35 / 0.3) and galaxy stellar mass (≈ 0.5).

findings.claim: Hatton et al. (2021) reconstruct the global ocean spectrum. Biomass in most order-of-magnitude body-mass classes is close to 1 Gt wet weight; bacteria sit well above this level and large marine mammals well below it. The fitted exponent for abundance per decade bin in the upper ~200 m is -1.04 (95% CI -1.05 to -1.02), so biomass per log mass scales as m^-0.04 (the repo's -0.039 is a re-expression of this). Humans appear to have truncated the upper third of the spectrum; the authors' reference baseline is pre-1850.
findings.citation: Hatton, I.A., Heneghan, R.F., Bar-On, Y.M., Galbraith, E.D. (2021) The global ocean size spectrum from bacteria to whales. Science Advances 7(46): eabh3732. doi:10.1126/sciadv.abh3732
findings.formula_or_number: N per decade ∝ m^-1.04 [−1.05, −1.02]; biomass/log m ∝ m^-0.04; ~1 Gt per decade
findings.relevance: This is the strongest evidence for approximate O_log in biomass, over roughly 16+ decades. The small negative slope is systematic and the CI excludes 0.
