Both ends of the spectrum deviate (a bacterial excess at the bottom, a mammal deficit at the top). Any O_log paper must predict the −0.04 slope, not only the 0.

findings.claim: Andersen & Beyer (2006) derive the spectrum exponent from individual-level processes (encounter, consumption, metabolism) under a constant-satiation assumption. Number density scales as w^-2.05, independent of the predator/prey size ratio. The authors describe this as the first derivation of the exponent from individual-level processes alone.
findings.citation: Andersen, K.H., Beyer, J.E. (2006) Asymptotic size determines species abundance in the marine size spectrum. American Naturalist 168: 54–61. doi:10.1086/504849
findings.formula_or_number: N(w) ∝ w^-2.05 → biomass per log w ∝ w^-0.05
findings.relevance: This is a mechanistic prediction of both the near-flatness and the size of the deviation: −0.05 predicted versus −0.04 [−0.05, −0.02] observed by Hatton. Predicted density exponent 2.05; Hatton's CI is 2.02–2.05. An 'indifference' baseline of exactly 0 does worse than this existing theory unless the constraint terms are specified in advance.

findings.claim: In the Andersen-group framework the community spectrum scales as w^-λ with λ = 2 + q − n ≈ 2, where q is the search/clearance-volume exponent and n is the consumption/metabolic exponent. Expected biomass across maturation-size groups scales as m*^(n−q). Typical parameters are q = 0.8 (range 0.62–1, citing Andersen & Beyer 2006) and n = 0.75 (2/3–1). My reconstruction of the closure (not confirmed in the full text): predation mortality scales as w^(1+q−λ) and must match the growth-scaled mortality w^(n−1), which gives λ = 2 + q − n.
findings.citation: Hartvig, M., Andersen, K.H., Beyer, J.E. (2011) Food web framework for size-structured populations. Journal of Theoretical Biology 272: 113–122 (arXiv:1004.4138); parameter tables in Andersen-group papers
findings.formula_or_number: λ = 2 + q − n; biomass/log w ∝ w^(n−q); flat iff q = n; with q=0.8, n=0.75 → λ=2.05
findings.relevance: Flatness becomes a codimension-one condition, q = n: encounter rate and metabolic demand scale with the same exponent. That is a scale-invariance condition, not a conservation law. The deviation is predicted as n − q from independently measurable physiology. Only the formula was seen in search snippets; the closure derivation is my reconstruction.

findings.claim: Capitán & Delius (2010) derive a scale-invariant size-spectrum model (predation, reproduction, maintenance, intrinsic mortality) from a Markov process. The power-law exponent is 'fixed solely by the scaling properties of the parameters', meaning the relative scaling of density-dependent (predation) and density-independent rates. It does not depend on details such as the preferred PPMR. When only predation is modelled, there are not enough scaling relations to fix the steady-state exponent, and it depends on model details. Including maintenance and reproduction stabilizes the steady state.
findings.citation: Capitán, J.A., Delius, G.W. (2010) Scale-invariant model of marine population dynamics. Physical Review E 81: 061901 (arXiv:1003.4674)
findings.formula_or_number: exponent set by relative scaling of density-dependent vs density-independent rates
findings.relevance: This is direct evidence against the working hypothesis that resource (mass) conservation plus scale-free dynamics fixes ζ = 1 by itself. In predation-driven, mass-conserving models the exponent is not pinned by conservation; it needs extra scaling relations.

findings.claim: The jump-growth model has a power-law steady state consistent with the approximate constancy of mass density per logarithmic body-mass interval. The authors note that predation alone cannot have a nontrivial steady state, and that the power law must break down at very small and very large sizes. Simulations show two classes of attractors, steady states and travelling waves. The stability analysis finds the McKendrick–von Foerster steady state without diffusion unstable in all cases. Stability is favoured by a small preferred PPMR, broad diet and high feeding efficiency.
findings.citation: Datta, S., Delius, G.W., Law, R. (2010) A jump-growth model for predator–prey dynamics: derivation and application to marine ecosystems. Bulletin of Mathematical Biology 72: 1361–1382, doi:10.1007/s11538-009-9496-5; Datta, S., Delius, G.W., Law, R., Plank, M.J. (2011) A stability analysis of the power-law steady state of marine size spectra. Journal of Mathematical Biology 63: 779–799 (arXiv:1001.3826)
findings.formula_or_number: steady state φ ∝ w^-γ with γ≈2; stability requires small PPMR, broad diet, high efficiency
findings.relevance: Flat spectra are stationary states only in part of parameter space; elsewhere the dynamics are oscillatory (travelling waves). Calling O_log an attractor or natural law must confront these dynamical regimes, which these papers already characterize.

findings.claim: Benoît & Rochet (2004) build a continuous model in which predation is the only process governing energy flow. Linear (power-law) size spectra are stationary solutions. Realistic fishing should change spectrum curvature and stability rather than slope. The 2003 ICES version adds that the slope is insensitive to prey-size breadth, search volume and assimilation efficiency.
findings.citation: Benoît, E., Rochet, M.-J. (2004) A continuous model of biomass size spectra governed by predation and the effects of fishing on them. Journal of Theoretical Biology 226: 9–21
findings.formula_or_number: power-law spectra stationary; fishing → curvature, not slope
findings.relevance: This is prior art for a predation/energy-flux model with power-law stationary solutions. Its claim that the slope does not depend on search volume conflicts with λ = 2 + q − n, so the theories disagree on which parameters set the deviation. A new paper must pick a closure and justify it.

findings.claim: Platt & Denman (1977) give a steady-state energy-flow theory over geometric size classes. Total biomass per size class falls as b(w2)/b(w1) ≈ (w2/w1)^-0.22, using the weight-specific metabolic exponent of −0.22. With carbon units the normalized slope is about −1.22. A Dalhousie thesis reports offshore NBSS slopes of about −1.0 in biovolume and −1.1 in carbon, and links the carbon value to the Platt–Denman model.
findings.citation: Platt, T., Denman, K. (1977) Organisation in the pelagic ecosystem. Helgoländer wissenschaftliche Meeresuntersuchungen 30: 575–581, doi:10.1007/BF02207862; Platt & Denman (1978) Rapp. P.-v. Réun. Cons. int. Explor. Mer 173: 60–65 (latter not verified); Quiñones-Bergeret thesis (Dalhousie)
findings.relevance: This is the original 'energy cascade through size' theory from physical oceanographers. It predicts a deviation from flatness about 5× larger than Hatton observes. A physics-style cascade framing of orthopolity is therefore ~50 years old. The currency (biovolume vs carbon) shifts the slope by ~0.1–0.2.

findings.claim: Zhou & Huntley (1997) derive a mass-conservation (continuity) theory over body weight and growth rate. At steady state, the normalized biomass spectrum slope is set by the ratio of intrinsic rate of increase to weight-specific individual growth rate. Spectra can therefore be inverted to estimate growth.
findings.citation: Zhou, M., Huntley, M.E. (1997) Population dynamics theory of plankton based on biomass spectra. Marine Ecology Progress Series 159: 61–73. doi:10.3354/meps159061
findings.formula_or_number: NBSS slope = f(intrinsic rate of increase / weight-specific growth rate)
findings.relevance: In continuity-equation models the exponent is a mortality(loss)/growth ratio, not a conservation-fixed constant. This is the ecological analogue of the Gabaix exponent formula, and here it is not pinned at the marginal value. The steady state with g ∝ w^n and μ = μ0 w^(n−1) gives λ = n + μ0/a (my derivation, standard McKendrick–von Foerster result).

findings.claim: Trophic-transfer theory: if each trophic step multiplies body mass by PPMR (β) and energy flux by TE, and production/biomass scales as m^(n−1) with n ≈ 3/4, then the abundance-per-log-bin slope is −n + log TE/log β. The biomass-per-log-bin slope is s_B = (1−n) + log TE/log β ≈ 1/4 + log TE/log β. Mehner et al. state that the NBSS slope of multi-trophic communities is exactly −1.0 if TE = 10% and PPMR = 10^4. Woodson et al. are cited (via Schwamborn) as using β = 0.25 + log(TE)/log(PPMR).
findings.citation: Mehner, T. et al. (2018) Empirical correspondence between trophic transfer efficiency in freshwater food webs and the slope of their size spectra. Ecology 99(6): 1463–1472, doi:10.1002/ecy.2347; earlier formulations attributed to Borgmann (1987) CJFAS 44(Suppl 2): 136–140, Brown & Gillooly (2003) PNAS, Brown et al. (2004) Ecology 85: 1771–1789, Trebilco et al. (2013) TREE 28: 423–431 (exact equations in these not verified)
findings.formula_or_number: s_B = (1−n) + ln TE/ln PPMR; flat iff TE = PPMR^-(1−n) ≈ PPMR^-1/4 (e.g., TE 0.1, PPMR 10^4)
findings.relevance: This is exactly 'flat spectrum as baseline, deviations predicted by TE and PPMR', and it is textbook. Flatness is a special case (TE = PPMR^-1/4), not a default. The sensitivity is ∂s_B/∂log10 TE = 1/log10 PPMR (0.25–0.5 per decade of TE for PPMR 10^2–10^4). The 1/4 term and the attributions to Borgmann, Brown and Trebilco are not verified from full texts; Mehner's statement is.

findings.claim: Jennings & Mackinson (2003) formalized and tested the energy-availability model using PPMR from δ15N and transfer efficiency. For the central North Sea they predict abundance and biomass slopes of about −1.2 and −0.2 versus body mass, matching empirical estimates, and explain this by a small PPMR (~106:1). Energetic equivalence predicts −0.75 when organisms share one energy source. They predict steeper relationships in more stable environments, which favour low PPMR and long food chains. Consistency check (my arithmetic): log(0.125)/log(106) = −0.446, so the slopes are −0.75 − 0.446 ≈ −1.20 and −0.20.
findings.citation: Jennings, S., Mackinson, S. (2003) Abundance–body mass relationships in size-structured food webs. Ecology Letters 6: 971–974
findings.formula_or_number: predicted N ∝ M^-1.2, B ∝ M^-0.2 at PPMR≈106, TE≈0.125
findings.relevance: This is a quantitative, independently parameterized and successfully tested prediction of a deviation from flatness (biomass slope −0.2). It is the bar an orthopolity paper must meet. It also shows that a non-flat system can be fully explained without invoking a 'law' of flatness.

findings.claim: For the central North Sea, Jennings, Warr & Mackinson (2002) estimate transfer efficiencies of 3.7–12.4% and a mean predator:prey body-mass ratio of 109:1 from size-based production and δ15N. The estimates are sensitive to the assumed δ15N fractionation. Excluding fished large size classes raises the TE estimates (5.7% excluding >1024 g; 12.4% excluding >512 g, per a Cefas summary).
findings.citation: Jennings, S., Warr, K.J., Mackinson, S. (2002) Use of size-based production and stable isotope analyses to predict trophic transfer efficiencies and predator–prey body mass ratios in food webs. Marine Ecology Progress Series 240: 11–20
findings.relevance: Provides independent TE/PPMR inputs for a test. With PPMR ≈ 10^2, flatness would require TE ≈ 0.32, outside the measured range. The North Sea should be (and is) bottom-heavy.

findings.claim: Barnes et al. (2010) compile ~30,000 individual feeding records from 21 marine locations, with predators spanning 10 orders of magnitude in mass. PPMR increases with predator mass, implying a nonlinear relation between log mass and trophic level and decreasing transfer efficiency with size. The increase is not significantly affected by temperature, latitude, depth or primary production.
findings.citation: Barnes, C., Maxwell, D., Reuman, D.C., Jennings, S. (2010) Global patterns in predator–prey size relationships reveal size dependency of trophic transfer efficiency. Ecology 91(1): 222–232
findings.relevance: If PPMR and TE drift with size, s_B = 1/4 + log TE/log PPMR is size-dependent. This predicts curvature in log-log spectra rather than a single universal slope, and a clean O_log power law should not be expected over the whole range.

findings.claim: In four lake food webs (two shallow eutrophic lakes, each divided in half), trophic transfer efficiencies were 1.0–3.6%, well below 10%. The NBSS slopes were correspondingly steeper than −1 (−1.14 to −1.19), consistent with the TE-slope theory.
findings.citation: Mehner, T., Lischke, B., Scharnweber, K., Attermeyer, K., Brothers, S., Gaedke, U., Hilt, S., Brucet, S. (2018) Ecology 99(6): 1463–1472. doi:10.1002/ecy.2347
findings.relevance: This is a direct empirical test linking measured TE to the deviation from −1, in the direction trophic theory predicts. Flatness fails where TE is low. Check (my arithmetic): s_B ≈ −0.16 with TE ≈ 0.02 implies PPMR ≈ 10^4. The author list is from memory.

findings.claim: Atkinson et al. (2021) combine a 6-year weekly plankton time series (Plymouth L4) with a global meta-analysis. Normalized spectra are steeper than −1 (median −1.11), implying TE ≈ 3.5% or PPMR ≈ 569, much lower than commonly quoted values. Slope versus plankton biomass is dome-shaped, steepening under both increasingly oligotrophic and increasingly eutrophic conditions. Summer nutrient starvation reduces transfer efficiency and steepens slopes; storms produce steep slopes with recovery within months. They recommend carbon units and a >10^7 mass range.
findings.citation: Atkinson, A., et al. (2021) Increasing nutrient stress reduces the efficiency of energy transfer through planktonic size spectra. Limnology and Oceanography 66(2): 422–437. doi:10.1002/lno.11613
findings.formula_or_number: median NBSS −1.11 → TE 3.5% or PPMR 569; dome-shaped slope vs biomass
findings.relevance: The central tendency of plankton spectra in this meta-analysis is measurably steeper than O_log. Slope covaries non-monotonically with trophic state, so a single 'indifference' value with ad hoc constraints is weaker than an explicit TE model.

findings.claim: Atkinson et al. (2024) use in situ size spectra and a global compilation of pelagic slopes. Spectra steepen as phytoplankton biomass decreases, indicating strong trophic amplification: a 16% phytoplankton decline this century could translate into ~38% less fish biomass supported in the mid-latitude ocean. The amplification arises mainly from temperature/nutrient control of the phytoplankton baseline, not from direct thermal effects on consumers.
findings.citation: Atkinson, A., et al. (2024) Steeper size spectra with decreasing phytoplankton biomass indicate strong trophic amplification and future fish declines. Nature Communications 15: 381. doi:10.1038/s41467-023-44406-5
findings.relevance: Slope systematically covaries with productivity, so nature is not 'indifferent' to resource supply in this sense. Any orthopolity deviation model must predict this sign and magnitude from first principles.

findings.claim: Blanchard et al. (2009) split North Sea community data into predator and detritivore groups. Abundance-mass slopes for fish and epifaunal predators (−1.2 to −2.25) were significantly steeper than for infaunal detritivores (−0.56 to −0.87). A coupled size-spectrum model reproduces this: an unstructured, shared detrital resource yields shallower slopes, while size-structured predation yields steeper ones. Harvesting large predators steepens the predator spectrum.
findings.citation: Blanchard, J.L., Jennings, S., Law, R., Castle, M.D., McCloghrie, P., Rochet, M.-J., Benoît, E. (2009) How does abundance scale with body size in coupled size-structured food webs? Journal of Animal Ecology 78(1): 270–280. doi:10.1111/j.1365-2656.2008.01466.x
findings.relevance: These are large deviations in both directions within one ecosystem, set by feeding mode. If these are log-bin abundance slopes, ζ ranges from ~0.6 to ~2.3. O_log holds only for a particular aggregation (whole community) and not for its components, which weakens a 'general property of real systems' claim.

findings.claim: Cavender-Bares, Rinaldo & Chisholm (2001) measured microbial size spectra across the western North Atlantic and in enrichment experiments. Slopes ranged from −1.0 (biomass equal across classes) to −1.4 (more biomass in small classes), with no clear link between nutrient level and slope. Shapes were smooth and log-linear during the Sargasso Sea spring bloom but distinctly non-log-linear in coastal waters. In enriched bottles, succession turned smooth power laws into spectra with preferred sizes; IronEx II spectra stayed stable.
findings.citation: Cavender-Bares, K.K., Rinaldo, A., Chisholm, S.W. (2001) Microbial size spectra from natural and nutrient enriched ecosystems. Limnology and Oceanography 46(4): 778–789
findings.relevance: At the microbial end, O_log is the upper bound of observed slopes, not their centre, and power-law form itself breaks down under perturbation.

findings.claim: In freshwater streams, individual size distributions (individual-level power-law fits) have exponent λ ≈ −1.2: mean −1.2, sd 0.04, from 2.4 million body sizes; 133 ISDs from 22 NEON streams ranged −1.47 to −1.14, far shallower than the Sheldon value −2. The authors interpret this as a surplus of large individuals, requiring subsidies to large predators and/or metabolic scaling ~0.4. Pomeranz et al. (2022) found ISDs steepen with mean annual temperature (median about −1.2 to −1.3 across a 29 °C range). The published Ecology Letters version reports temperature effects that depend on resource supply (organic matter). A 2026 abstract warns that undersampling small individuals biases λ.
findings.citation: Gjoni, V., Pomeranz, J.P.F., Junker, J.R., Wesner, J.S. (2024) bioRxiv doi:10.1101/2024.01.09.574822; published as 'Temperature and resource supply drive continental variation in size structure of freshwater food webs', Ecology Letters, doi:10.1111/ele.70437; Pomeranz, J.P.F., Junker, J.R., Wesner, J.S. (2022) Global Change Biology 28, doi:10.1111/gcb.15862
findings.formula_or_number: ISD λ ≈ −1.2 (Sheldon = −2) → biomass/log m ∝ m^+0.8, ζ ≈ 0.2
findings.relevance: This is a large, statistically precise departure from O_log (top-heavy) in a whole class of ecosystems. Calling it a 'constraint' (allochthonous subsidies, open system) is defensible only if the deviation is predicted from measured subsidy flux, otherwise it is unfalsifiable. Caveats: truncated size domain, gear selectivity, and the preprint vs published versions differ.

findings.claim: Warming experiments disagree in direction. In freshwater mesocosms, ~4 °C warming steepened the community size spectrum, mainly by favouring small phytoplankton, and cut phytoplankton mean and maximum size by about an order of magnitude (Yvon-Durocher et al. 2011). Across 13 Icelandic streams spanning 5–25 °C, size structure changed opposite to the expected steepening, attributed to nutrient supply rising with temperature (O'Gorman et al. 2017).
findings.citation: Yvon-Durocher, G., Montoya, J.M., Trimmer, M., Woodward, G. (2011) Warming alters the size spectrum and shifts the distribution of biomass in freshwater ecosystems. Global Change Biology 17: 1681–1694; O'Gorman, E.J., et al. (2017) Unexpected changes in community size structure in a natural warming experiment. Nature Climate Change 7(9): 659–663
findings.relevance: Temperature effects on slope depend on context (nutrient covariation). Deviation predictions must include resource supply as well as temperature. GCB volume/pages for Yvon-Durocher are from memory.

findings.claim: Across Australian reefs, community-level predator–prey mass ratios were positively related to size-spectrum slopes, broadly consistent with theory. The pattern was also influenced by the latitudinal temperature gradient.
findings.citation: Coghlan, A.R., et al. (2022) Community size structure varies with predator–prey size relationships and temperature across Australian reefs. Ecology and Evolution 12: e8789
findings.relevance: This is empirical covariation of slope with PPMR in the direction s_B = 1/4 + log TE/log PPMR predicts. It supports the existing TE/PPMR deviation theory, not an independent orthopolity law. Article number is from memory.

findings.claim: Fishing removes large size classes and steepens spectra. In the North Sea, current biomass of 4–16 kg and 16–66 kg fish is estimated to be 97.4% and 99.2% below unexploited levels; total biomass of fish of 64 g–66 kg is 38% lower; turnover time falls from 3.5 to 1.9 years. On Fijian reefs, slopes steepened and heights declined with fishing intensity. Hatton et al. (2021) report truncation of the upper third of the ocean spectrum.
findings.citation: Jennings, S., Blanchard, J.L. (2004) Fish abundance with no fishing: predictions based on macroecological theory. Journal of Animal Ecology 73: 632–642, doi:10.1111/j.0021-8790.2004.00839.x; Graham, N.A.J., Dulvy, N.K., Jennings, S., Polunin, N.V.C. (2005) Size-spectra as indicators of the effects of fishing on coral reef fish assemblages. Coral Reefs 24: 118–124
findings.relevance: These are textbook 'externally imposed constraint' deviations, already quantified with size-spectrum theory used as an unexploited baseline. Orthopolity adds nothing here unless it changes the baseline prediction. Graham et al. journal details are from memory.

findings.claim: Hatton et al. (2015) find, across 2,260 communities (large mammals, invertebrates, plants, plankton), that predator biomass scales sublinearly with prey biomass, with exponents often near 3/4. Community production scales with biomass with a similar exponent. Perkins et al. (2022) find the same ~3/4 predator–prey biomass scaling within and across 141 complex food webs.
findings.citation: Hatton, I.A., McCann, K.S., Fryxell, J.M., Davies, T.J., Smerlak, M., Sinclair, A.R.E., Loreau, M. (2015) The predator–prey power law: biomass scaling across terrestrial and aquatic biomes. Science 349: aac6284, doi:10.1126/science.aac6284; Perkins, D.M., Hatton, I.A., Gauzens, B., et al. (2022) Nature Communications 13: 4990, doi:10.1038/s41467-022-32578-5
findings.relevance: This competing cross-system 'law' says pyramid shape is not invariant: the predator/prey ratio falls as B^-1/4. If trophic levels map to fixed mass ratios, then ∂s_B/∂log10 B_prey ≈ −0.25/log10 PPMR (my derivation), so richer systems should be more bottom-heavy. This conflicts with Atkinson 2024's steepening at low productivity, so neither simple rule is universal. Author list partly from memory; exponent and dataset size verified.

findings.claim: Trebilco et al. (2013) argue that biomass pyramids and size spectra carry the same information, so size-based and metabolic theory constrain pyramid shape. Bottom-heavy pyramids should be the norm; top-heavy ones indicate overestimated predator abundance or energy subsidies.
findings.citation: Trebilco, R., Baum, J.K., Salomon, A.K., Dulvy, N.K. (2013) Ecosystem ecology: size-based constraints on the pyramids of life. Trends in Ecology & Evolution 28(7): 423–431. doi:10.1016/j.tree.2013.03.008
findings.relevance: This already frames non-flat or inverted structures as constraint-driven deviations (subsidies) from a size-based baseline, the same logical structure as 'deviations imposed by constraints'.

findings.claim: Woodson et al. (2018) show that generalist predation and large animals feeding lower in the food web than their size predicts can shift ecosystems from a bottom-heavy pyramid to a top-heavy hourglass, especially in the ocean. Woodson et al. (2020) find intermediate food-web connectance yields inverted trophic structure more often than size-only theory predicts. They suggest observed bottom-heavy marine structure may partly reflect human removals.
findings.citation: Woodson, C.B., Schramski, J.R., Joye, S.B. (2018) A unifying theory for top-heavy ecosystem structure in the ocean. Nature Communications 9: 23, doi:10.1038/s41467-017-02450-y; Woodson, C.B., Schramski, J.R., Joye, S.B. (2020) Food web complexity weakens size-based constraints on the pyramids of life. Proceedings of the Royal Society B (data: doi:10.5061/dryad.xgxd254dx)
findings.relevance: This gives mechanistic routes to persistent ζ<1 in closed systems without external subsidies. It challenges reading O_log as a universal attractor and offers an alternative 'constraint' with its own quantitative model. The 2020 journal is inferred, not seen.

findings.claim: In METE (Harte 2011), the ecosystem structure function is R(n,ε) ∝ exp(−λ1 n − λ2 n ε) (form from memory). I computed Ψ(ε) = Σ n R(n,ε) numerically for S0 = 50, N0 = 5000, E0 = 5×10^5 (fitted λ1 ≈ 1.44×10^-3, λ2 ≈ 1.01×10^-4). The local log-slope of Ψ is −1.97 to −2.01 for ε ≈ 10^3–3×10^3, and within ±0.25 of −2 from ε ≈ 10^2 to 10^4. Below λ1/λ2 ≈ 14 it is shallower, and above 1/λ2 ≈ 10^4 an exponential cutoff takes over. So MaxEnt gives approximately equal total metabolic rate per log ε over a window bounded by the state variables.
findings.citation: Harte, J. (2011) Maximum Entropy and Ecology. Oxford University Press (ch. 7); Brummer, A.B., Newman, E.A. (2019) Derivations of the core functions of the Maximum Entropy Theory of Ecology. Entropy 21: 712, doi:10.3390/e21070712; own computation (scratchpad mete.py)
findings.formula_or_number: Ψ(ε) ∝ ε^-2 for λ1/λ2 ≪ ε ≪ 1/λ2; implies metabolic rate per log ε flat; with ε ∝ m^3/4, biomass per log m ∝ m^+1/4
findings.relevance: MaxEnt reproduces O_log only in the constrained currency (metabolic rate) and only over a finite window. Translated to biomass under ε ∝ m^3/4, it predicts energetic equivalence (abundance per log ∝ m^-3/4), not Sheldon flatness. MaxEnt therefore cannot make both biomass and energy flat; choosing the resource is not innocuous.

findings.claim: In a test of METE on 60 forest communities (>300,000 individuals, ~2,000 species), METE captured 96% of variation in the rank species-abundance distribution and 89% in the individual size/energy distribution. It failed badly on the size–density relationship (R² ≈ −2.24) and on intraspecific size distributions.
findings.citation: Xiao, X., McGlinn, D.J., White, E.P. (2015) A strong test of the maximum entropy theory of ecology. American Naturalist 185(3): E70–E80. doi:10.1086/679576
findings.formula_or_number: SAD R²≈0.96; ISD R²≈0.89; SDR R²≈−2.24
findings.relevance: A MaxEnt 'indifference' derivation can fit the aggregate distribution while failing the size–density (allocation) relation, which is precisely the orthopolity-relevant quantity. MaxEnt is not yet empirical support for O_log as a law.

findings.claim: Metzig & Colijn (2020) infer stationary size distributions by maximizing Gibbs–Shannon entropy for a preferential-attachment process with exit (constant system size). Given mean size and turnover rate, the method yields the power-law exponent and an exponential cutoff, so the exponent depends on those constraints and is not universal. A 2001 Ecological Modelling paper optimizing size distributions with Lagrange multipliers finds a flat biomass spectrum only for particular multiplier values (λ2 → 0 or large negative λ2), while positive λ2 gives biomass increasing with mass.
findings.citation: Metzig, C., Colijn, C. (2020) A maximum entropy method for the prediction of size distributions. Entropy 22(3): 312, doi:10.3390/e22030312; [authors not verified, possibly Han B.-P. & Straškraba M.] (2001) Size dependence of biomass spectra and abundance spectra: the optimal distributions. Ecological Modelling 145: 175–187
findings.formula_or_number: exponent = f(mean size, turnover); flat biomass only for specific multiplier
findings.relevance: 'O_log is the maximum-entropy state' is not generic. MaxEnt gives a family of exponents, and ζ = 1 needs a specific constraint (e.g., the Gabaix-like limit of vanishing turnover/entry). The orthopolity paper must name that constraint and justify it independently.

findings.claim: Camacho & Solé (2001), physicists, model a size spectrum in which every individual can prey on all smaller ones, with reproduction and natural mortality. Intrinsic dynamics produce a power-law size distribution with an exponent in agreement with field data, and predation is the main mechanism generating the exponent. The 1999 Santa Fe Institute working paper was titled 'Scaling and Zipf's Law in Ecological Size Spectra'.
findings.citation: Camacho, J., Solé, R.V. (2001) Scaling in ecological size spectra. Europhysics Letters 55(6): 774–780, doi:10.1209/epl/i2001-00347-0; Santa Fe Institute WP 99-12-076
findings.formula_or_number: power-law exponent from predation dynamics (value not retrieved)
findings.relevance: This is prior art for a physics-style, Zipf-law framing of the ecological size spectrum. A 'ζ = 1 in resource' reframing for ecology is not new terminology-free territory.

findings.claim: Rinaldo et al. (2002) develop a theory linking community planktonic size spectra to species-level size distributions. If the community spectrum is a power law (linked to self-organized criticality), a second power law follows relating each species' total abundance to its mean cell size. They test it on Atlantic microbial datasets.
findings.citation: Rinaldo, A., Maritan, A., Cavender-Bares, K.K., Chisholm, S.W. (2002) Cross-scale ecological dynamics and microbial size spectra in marine ecosystems. Proceedings of the Royal Society B 269: 2051–2059. doi:10.1098/rspb.2002.2102
findings.formula_or_number: community power law ⇒ species abundance–size power law
findings.relevance: This is statistical-physics prior art (criticality, cross-scale consistency) for the size spectrum. It also gives a derived, testable cross-scale prediction, the kind of output an orthopolity paper would need.

findings.claim: Cuesta, Delius & Law (2018) build a trait-based plankton model with growth from resource consumption and predation on smaller cells, death from predation, and flexible cell division. Coexistence is facilitated by allometric scaling of four physiological rates. Two of these allometries have empirical support; the other two emerge from predator–prey interactions exactly when abundances follow a Sheldon spectrum.
findings.citation: Cuesta, J.A., Delius, G.W., Law, R. (2018) Sheldon spectrum and the plankton paradox: two sides of the same coin — a trait-based plankton size-spectrum model. Journal of Mathematical Biology 76: 67–96. doi:10.1007/s00285-017-1132-7
findings.formula_or_number: Sheldon spectrum ⇔ self-consistent allometries enabling coexistence
findings.relevance: Here the Sheldon spectrum is a self-consistency condition of a mechanistic model, a stronger and more specific claim than an 'indifference' principle. It is closely related to any 'O_log as stationary state' claim.

findings.claim: Schwamborn's 2025 arXiv preprint (v4, Jan 2026; not peer reviewed) names a 'constant size spectra – variable trophic dynamics paradox': slopes near b = −1 in polar and tropical seas despite highly variable trophic pyramids and PPMR spanning orders of magnitude. It proposes a predator-prey-efficiency theory of size spectra (PETS) with an equilibrium constant c = E/log10(PPMR) fixed at −1, where E = d log10 B/d TL. Under Kleiber (R ∝ M^0.75) and Fenchel (g/M ∝ M^-0.25) scaling, b = c. Size-selective foraging is argued to hold the size spectrum steady while trophic-level biomass varies; stress and non-equilibrium effects produce deviations.
findings.citation: Schwamborn, R. (2025) Towards a compleat theory of ecosystem size spectra. arXiv:2509.00023 (v1 Aug 2025; v4 Jan 2026)
findings.formula_or_number: c = E / log10(PPMR) = −1; b = c under Kleiber/Fenchel scaling
findings.relevance: This is the closest current prior art to orthopolity: an invariant −1 slope as an equilibrium constant with stress-induced deviations, written from an aquatic-ecology perspective. Its derivation of c = −1 was not checked (snippets only). An orthopolity paper must cite it and differ from it explicitly.

findings.claim: Size-spectrum slopes depend on the currency and representation used. Offshore NBSS slopes are about −1.0 in biovolume units and −1.1 in carbon units. Abundance-based spectra are steeper than NBSS (one 2025 study: NBSS −1 to −0.8 vs abundance-vs-individual-biovolume −2 to −1.7). Schwamborn's 2026 preprint argues that NBSS plots often carry pseudo-abundance or 'biomass flux' units rather than biomass, and proposes back-transformed spectra.
findings.citation: Schwamborn, R. (2026) Is normalized biomass really abundance? arXiv:2602.01496; Quiñones-Bergeret, R. (Dalhousie University thesis); Atkinson et al. (2021) L&O 66: 422–437
findings.relevance: The departure from O_log at stake (~0.05–0.15 in slope) is the same size as currency and binning artifacts. A strong paper must fix the resource (carbon biomass vs biovolume vs energy) a priori and use individual-level MLE (e.g., Edwards et al. 2017) rather than binned NBSS.

findings.claim: Gaedke & Straile (1994) note that spectrum slope can indicate trophic transfer efficiency (high prey biomass relative to predators means low efficiency), crediting the method to Platt & Denman (1978) and Gaedke (1993). In Lake Constance, early-spring spectra are steep (slope −1.16, small-organism dominance, low transfer efficiency) and shift to about −0.94 by early summer.
findings.citation: Gaedke, U. (1993) Ecosystem analysis based on biomass size distributions: a case study of a plankton community in a large lake. Limnology and Oceanography 38(1): 112–127, doi:10.4319/lo.1993.38.1.0112; Gaedke, U., Straile, D. (1994) Ecological Modelling (title/pages not verified); IGB dataset documentation
findings.relevance: Within a single system, the slope crosses −1 seasonally in step with transfer efficiency. Flatness is a transient crossing, not a maintained state, and the slope-as-TE-indicator inversion is 30-year-old practice.

findings.claim: Andersen, Beyer & Lundberg (2009) derive individual and trophic efficiencies from individual-level mechanisms in size-structured communities, linking Lindeman trophic theory to size-spectrum theory. The mass-transfer definition of trophic efficiency holds only if somatic growth is negligible; including growth makes average individual growth efficiency smaller than trophic efficiency. Background: the community exponent λ depends mainly on PPMR and individual growth efficiency.
findings.citation: Andersen, K.H., Beyer, J.E., Lundberg, P. (2009) Trophic and individual efficiencies of size-structured communities. Proceedings of the Royal Society B 276(1654): 109–114. doi:10.1098/rspb.2008.0951
findings.relevance: A TE-based deviation test must define TE consistently (Lindeman vs individual efficiency), or the predicted slopes are ambiguous by a non-trivial amount.

findings.claim: Derived (my arithmetic, not from a single source): combining the encounter result s_B = n − q with the trophic result s_B = (1−n) + ln TE/ln PPMR gives an emergent efficiency TE = PPMR^(2n−q−1). For n = 0.75 and q = 0.8 that is PPMR^-0.3: 0.25 at PPMR 10^2, 0.13 at 10^3, 0.063 at 10^4. The flatness 'tuning' TE = PPMR^-(1−n) follows automatically when q = n.
findings.citation: Derived from Hartvig et al. (2011) and the Mehner et al. (2018)/Jennings & Mackinson (2003) TE–PPMR relation
findings.formula_or_number: TE_emergent = PPMR^(2n−q−1); flat iff q = n
findings.relevance: This answers 'why would TE ≈ PPMR^-1/4?' inside existing theory: when encounter and metabolism scale alike (q ≈ n), the flat spectrum is robust to PPMR and TE adjusts. For novelty, orthopolity would need to explain why q ≈ n (or why systems self-organize to it), not merely posit flatness.

findings.claim: Derived (my arithmetic): if the conserved quantity were the energy flux through size (a Kolmogorov-like constant cascade flux with no losses), with mass-specific production ∝ m^-1/4, biomass per log mass would scale as m^+1/4 (λ = 1 + n = 1.75), a 10^4-fold rise over 16 decades. Hatton's −0.04 excludes this. Conversely, flat biomass implies energy flux per log mass ∝ m^-1/4, falling ~10^4-fold from bacteria to whales, i.e., dissipation of exactly a factor TE per trophic step.
findings.citation: Derived; production/biomass ∝ m^-1/4 from metabolic scaling (e.g., Brown et al. 2004 Ecology 85: 1771–1789; not verified from full text); Hatton et al. (2021)
findings.formula_or_number: constant flux ⇒ biomass/log m ∝ m^(1−n) ≈ m^0.25; flat biomass ⇒ flux ∝ m^(n−1) ≈ m^-0.25
findings.relevance: 'Nature doesn't care about concentration' is ambiguous between stock and flux, and the two give exponents differing by 1/4. Ocean data favour equal stock, not equal flux, the opposite of naive cascade intuition. Single-trophic assemblages sharing one resource follow energetic equivalence (abundance per log ∝ m^-3/4; Jennings & Mackinson 2003), i.e., equal flux. The equalized resource is therefore system-dependent.

res.novelty_assessment:
The idea of a flat spectrum (equal biomass per log mass) as a baseline, with deviations predicted by transfer efficiency (TE) and predator–prey mass ratio (PPMR), is not novel. It is the standard view in aquatic size-spectrum ecology. The lineage is long:
- Sheldon et al. 1972.
- Platt & Denman 1977/78: an energy-cascade theory predicting biomass per log class ∝ w^-0.22.
- Borgmann 1987; Gaedke 1993; Gaedke & Straile 1994, who use spectrum slope to infer TE.
- Jennings & Mackinson 2003: a tested, independently parameterized prediction of −1.2 abundance and −0.2 biomass slopes for the North Sea.
- Brown et al. 2004; Trebilco et al. 2013.
- Mehner et al. 2018, who state that the slope is exactly −1 if TE = 10% and PPMR = 10^4.
- Atkinson et al. 2021, who invert the median slope −1.11 to TE ≈ 3.5% or PPMR ≈ 569.

The encounter-based theory goes further. Andersen & Beyer 2006 and Hartvig et al. 2011 give λ = 2 + q − n ≈ 2.05, which predicts both the near-flatness and the observed small negative residual: biomass per log mass ∝ m^-0.05, against Hatton's m^-0.04 with CI [−0.05, −0.02]. Flatness then becomes the condition q = n. Physicists have already worked on this problem:
- Camacho & Solé 1999/2001, including an SFI working paper titled 'Scaling and Zipf's Law in Ecological Size Spectra'.
- Rinaldo et al. 2002 (self-organized criticality).
- Capitán & Delius 2010, who find the exponent set by relative scaling of density-dependent and density-independent rates and not fixed by predation and mass balance alone.
- Datta et al. 2010/2011 and Cuesta et al. 2018, who treat the Sheldon spectrum as a self-consistency or stationary state with characterized stability.

Schwamborn's 2025 arXiv preprint (PETS) is the closest prior art: it calls slope −1 an 'equilibrium constant' with stress and non-equilibrium deviations, the same logical shape as the orthopolity claim. On MaxEnt, METE yields ε^-2 (equal metabolic rate per log ε) only over a finite window, in the energy currency rather than biomass. Other MaxEnt size-distribution methods (Metzig & Colijn 2020; the 2001 Ecological Modelling optimization paper) give exponents that depend on the constraints, not a universal ζ = 1.

What could still be novel:
1. A cross-domain unifying condition for ζ = 1 in a named conserved resource, with the same mathematical criterion applied to earthquakes, flares and ecology.
2. An explanation of why real systems sit near the codimension-one point (q ≈ n, equivalently TE ≈ PPMR^-1/4), rather than assuming it.
3. Pre-registered, out-of-sample deviation predictions in systems where no mechanistic size-spectrum model has been fitted.

Relabelling the Sheldon spectrum as orthopolity, or asserting 'deviations are constraints', would be judged derivative.
res.implications:
What an ecological section must beat:

(a) Location. Hatton's ocean slope of −0.04 ± ~0.015 is already predicted at about −0.05 by λ = 2 + q − n from independently measured physiology. Predicting exactly 0 is worse unless the paper supplies a constraint term computed a priori.

(b) Covariation. Across systems the slope tracks TE and PPMR as s_B = (1−n) + ln TE/ln PPMR:
- Mehner 2018: four lake webs with TTE 1–3.6% and NBSS −1.14 to −1.19.
- Jennings & Mackinson 2003: North Sea, PPMR ~10^2, slope −0.2.
- Coghlan 2022: reef slopes increase with community PPMR.
- Atkinson 2021/2024: dome-shaped slope versus plankton biomass, steeper with lower phytoplankton biomass.

(c) Large, systematic counterexamples. Each needs a quantitative, a-priori explanation:
- Freshwater stream ISDs λ ≈ −1.2 (ζ ≈ 0.2, strongly top-heavy).
- North Sea detritivores −0.56 to −0.87 versus predators −1.2 to −2.25.
- Microbial slopes −1.0 to −1.4.
- Seasonal crossing of −1 in Lake Constance.
- Top-heavy structures from generalist predation (Woodson 2018).
- The cross-system predator ∝ prey^0.75 law (Hatton 2015), implying pyramid shape changes with productivity.

(d) Resource ambiguity. Equal biomass (Sheldon, size-structured food webs) and equal energy flux (energetic equivalence, shared-resource guilds; METE's ε^-2 window) differ by 1/4 in exponent. Ocean data reject constant flux, which would give biomass ∝ m^+0.25. A 'law' must say which resource is equalized and why that choice changes between systems.

(e) Mechanism. The working hypothesis (Gabaix-type conservation plus reflecting barrier gives ζ → 1) is not the operative mechanism in size-structured ecology. In continuity-equation and jump-growth models the exponent is set by mortality/growth or encounter/metabolism scaling ratios (Zhou & Huntley 1997; Capitán & Delius 2010), not by conservation alone. In ecology, ζ = 1 is a tuned case, not a generic attractor.

Testable deviation predictions a strong paper could pre-register:
1. Δs_B = Δln TE/ln PPMR. For PPMR 10^3, halving TE from 10% to 5% steepens s_B by −0.10. Test with paired TE (production-based) and PPMR (gut content or δ15N) measurements across systems.
2. s_B = n − q. Communities dominated by feeders with larger clearance-rate exponents (q > n) should be steeper by q − n; with n ≈ 0.75 and q ≈ 1, s_B ≈ −0.25. This differs from the TE route and can discriminate between them.
3. Size-dependent PPMR (Barnes 2010) predicts a concave spectrum: the local slope steepens with size by d(ln TE/ln PPMR)/d ln m, testable as curvature in individual-level MLE fits.
4. From Hatton 2015 (my derivation), ∂s_B/∂log10(prey biomass) ≈ −0.25/log10 PPMR, about −0.08 per decade of biomass at PPMR 10^3. This contradicts Atkinson's oligotrophic steepening, a sharp discriminating test.
5. Boundary effects: a finite plateau between the bacterial excess and the mammal deficit, with fishing truncation of the top (−97 to −99% for large North Sea fish).
6. Open systems: stream ζ_obs − 1 ≈ −0.8 should scale with measured allochthonous subsidy flux relative to in-situ primary production.

Design requirements:
- Fix the resource (carbon biomass) a priori.
- Use individual-level MLE (bounded power law) rather than NBSS bins, given the unit artifacts of ~0.1 in slope.
- Set equivalence tolerances smaller than the mechanistic alternatives' differences (~0.05).
- Compare O_log + constraint models against λ = 2 + q − n and TE/PPMR models out of sample, using information criteria or held-out systems.

Without these, the ecological evidence supports 'approximate flatness as a common, mechanistically explained special case' rather than a general law.

findings.claim: Cleanest rigorous form of candidate theorem (6). Let u = ln(k/k0) on an interval U, let rho(u) = (1/R) dR/du be the resource-weighted (q-size-biased) law of log-size, and take du as reference measure. du is the image of the Haar measure dk/k of the dilation group. For constraints E_rho[T_j] = c_j, if some lambda* in the interior of {lambda : Z(lambda) = integral over U of exp(-lambda.T) du < inf} reproduces c, then rho* = exp(-lambda*.T)/Z(lambda*) is the a.e.-unique maximizer of h(rho) = -integral rho ln rho du among feasible densities. Proof: h(rho) = -KL(rho||rho*) + lambda*.c + ln Z(lambda*) <= h(rho*) (Gibbs inequality). Corollaries. (i) No constraint, U = [ln a, ln b]: rho = 1/L with L = ln(b/a), which is O_log; dN/dk = R/(L k qbar(k)). (ii) T = u: rho proportional to k^-lambda1 and dN/dk proportional to k^(-1-lambda1)/qbar. Any exponent is attainable. O_log holds iff lambda1 = 0; within this tilt family that is equivalent to a resource-weighted geometric-mean size of sqrt(ab). (iii) T = k: rho proportional to exp(-lambda2 k) and dN/dk proportional to exp(-lambda2 k)/(k qbar), a Schechter/gamma-type upper cutoff with alpha = -(d+1); U may be unbounded above. (iv) Fixing the count N as well as R is equivalent to E_rho[1/qbar] = N/R. This gives rho proportional to exp(-lambdaN/qbar); for qbar proportional to k^d, dN/dk is proportional to k^-(d+1) exp(-c k^-d), a Frechet-shaped LOWER cutoff. (v) Combining (ii)-(iv) with d = 1 gives the generalized-inverse-Gaussian family k^(-2-lambda1) exp(-c/k - lambda2 k).
findings.citation: Own derivation in this task. Gibbs inequality / exponential-family MaxEnt as in Cover & Thomas, Elements of Information Theory, 2nd ed. (Wiley 2006), Thm 12.1.1 (cited from memory).
findings.relevance: Part (i) is true but tautological: with no constraints, the MaxEnt law is the normalized reference measure. All content lies in three choices. First, the entropy is taken of the RESOURCE-weighted law rather than the count law. Second, du is the reference. Third, no other constraint is active. Correction to the candidate: conservation of count and resource gives a lower cutoff (iv), not the upper exponential cutoff. An upper Schechter/tapered cutoff needs a constraint on E_R[k] = sum(q_i k_i)/sum(q_i), which has no obvious conservation-law origin. Count-level MaxEnt (Main & Burton; Sornette & Sornette; Pueyo) gets an UPPER cutoff from the same mean-resource constraint. The two entropies are therefore not equivalent, and cutoff placement could discriminate between them.
findings.formula_or_number: rho* = exp(-lambda.T)/Z; O_log: dN/dk = R/(ln(b/a) k qbar(k)); count+resource conservation: dN/dk ∝ k^-(d+1) exp(-c k^-d); E_R[k] constraint: dN/dk ∝ k^-(d+1) exp(-lambda2 k)

findings.claim: Symmetry characterization. The Radon measures on (0,inf) that are relatively invariant under dilations k -> ck (nu∘D_c = chi(c) nu, with chi a continuous character) are exactly nu_gamma = C k^(-1-gamma) dk, with chi(c) = c^-gamma. With qbar proportional to k^d, the resource measure qbar·nu_gamma has character c^(d-gamma) and is exactly invariant iff gamma = d, which is O_log. The count measure is exactly invariant iff gamma = 0: log-uniform counts, i.e. Benford, i.e. O_log with q ≡ 1.
findings.citation: Own derivation (continuous homomorphisms of (R>0,×) into (R>0,×) are power maps; uniqueness of Haar measure up to a constant).
findings.relevance: Scale symmetry alone yields only the one-parameter power family (the classical result that scale invariance implies a power law); it cannot pick the exponent. O_log adds a postulate: the conserved resource, not the count or any other weight, carries the trivial character. Jaynes-style group invariance does not say which measure must be exactly invariant. On a bounded support no nonzero measure is exactly dilation-invariant, so the symmetry can hold only in the interior, away from cutoffs. O_log is preserved by the affine group u -> s u + t, i.e. by power reparametrizations k -> c k^s. This matches the repo paper's §2.2 statement.
findings.formula_or_number: nu_gamma = k^(-1-gamma) dk; resource character c^(d-gamma); O_log <=> gamma = d

findings.claim: Vacuity lemma. For any count density proportional to k^-alpha (alpha > 1), the weight q proportional to k^(alpha-1) satisfies O_log exactly. More generally, any p_N is the Haar-uniform MaxEnt solution for q = 1/(k p_N(k)). The statement 'orthopolity holds for SOME resource' is therefore empty. It has content only for a resource fixed a priori: conserved or extensive, additive, and independently measured, with an independently measured cost exponent d.
findings.citation: Own derivation; same point as repo docs/paper.md §2.3 ('the resource must not be fitted').
findings.relevance: Example: for earthquakes the conserved additive quantities, seismic moment and radiated energy, fail O_log. Rupture area passes (zeta_A ≈ b ≈ 1.00 in the repo results), but area is selected after the fact through M0 ∝ A^(3/2). That selection is exactly the freedom the lemma warns about. A paper must pre-register q and d per system.
findings.formula_or_number: q ∝ k^(alpha-1) makes any power law orthopolic

findings.claim: Jaynes (1968) introduced the principle of transformation groups: a problem's symmetry group determines the prior. Invariance of a scale parameter under rescaling gives p(sigma) ∝ 1/sigma, which is uniform in ln sigma. Jaynes' 'limiting density of discrete points' replaces Shannon's continuous entropy with H = -∫ p ln(p/m) dx, where m is an invariant measure. This makes MaxEnt coordinate-invariant, and with no constraints it returns m itself.
findings.citation: Jaynes, E. T. (1968). Prior probabilities. IEEE Transactions on Systems Science and Cybernetics SSC-4(3), 227–241. Jaynes, E. T. (1957) Phys. Rev. 106, 620–630 (LDDP background).
findings.relevance: This supplies the Haar reference measure m(k) ∝ 1/k and shows why MaxEnt without constraints just returns m. Jaynes' argument concerns a prior for a parameter under ignorance, not the physical frequency distribution of a resource. Applying m to resource quanta rather than to objects is a further, physical assumption (see the symmetry characterization finding). Verified from a bibliographic record and secondary encyclopedic summaries; full text not accessible.

findings.claim: The Jeffreys prior, proportional to the square root of det(Fisher information), is invariant under reparametrization. For a scale parameter with location fixed it is ∝ 1/sigma, i.e. uniform on a log scale.
findings.citation: Jeffreys, H. (1946). An invariant form for the prior probability in estimation problems. Proc. R. Soc. Lond. A 186(1007), 453–461. doi:10.1098/rspa.1946.0056
findings.relevance: This is the standard justification for calling dk/k the 'scale-invariant (Jeffreys) reference measure' in the candidate theorem. It is a statistical-inference device, not a physical law of allocation.

findings.claim: Frank (2009) treats common distributions as consequences of informational constraints plus measurement scale. A scale-invariant pattern implies a power law. Aggregation that preserves only the geometric mean attracts to a power law; preserving only the arithmetic mean attracts to an exponential.
findings.citation: Frank, S. A. (2009). The common patterns of nature. Journal of Evolutionary Biology 22(8), 1563–1585. doi:10.1111/j.1420-9101.2009.01775.x
findings.relevance: This is the closest methodological sibling. In Frank's language, O_log is a log-scale MaxEnt in which the resource-weighted measure carries no geometric-mean constraint. The power-law and cutoff corollaries are already in this framework at the count level. Verified from abstract and snippets only.
findings.formula_or_number: <ln x> constraint -> power law; <x> constraint -> exponential

findings.claim: Frank & Smith treat measurement scale T(y) as an information constraint. A log scale yields power laws (densities 'linear in y^c'). A log-linear scale yields the gamma (power law with exponential cutoff), and the inverse linear-log scale yields Student-type laws. The constraint E[f + b log f] gives the density ∝ f^(-lambda b) e^(-lambda f). They classify Pearson-type families by scale change.
findings.citation: Frank, S. A. & Smith, D. E. (2010). Measurement invariance, entropy, and probability. Entropy 12(3), 289–303. doi:10.3390/e12030289. Frank, S. A. & Smith, E. (2011). A simple derivation and classification of common probability distributions based on information symmetry and measurement scale. J. Evol. Biol. 24, 469–484. doi:10.1111/j.1420-9101.2010.02204.x
findings.relevance: Corollaries (ii) and (iii) of the theorem, and their combination into a power law with exponential cutoff, are count-level special cases of this framework. The resource-weighted variant changes only which density is maximized. Frank (2011), 'Measurement scale in maximum entropy models of species abundance' (J. Evol. Biol. 24, 485–496), applies the framework to species abundance.

findings.claim: Frank (2016) analyses power-law size distributions through shift, stretch and rotational invariances. Stretch invariance is tied to a conserved total 'such as the total biomass and consequently the average size'. Frank (2019) presents Zipf's law and the log series as opposite endpoints of one theory, based on conserved average values and the associated scale invariances. Frank & Bascompte (2019) derive the log series from invariance to additive and multiplicative change of abundance.
findings.citation: Frank, S. A. (2016). The invariances of power law size distributions. F1000Research 5, 2074. doi:10.12688/f1000research.9452.3. Frank, S. A. (2019). The common patterns of abundance: the log series and Zipf's law. F1000Research 8, 334. doi:10.12688/f1000research.18681.1. Frank, S. A. & Bascompte, J. (2019). Invariance in ecological pattern. F1000Research 8, 2093. doi:10.12688/f1000research.21586.1
findings.relevance: This is the strongest novelty threat to 'orthopolity as an invariance + conservation principle'. Frank already links conserved totals (biomass) to scale invariance in size distributions and places Zipf (zeta = 1) inside a conserved-average/scale-invariance theory. Only abstracts were checked. The full texts could not be read because the network blocked arXiv, PMC and doi.org fetches. They must be read before any priority claim.

findings.claim: Visser (2013) shows that maximizing Shannon entropy with the single constraint <ln n> = chi gives a pure power law p_n = n^-z/zeta(z). The exponent z is the Lagrange multiplier fixed by the value of chi.
findings.citation: Visser, M. (2013). Zipf's law, power laws and maximum entropy. New Journal of Physics 15, 043021. doi:10.1088/1367-2630/15/4/043021
findings.relevance: At the count level MaxEnt does not select z = 2 (zeta = 1). It reproduces whatever log-moment is imposed. O_log corresponds to one specific value. In the resource variable with an unbounded top that value is E_N[ln(q/q_min)] = 1/zeta = 1, the Hill-estimator form. So O_log is a restriction on the constraint value, not a MaxEnt output.

findings.claim: Pueyo, He & Zillio (2007) adopt a scale-invariant prior P(n) = A/n, which they argue carries no information about scale or sample size. MaxEnt with a mean constraint then gives Fisher's log series P(n) ∝ e^(-beta n)/n, and an extra constraint gives a gamma family that subsumes the log series, geometric and power laws. Bowler & Kelly accept the 1/n factor but attribute it to per-capita birth–death dynamics rather than invariance. Frank (2011) argued for a log-linear scale, and Pueyo (2012, Ecology and Evolution) replied.
findings.citation: Pueyo, S., He, F. & Zillio, T. (2007). The maximum entropy formalism and the idiosyncratic theory of biodiversity. Ecology Letters 10(11), 1017–1028. doi:10.1111/j.1461-0248.2007.01096.x. Bowler, M. G. & Kelly, C. K. (2010) arXiv:1004.2271. Bowler (2012) 'Of priors and prejudice' arXiv:1205.1946.
findings.relevance: This is exactly corollary (iii) (Haar/1/n reference plus a linear constraint giving an exponential cutoff) for d = 0, justified by scale invariance. It is published and debated. Even in its most successful ecological use, the invariance justification is contested and a dynamical origin is preferred by critics.

findings.claim: In METE (Harte et al. 2008; Harte 2011), MaxEnt over species abundance n and individual metabolic rate eps under the state variables S0, N0, E0 gives the structure function R(n,eps) ∝ exp(-lambda1 n - lambda2 n eps). Own derivation: the individual metabolic-rate distribution is Psi(eps) ∝ sum_n n exp(-(lambda1 + lambda2 eps) n) = e^-g/(1-e^-g)^2, which is ≈ g^-2 for g = lambda1 + lambda2 eps << 1. Psi therefore approaches eps^-2, i.e. O_log in metabolic energy (zeta = 1), but only between a knee at lambda1/lambda2 and a cutoff at 1/lambda2 ≈ E0/S0. Numerically, with S0 = 100, N0 = 10^4 and E0 = 10^6, the local log-slope is -1.75 at eps = 100, -1.97 at 10^3, -2.01 at 3×10^3 and -2.17 at 10^4, and falls steeply beyond.
findings.citation: Harte, J., Zillio, T., Conlisk, E. & Smith, A. B. (2008). Maximum entropy and the state-variable approach to macroecology. Ecology 89, 2700–2711. Harte, J. (2011). Maximum Entropy and Ecology. Oxford University Press. R(n,eps) form as restated in Xiao et al. arXiv:1308.0731. The Psi asymptotics are own derivation and computation (scratchpad mete_psi.py).
findings.relevance: A published MaxEnt theory already yields approximately O_log for an energetic resource over roughly 1 to 1.5 decades, with calculable knee and cutoff. This is partial support and a novelty threat. Note that the eps^-2 comes from summing abundance-weighted exponentials, not from a Haar-reference resource MaxEnt. Not confirmed that Harte states eps^-2 explicitly; Harte (2011) Ch. 7 should be checked. The citation and the R(n,eps) form are verified.
findings.formula_or_number: Psi(eps) ≈ (lambda1 + lambda2 eps)^-2; local slope ≈ -2 for ~3×10^2 < eps < ~5×10^3

findings.claim: In 60 forest communities (more than 300,000 individuals, about 2,000 species), METE captured 96% of the variation in rank species-abundance and 89% in rank individual-size distributions. It performed poorly for the size–density relationship and for intraspecific size distributions. A separate 2012 ESA abstract (Barro Colorado Island and Sherman plots) reported that METE overpredicts energy use by high-metabolic-rate individuals.
findings.citation: Xiao, X., McGlinn, D. J. & White, E. P. (2015). A strong test of the maximum entropy theory of ecology. American Naturalist 185(3), E70–E80. doi:10.1086/679576. ESA 2012 abstract PS 57-165.
findings.relevance: The MaxEnt energetic prediction that comes closest to O_log fails in its tail and in its size–density predictions. Real upper tails are steeper than eps^-2, i.e. zeta > 1 (bottom-heavy). Page range E70–E80 from memory; volume, issue and DOI verified.

findings.claim: Base-invariance implies Benford's law: every base-invariant significand distribution is a convex combination of a point mass and the log-Lebesgue measure. Random samples from random distributions converge to Benford (Hill 1995b). Scale invariance implies Benford, and Benford is the unique scale-invariant first-digit law (Pinkham 1961).
findings.citation: Hill, T. P. (1995a). Base-invariance implies Benford's law. Proc. Amer. Math. Soc. 123(3), 887–895. doi:10.1090/S0002-9939-1995-1233974-8. Hill, T. P. (1995b). A statistical derivation of the significant-digit law. Statistical Science 10(4), 354–363. doi:10.1214/ss/1177009869. Pinkham, R. S. (1961). On the distribution of first significant digits. Ann. Math. Statist. 32(4), 1223–1230.
findings.relevance: The Benford literature is the mature mathematics of 'scale indifference', but at the COUNT level. Benford equals O_log with q ≡ 1 (d = 0), whose count exponent is 1, not d + 1.

findings.claim: Allaart (1997) proved Nigrini's sum-invariance observation: Benford's law is the unique distribution for which the expected sum of all elements with given first k significant digits is constant for every k. Own mapping: count-Benford means log-uniform counts, which means equal value-sums per digit block. That is linear-measure orthopolity with q = k, the 2017 linear version, not O_log with q = k.
findings.citation: Allaart, P. C. (1997). An invariant-sum characterization of Benford's law. Journal of Applied Probability 34(1), 288–291. Nigrini summation test: Nigrini, M. (2012) Benford's Law, Wiley (ch. 5).
findings.relevance: Benford's law is itself a published 'equal resource per class' theorem (forensic accounting uses it as the summation test). It corresponds to the 2017 linear-allocation version, so it is prior art for that version and a counter-model to O_log with q = k. The theorem is verified; the mapping to orthopolity is own derivation.
findings.formula_or_number: value-weighted digit fractions = 1/9 each under count-Benford

findings.claim: Resource-weighted Benford (own derivation). O_log implies that the fraction of TOTAL RESOURCE held by objects whose size has leading digit D is log10(1 + 1/D): exact on supports spanning an integer number of decades, approximate on wide supports. Count-weighted digits follow P(D) = (D^-d - (D+1)^-d)/(1 - 10^-d); for q = k these are 0.556, 0.185, 0.093, 0.056, 0.037, 0.026, 0.020, 0.015, 0.012. For a resource tilt beta per ln k, the resource-weighted digit law is ((D+1)^beta - D^beta)/(10^beta - 1). For beta = -0.039 (the Hatton-type slope), P_w(1) moves only from 0.3010 to 0.3105. A digit test sees only the profile folded modulo one decade. Its Fisher information on beta at beta = 0 is (1/M)^2 of a direct slope fit over M decades: 0.111 for 3 decades, 0.0039 for 16, 0.0019 for 23.
findings.citation: Own derivation and computation (scratchpad checks.py). No published statement of value- or resource-weighted Benford was found by search.
findings.relevance: The test is testable and unit-free. It discriminates O_log (resource-weighted Benford) from count-log-uniformity (resource fractions 1/9 each). It is necessary, not sufficient: broad humps and curvature over many decades average out in the fold, and it is far less powerful than a direct slope or profile test. It is too weak to discriminate and should not be a primary test; at most a side remark. Possibly novel as a statement, but minor.

findings.claim: Pietronero et al. (2001) derived a generalized Benford law for power-law data P(N) ∝ N^-alpha. Benford is the case alpha = 1, the paper relates the law to Zipf's law, and it notes that many real data sets have alpha ≈ 2.
findings.citation: Pietronero, L., Tosatti, E., Tosatti, V. & Vespignani, A. (2001). Explaining the uneven distribution of numbers in nature: the laws of Benford and Zipf. Physica A 293(1–2), 297–304. doi:10.1016/S0378-4371(00)00633-6
findings.relevance: The count-level digit law implied by O_log with d = 1 (alpha = 2) is already in this paper, so the resource-weighted Benford adds only a reweighting. The alpha ≈ 2 remark is verified via a secondary restatement (Altamirano & Robledo).

findings.claim: Friar, Goldman & Pérez-Mercader (2016) show that the reciprocal (1/x, log-uniform) distribution results uniquely from requiring maximum entropy for size-class distributions with uniform log bin sizes.
findings.citation: Friar, J. L., Goldman, T. & Pérez-Mercader, J. (2016). Ubiquity of Benford's law and emergence of the reciprocal distribution. Physics Letters A 380(22), 1895–1899.
findings.relevance: This is the published count-level version of corollary (i): MaxEnt over equal log bins gives log-uniformity. Orthopolity's only change is to apply it to resource rather than counts.

findings.claim: Kesten–Goldie theorem: for X_{t+1} = A_t X_t + B_t with i.i.d. (A,B), A > 0, B > 0, E[ln A] < 0, ln A non-arithmetic, E[A^kappa] = 1, E[A^kappa ln+ A] < inf and E[B^kappa] < inf, the stationary law has P(X > x) ~ C x^-kappa. Own corollary for X = resource: zeta = 1 iff E[A] = 1 (resource conserved in expectation under scale-free multiplicative change); E[A] < 1 gives zeta > 1 (bottom-heavy) and E[A] > 1 gives zeta < 1 (top-heavy), by log-convexity of kappa -> E[A^kappa]. At E[A] = 1, E[X_t] grows linearly: the stationary law exists but has infinite mean. For lognormal A, zeta = 1 - 2 ln E[A]/sigma^2. Simulation with 200,000 copies, 4,000 steps, sigma = 0.3, B = 1: E[A] = 1.00 gives a ccdf slope of 0.997 and Hill estimates of 1.04–1.06, with resource per ln-size bin flat to about ±10% in the tail. E[A] = 0.97 gives 1.58–1.71 (theory 1.677). E[A] = 1.03 gives 0.34 (theory 0.343).
findings.citation: Kesten, H. (1973). Random difference equations and renewal theory for products of random matrices. Acta Mathematica 131, 207–248. doi:10.1007/BF02392040. Goldie, C. M. (1991). Implicit renewal theory and tails of solutions of random equations. Ann. Appl. Probab. 1(1), 126–166. doi:10.1214/aoap/1177005985. Corollary and simulation are own work (scratchpad checks.py).
findings.relevance: This is the non-tautological content that the MaxEnt route lacks. O_log is equivalent to a measurable dynamical condition, E[A] = 1 for per-object resource multipliers, and that condition can be tested from object-level growth data independently of the size distribution. It also undermines robustness: zeta = 1 is a knife-edge, since a 3% imbalance moves zeta to 1.68 or 0.34, unless something enforces the conservation exactly. The theorem conditions are verified; the corollary and numbers are own derivation and computation.
findings.formula_or_number: E[A^zeta] = 1; zeta = 1 <=> E[A] = 1; lognormal: zeta = 1 - 2 ln E[A]/sigma^2

findings.claim: Gabaix (1999): if cities follow proportional (Gibrat) growth with a common mean and variance of normalized size (normalized multipliers with E[gamma] = 1), plus a reflecting lower barrier, the steady state is Zipf's law with exponent ≈ 1. The finite-barrier formula zeta = 1/(1 - s_min/s̄) was not found in the retrieved text. It follows because stationary normalized sizes are an exact Pareto from the floor with mean s̄: zeta s_min/(zeta - 1) = s̄. Own simulation (N = 20,000, sigma = 0.1 per step, 6,000 steps): s_min/s̄ = 0.2 gives Hill estimates of 1.31–1.40 (formula 1.25); 0.4 gives 1.42–1.56 (formula 1.667); 0.05 gives 0.86–0.90 (formula 1.053), not converged or finite-N limited.
findings.citation: Gabaix, X. (1999). Zipf's law for cities: an explanation. Quarterly Journal of Economics 114(3), 739–767.
findings.relevance: In a closed system with fixed total and fixed number, normalization enforces E[A] = 1 for normalized sizes. The deviation from zeta = 1 is then a calculable finite-floor correction. This is precisely the authors' 'conservation + constraint-induced deviations' intuition, already published. The mechanism is verified; the s_min formula is unverified in text but derived here.

findings.claim: Levy & Solomon (1996) interpret power laws as Boltzmann laws in the logarithmic variable, with the exponent tied to the system's constraints (lower bound) and the fluctuation dispersion. Sornette & Cont (1997) show the exponent solves <lambda^mu> = 1 and is controlled by extreme excursions of the drifting log-walk, not its average behaviour. On that basis they argue the Levy–Solomon equilibrium analogy is ruled out.
findings.citation: Levy, M. & Solomon, S. (1996). Power laws are logarithmic Boltzmann laws. Int. J. Mod. Phys. C 7(4), 595–601. Sornette, D. & Cont, R. (1997). Convergent multiplicative processes repelled from zero: power laws and truncated power laws. J. Phys. I France 7, 431–444. doi:10.1051/jp1:1997169
findings.relevance: 'Power law = MaxEnt/Boltzmann in log-size' is 30-year-old prior art. The strongest objection to reading it as an equilibrium-entropy principle comes from the multiplicative-process literature itself: the exponent is set by rare excursions (the Kesten condition), not by entropy maximization.

findings.claim: Malevergne, Saichev & Sornette (2013) show that with Gibrat growth at all sizes plus random firm births and deaths, Zipf's law holds under a balance condition between the effective growth rate of incumbents (including exits) and the growth rate of investment in entrants. They read Zipf as the signature of the allocation that maximizes sustainable growth when firms cannot consume more resources than available. Their book classifies deviation mechanisms: time-varying creation, exits from capital shortfall or shocks, and coupling of birth rate to aggregate growth.
findings.citation: Malevergne, Y., Saichev, A. & Sornette, D. (2013). Zipf's law and maximum sustainable growth. J. Economic Dynamics and Control 37(6), 1195–1212. doi:10.1016/j.jedc.2013.02.004. Saichev, A., Malevergne, Y. & Sornette, D. (2010). Theory of Zipf's Law and Beyond. Lecture Notes in Economics and Mathematical Systems 632, Springer. doi:10.1007/978-3-642-02946-2
findings.relevance: The working hypothesis is already a published research programme for firms: zeta = 1 as the stationary state under resource balance, with calculable deviations from entry/exit imbalance. An orthopolity paper must cite it and show what it adds.

findings.claim: Hernando et al. derive Zipf's law as the equilibrium density of a 'scale-free ideal gas' from an extreme-information (Fisher) variational principle. Their model is non-interacting elements with stochastic proportional growth; a harmonic constraint gives a lognormal. They test it on election results, city populations and journal citations.
findings.citation: Hernando, A., Puigdomènech, D., Villuendas, D. & Vesperinas, C. (2009) arXiv:0902.2738. Hernando, A., Vesperinas, C. & Plastino, A. (2010). Fisher information and the thermodynamics of scale-invariant systems. Physica A 389(3), 490–498. Hernando et al. (2010) Zipf's law from a Fisher variational-principle. Physics Letters A 374(1), 18–21.
findings.relevance: 'Zipf (zeta = 1) as the equilibrium/variational state of a scale-invariant system' is published. A paper framing orthopolity as a variational or equilibrium property would need to distinguish itself from this.

findings.claim: Mazzarisi, de Azevedo-Lopes, Arenzon & Corberi (2021) link Zipf's law to maximal diversity of component sizes. The diversity law naturally selects the size-distribution exponent tau = 2, which they identify as maximal diversity.
findings.citation: Mazzarisi, O., de Azevedo-Lopes, A., Arenzon, J. J. & Corberi, F. (2021). Maximal diversity and Zipf's law. Physical Review Letters 127, 128301. doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.127.128301
findings.relevance: A published extremal principle singles out exactly tau = 2, i.e. density exponent 2 and zeta = 1, the O_log case for q = k. This is a direct novelty threat to any 'mathematical principle selects zeta = 1' claim.

findings.claim: Corominas-Murtra & Solé (2010) argue that Zipf's law is an inevitable outcome of a general class of stochastic systems with unbounded state space. Under a power-law ansatz the only large-system solution of their condition is exponent 1.
findings.citation: Corominas-Murtra, B. & Solé, R. V. (2010). Universality of Zipf's law. Physical Review E 82, 011102.
findings.relevance: This is a further published 'zeta = 1 is universal' derivation. It shows the claim is not new and has competing derivations with different assumptions.

findings.claim: Main & Burton (1984) used information theory (MaxEnt) to derive a modified, gamma-type frequency–size distribution of earthquakes. Sornette & Sornette (1999) argue that if the Gutenberg–Richter power law holds 'in absence of any condition', imposing constraints (finite moment release rate, observed maximum) makes the Gamma distribution the best model, independent of the constraint's nature.
findings.citation: Main, I. G. & Burton, P. W. (1984). Information theory and the earthquake frequency-magnitude distribution. Bull. Seismol. Soc. Am. 74, 1409–1426. Sornette, D. & Sornette, A. (1999). General theory of the modified Gutenberg-Richter law for large seismic moments. Bull. Seismol. Soc. Am. 89(4), 1121–1130. doi:10.1785/BSSA0890041121
findings.relevance: This is prior art for corollary (iii) in seismology, with the same logic of 'unconstrained power law + linear constraint gives an exponential cutoff'. It is count-level and relative to a GR reference with beta ≈ 2/3, not O_log (beta = 1). The Main & Burton content is verified only via secondary descriptions.

findings.claim: Kagan (2002) reports a universal moment-distribution exponent beta = 0.60–0.65 for moderate earthquakes, with corner moment ≈ 10^21 N m (m_c ≈ 8.0) for subduction zones. A corner is required to keep the moment flux finite; Part II applies a moment-conservation principle.
findings.citation: Kagan, Y. Y. (2002). Seismic moment distribution revisited: I. Statistical results. Geophys. J. Int. 148(3), 520–541. Kagan, Y. Y. (2002). II. Moment conservation principle. Geophys. J. Int. 149(3), 731–754.
findings.relevance: In the physically conserved, additive resource (seismic moment), zeta_M0 ≈ 0.63, whereas O_log needs 1 (b = 1.5). Resource per ln M0 scales as M0^0.37, which is top-heavy, and the active constraint is the corner. In MaxEnt language this is a large nonzero lambda1, so O_log is not the reference state.
findings.formula_or_number: beta = 0.60–0.65; moment per ln M0 ∝ M0^(1-beta)

findings.claim: The Schechter (1976) form phi(L) = phi*(L/L*)^alpha exp(-L/L*) fits galaxy luminosity functions. Local faint-end slopes are alpha ≈ -1.05 (SDSS r band, Blanton et al. 2003), steepening to ≈ -1.3 at the faint end (Blanton et al. 2005); 2dFGRS gives ≈ -1.21.
findings.citation: Schechter, P. (1976). An analytic expression for the luminosity function for galaxies. Astrophysical Journal 203, 297–306. Faint-end values as restated in later literature (e.g., COSMOS faint-end paper arXiv:0708.1545).
findings.relevance: O_log in luminosity would require alpha = -2. Observed light per ln L scales as L^(alpha+2) ≈ L^0.7–0.95 below L*, so the light is concentrated at a characteristic scale. This is a major counterexample with an additive resource. The Schechter shape matches corollary (iii) only with a strongly active log-constraint. The alpha values are verified via secondary sources.

findings.claim: The stellar IMF (Kroupa 2001) has dN/dm ∝ m^-alpha with alpha = 1.3 ± 0.5 for 0.08–0.5 Msun and 2.3 ± 0.3 above 0.5 Msun. Salpeter's index is 2.35 for 0.4–10 Msun.
findings.citation: Kroupa, P. (2001). On the variation of the initial mass function. MNRAS 322, 231–246. Salpeter, E. E. (1955). ApJ 121, 161.
findings.relevance: Stellar mass per ln m scales as m^(2-alpha), i.e. m^0.7 below 0.5 Msun and m^-0.3 above. Mass is peaked near 0.5 Msun, not flat, so this mass resource is not orthopolic. The page range 231–246 is from memory.

findings.claim: Junge aerosol distributions dN/dlog r = c r^-nu have nu between 3 and 5, typically 4. nu = 3 is exactly equal volume per log radius (own algebra: dV/dlog r ∝ r^(3-nu)). Real distributions are multimodal.
findings.citation: Junge distribution as described in Selvam (arXiv:0908.2321) and related aerosol literature. Equal-volume interpretation is own derivation.
findings.relevance: This is prior art under another name: Junge nu = 3 is O_log for aerosol volume. The typical nu ≈ 4 gives volume per log r ∝ r^-1, bottom-heavy, so it is another counterexample to universality.

findings.claim: Sheldon, Prakash & Sutcliffe (1972) reported roughly equal concentrations of particulate material across logarithmic size classes, over about six orders of magnitude at about 80 stations. This is the 'Sheldon spectrum'. Platt & Denman (1977) derived biomass per geometric class ∝ (weight ratio)^-0.22 (normalized slope -1.22) from metabolic scaling. Andersen & Beyer (2006) derived abundance ∝ w^-2.05 from individual-level physiology, and the size-spectrum food-web framework gives lambda = 2 + q - n ≈ 2.
findings.citation: Sheldon, R. W., Prakash, A. & Sutcliffe, W. H. (1972). Limnol. Oceanogr. 17, 327–340. Platt, T. & Denman, K. (1977). Organisation in the pelagic ecosystem. Helgoländer wiss. Meeresunters. 30, 575–581. Andersen, K. H. & Beyer, J. E. (2006). Asymptotic size determines species abundance in the marine size spectrum. Am. Nat. 168, 54–61. doi:10.1086/504849. Hartvig et al. arXiv:1004.4138.
findings.relevance: In ecology, O_log for biomass is a known first approximation, and deviations from it have been calculated mechanistically for 50 years (-0.22, -0.05). This is the 'constraint gives calculable deviation' programme, already established there. It supports the framing but removes novelty. The Platt & Denman page range is from memory.
findings.formula_or_number: biomass per class ∝ w^-0.22; N ∝ w^-2.05; lambda = 2+q-n

findings.claim: Pink noise (PSD ∝ 1/f) carries equal power per octave, i.e. constant power per log-frequency interval.
findings.citation: Standard signal-processing definition (Wikipedia 'Pink noise'; Cycling '74 pink~ documentation).
findings.relevance: This is the oldest familiar 'equal resource per log interval' statement under another name, with resource = variance and coordinate = frequency. It is a useful analogy, but neither generality nor novelty follows from it.

findings.claim: Newman (2005) shows that power laws with density exponent alpha ≤ 2 have no finite mean, and that the share of the total held by the top fraction P is W = P^((alpha-2)/(alpha-1)). Bouchaud & Mézard (2000) find a wealth-condensation transition in a stochastic exchange model; condensation is tied to a non-integrable tail (alpha < 1 in the tail convention w^(-1-alpha)).
findings.citation: Newman, M. E. J. (2005). Power laws, Pareto distributions and Zipf's law. Contemporary Physics 46(5), 323–351. Bouchaud, J.-P. & Mézard, M. (2000). Wealth condensation in a simple model of economy. Physica A 282(3), 536–545.
findings.relevance: zeta = 1 (alpha = 2) is by definition the boundary between finite-mean, bottom-heavy and infinite-mean, top-heavy or condensed regimes. Calling it 'marginal' describes the power family. It is not evidence that systems are attracted to the boundary.

findings.claim: The Dohnanyi (1969) collisional cascade gives a mass index ≈ 1.837, close to the commonly quoted 11/6. That corresponds to zeta_m ≈ 5/6 and mass per ln m ∝ m^(1/6).
findings.citation: Dohnanyi, J. S. (1969). Collisional model of asteroids and their debris. J. Geophys. Res. 74(10), 2531–2554.
findings.relevance: A steady cascade with constant mass flux gives a top-heavy deviation from O_log. That is calculable, which supports the 'deviation' framing, but it shows constant flux is not equal stock per scale. The observed belt also deviates from the simple law.

findings.claim: Weighted (size-biased) distributions: sampling with probability proportional to a weight w(x) turns f(x) into w(x) f(x)/E[w].
findings.citation: Patil, G. P. & Rao, C. R. (1978). Weighted distributions and size-biased sampling with applications to wildlife populations and human families. Biometrics 34(2), 179–189.
findings.relevance: The resource-weighted law rho is the q-size-biased distribution of ln k. 'Resource-weighted scale indifference' is precisely the statement that the q-size-biased law of ln k is uniform. Statistics already has standard machinery and terminology for this.

findings.claim: Peterson, Dixit & Dill (2013) obtain power-law tails from standard Boltzmann–Gibbs–Shannon MaxEnt by placing the nonextensivity in an energy-like cost with economies of scale. They report fits to 13 datasets.
findings.citation: Peterson, J., Dixit, P. D. & Dill, K. A. (2013). A maximum entropy framework for nonexponential distributions. PNAS 110(51), 20380–20385. doi:10.1073/pnas.1320578110
findings.relevance: This is another published route by which MaxEnt produces power laws with fitted, not predicted, exponents. MaxEnt plus a suitably chosen cost or measure can reproduce almost any tail, which reinforces the vacuity lemma.

res.novelty_assessment:
Short version: the mathematics is not novel. Only a narrow synthesis is defensible, and only with heavy attribution.

1. MaxEnt core. "Relative to the Haar/Jeffreys measure dk/k, the MaxEnt resource distribution on [ln a, ln b] is uniform" is the Gibbs inequality. Unconstrained MaxEnt returns the normalized reference measure (Jaynes 1957/1968, limiting density of discrete points).
