The power-law tilt from a log-moment constraint is published (Frank 2009; Frank & Smith 2010, 2011; Visser 2013). So is the exponential cutoff from a linear constraint with a 1/x reference: Pueyo, He & Zillio 2007 (log series); Main & Burton 1984; Sornette & Sornette 1999 (gamma for seismic moment). The count-level uniform-in-log result is Friar et al. 2016. Presented as a new theorem, this would rightly be rejected.

2. Symmetry. "Scale invariance implies a power law" is classical (Frank 2009, 2016; Pinkham 1961 and Hill 1995 for Benford). The characterization derived here, that O_log is the trivial character on the RESOURCE measure, was not found in that form, but it is a two-line observation.

3. zeta = 1 as special, equilibrium or attracting. Strong prior art:
- Levy & Solomon 1996
- Gabaix 1999
- Saichev, Malevergne & Sornette 2010 / Malevergne et al. 2013 (balance condition; deviations classified)
- Hernando et al. 2009–2010 (Zipf as equilibrium of a scale-free ideal gas)
- Corominas-Murtra & Solé 2010
- Mazzarisi et al. 2021 PRL (tau = 2 maximizes diversity)
- Frank 2019 (Zipf from conserved averages and scale invariance)
- Frank 2016 explicitly ties a conserved total (biomass) to scale invariance in size distributions.

4. The same statement under other names:
- Sheldon spectrum / equal biomass per log class (ecology); Platt & Denman and Andersen & Beyer already compute deviations
- Junge nu = 3 (aerosol volume)
- Fractal fragmentation with D = 3 (fragment mass)
- pink noise (power per octave)
- Zipf zeta = 1 (population per log class)
- b = 1.5 (equal seismic energy per magnitude)
- the q-size-biased law (Patil & Rao 1978)
- METE's intermediate eps^-2 regime (own derivation)
- Benford's law, which is the q ≡ 1 case. Its Allaart/Nigrini sum-invariance is linear-measure orthopolity with q = k, i.e. the 2017 version, not O_log.

5. Not found in searches, so possibly new but minor:
- (a) the explicit resource-weighted vs count-weighted MaxEnt contrast, with the vacuity lemma;
- (b) the observation that, in the resource-weighted formulation, conservation of count and resource gives a LOWER (Frechet-type) cutoff, while count-level MaxEnt gives an UPPER cutoff from the same constraint. This is a potential discriminating test;
- (c) a "resource-weighted Benford" law. It is testable but statistically weak (Fisher information on tilt about 1/M^2 of a direct slope fit) and adds little beyond Pietronero et al. 2001.

6. Caveat on verification. WebFetch failed (DNS), and the proxy blocked arXiv, doi.org, MDPI, PMC and publisher hosts. Every "verified" item was confirmed from search-engine abstracts, snippets or secondary summaries, not full texts. Before any priority claim, read the full texts of Frank 2016, Frank 2019, Harte 2011 ch. 7, and Gabaix 1999 (for the s_min formula).

rows.system: US firms (about 5.5 million US tax-paying firms, 1997 Census data)
rows.zeta_estimate: Employees: zeta = 1.059, a survival (Pareto) exponent from Axtell, so density alpha = 2.059. Receipts: zeta about 0.99 (secondary source). A later binned MLE on 2011 SBA data gives zeta = 1.0967 +/- 0.0020 (MPRA Paper 78985, as quoted). Axtell's own SE (about 0.05 from memory) was not verified.
rows.dynamics_class: Proportional (Gibrat) growth with entry and exit
rows.citation: Axtell, R. L. (2001) Zipf distribution of U.S. firm sizes. Science 293(5536):1818-1820, doi:10.1126/science.1062081. 1.059 confirmed via arXiv cond-mat/0401053; receipts 0.99 via arXiv 0704.2955; 2011 value via https://mpra.ub.uni-muenchen.de/78985/1/MPRA_paper_78985.pdf
rows.known_constraint_explaining_deviation: Small deviation. Size measures are not linearly related to each other (employees, receipts, assets), so at most one of them can have zeta exactly 1. The SBA binned data are top-coded.

rows.system: European firms (France, UK, Italy, Spain; Bureau van Dijk-type database)
rows.zeta_estimate: Pareto index mu = zeta: 0.886 +/- 0.005 (total assets, France); 0.896 +/- 0.011 (sales, France); 0.995 +/- 0.013 (employees, UK), 99% errors. The authors describe the index as 'close to unity in all the countries'.
rows.dynamics_class: Proportional growth (Gibrat's law holds in the upper tail)
rows.citation: Fujiwara, Y., Di Guilmi, C., Aoyama, H., Gallegati, M., Souma, W. (2004) Do Pareto-Zipf and Gibrat laws hold true? An analysis with European firms. Physica A 335:197-216; arXiv cond-mat/0310061
rows.known_constraint_explaining_deviation: Financial size measures sit slightly below 1 (top-heavy), possibly because of the finite sample or upper truncation of the database; headcount is closer to 1.

rows.system: US metropolitan areas (135 MSAs, 1991 Statistical Abstract)
rows.zeta_estimate: Rank-size OLS gives ln Rank = 10.53 - 1.005 ln Size, so zeta = 1.005 (naive SE 0.010, R^2 = 0.986). Gabaix's Monte Carlo shows OLS understates zeta by about 0.05 and that the true SE is about 0.1.
rows.dynamics_class: Proportional growth with a lower reflecting barrier (Gabaix model)
rows.citation: Gabaix, X. (1999) Zipf's law for cities: an explanation. Quarterly Journal of Economics 114(3):739-767. https://scholar.harvard.edu/sites/scholar.harvard.edu/files/xgabaix/files/zipfs_law.pdf
rows.known_constraint_explaining_deviation: Agrees with zeta = 1 within error for the top 135 metro areas only. The theory needs s_min/mean -> 0, which Blank & Solomon (2000) argued is incompatible with a finite number of units (as reported by Malevergne et al. 2013).

rows.system: Cities in 73 countries; meta-analyses of city Zipf exponents
rows.zeta_estimate: Soo 2005: Zipf (zeta = 1) rejected for 53/73 countries by OLS and 30/73 by Hill. OLS estimates are roughly normal; Hill estimates are bimodal. OLS is significantly above 1 in 39 countries and below 1 in 14. Mean about 1.11 (from a secondary thesis; not checked in Soo). Urban agglomerations: zeta significantly below 1 by OLS. Nitsch 2005 meta-analysis (515 estimates, 29 studies): combined estimate significantly above 1 (point value about 1.1 not verified). Cottineau 2017 (1,962 estimates, 86 studies): about 40% of variance comes from technical choices.
rows.dynamics_class: Proportional growth plus political and economic constraints
rows.citation: Soo, K. T. (2005) Regional Science and Urban Economics 35(3):239-263; Nitsch, V. (2005) Zipf zipped. Journal of Urban Economics 57(1):86-100; Cottineau, C. (2017) MetaZipf. PLoS ONE 12(8):e0183919
rows.known_constraint_explaining_deviation: City definition (administrative vs agglomeration), truncation point and estimator. Soo found that political-economy variables (primacy) explain cross-country variation better than economic geography.

rows.system: US administrative places, upper tail (2000 Census)
rows.zeta_estimate: Clauset et al. 2009: alpha = 2.37 +/- 0.08, so zeta = 1.37 (p = 0.76, moderate support). Newman 2005: alpha = 2.30(5), xmin = 40,000, so zeta = 1.30. Malevergne, Pisarenko & Sornette: top ~1000 cities zeta = 1.4 +/- 0.1, and zeta = 1 is rejected. Eeckhout 2004: the untruncated distribution is lognormal.
rows.dynamics_class: Proportional growth (Gibrat holds for all sizes per Eeckhout) with administrative fragmentation
rows.citation: Clauset, Shalizi & Newman (2009) SIAM Review 51(4):661-703 (value via Aschwanden & Scholkmann 2025, arXiv 2505.00748); Newman (2005) Contemporary Physics 46(5):323-351, arXiv cond-mat/0412004; Malevergne, Pisarenko & Sornette, arXiv 0909.1281; Eeckhout (2004) AER 94(5):1429-1451; Levy (2009) AER 99(4):1672-1675
rows.known_constraint_explaining_deviation: Legal boundaries split agglomerations into places, which steepens the tail. The result depends on the truncation point (Fazio & Modica, J. Regional Science 55(5):736-756), and the lognormal body hides any single exponent.

rows.system: 'Natural' cities by City Clustering Algorithm (USA, Great Britain)
rows.zeta_estimate: zeta close to 1 (Zipf) for population, down to about 12,000 inhabitants (US) and 5,000 (GB). City areas are also power-law distributed with exponent close to 1. Numerical CIs were not retrieved.
rows.dynamics_class: Proportional growth of contiguous settlements (percolation-like clustering)
rows.citation: Rozenfeld, H. D., Rybski, D., Gabaix, X., Makse, H. A. (2011) The area and population of cities. American Economic Review 101(5):2205-2225; arXiv 1001.5289
rows.known_constraint_explaining_deviation: None claimed. Compare the administrative-city row: the exponent depends on how the object is defined.

rows.system: Word frequencies (Moby Dick; large English corpora)
rows.extensive_variable: Token occurrences per word type (sums to text length)
rows.zeta_estimate: Clauset 2009 (Moby Dick): alpha = 1.95(2) at xmin = 7, so zeta = 0.95. Newman 2005: alpha = 2.20(1) at xmin = 1, so zeta = 1.20. Rank exponent about 1. Moreno-Sanchez et al. 2016 (31,075 Gutenberg texts): a pure power law fits more than 40% of texts over the full range (beta values not retrieved).
rows.dynamics_class: Proportional reuse with innovation (Simon/Yule-type preferential process)
rows.citation: Clauset et al. 2009 (value confirmed via poweRlaw docs, https://search.r-project.org/CRAN/refmans/poweRlaw/html/moby.html); Newman 2005; Moreno-Sanchez, Font-Clos & Corral (2016) PLoS ONE 11(1):e0147073
rows.known_constraint_explaining_deviation: Strong xmin dependence (0.95 vs 1.20). In Simon's model the innovation rate pushes zeta above 1 (from memory, not verified).

rows.system: US family names
rows.zeta_estimate: Newman 2005: alpha = 1.94(1), xmin = 10,000, so zeta = 0.94. Clauset 2009: alpha = 2.5(2) (xmin about 111,920), so zeta = 1.5 (from memory, not verified).
rows.dynamics_class: Multiplicative (patrilineal) inheritance with drift and immigration
rows.citation: Newman (2005) Contemporary Physics 46:323-351, Table I; Clauset et al. (2009)
rows.known_constraint_explaining_deviation: Large xmin and estimator dependence. Aschwanden & Scholkmann (2025) flag finite-size effects for names.

rows.system: Personal wealth, top tail (Forbes 400 US; rich lists)
rows.zeta_estimate: Klass et al. 2006 (Forbes 400, 1988-2003): average Pareto exponent 1.49. Levy & Solomon 1997 (1996 list): 1.36. Newman 2005: alpha = 2.09(4), xmin = $600m, so zeta = 1.09. Clauset 2009: power law rejected (p = 0.00; alpha = 2.3, so zeta = 1.3, from memory). Brzezinski 2014: power law consistent with only 35% of rich-list datasets; a CEPR paper finds top wealth fits Weibull better than Pareto.
rows.dynamics_class: Multiplicative investment returns (Kesten-type) with consumption and inheritance
rows.citation: Klass, Biham, Levy, Malcai & Solomon (2006) Economics Letters 90(2):290-295; Newman 2005; Clauset et al. 2009; Brzezinski, arXiv 1304.0212; CEPR DP18634 'Top Wealth Is Distributed Weibull, Not Pareto'
rows.known_constraint_explaining_deviation: Only 400 names; measurement error; taxation, consumption, estate splitting. Estimates range from 1.09 to 1.49 depending on estimator and year.

rows.system: Personal income, top tail (US tax data; France)
rows.zeta_estimate: US AGI (Feenberg & Poterba, as summarized): zeta = 1.83 (1951), 2.46 (1970), 1.59 (1990). France (WID top shares): about 1.5 prewar, about 2 postwar. Pareto's original range: 1.3-1.7. All above 1.
rows.citation: Feenberg & Poterba values as reported in arXiv 2206.04257 (Capital and Labor Income Pareto Exponents in the United States, 1916-2019); Toda & Wang, arXiv 1901.02471; Atkinson, Piketty & Saez (2011) JEL 49(1):3-71 (values not retrieved)
rows.known_constraint_explaining_deviation: Income is a flux, not a stock. Labor income is bounded by human capacity; progressive taxation and the regulatory regime shift zeta over time by about 1.

rows.system: US mutual funds
rows.zeta_estimate: No power-law tail. The upper tail is 'much better described by a log-normal than a power law', consistently over 15 years, so zeta = 1 is rejected (less concentrated than Zipf).
rows.dynamics_class: Random (Gibrat-like) growth with entry and exit, plus size-dependent drift and diffusion
rows.citation: Schwarzkopf, Y. & Farmer, J. D. (2010) An empirical study of the tails of mutual fund size. Physical Review E 81:066113, arXiv 1005.4976; companion: What drives mutual fund asset concentration?, arXiv 0807.3800
rows.known_constraint_explaining_deviation: Relaxation to the steady-state power law is 'extremely slow', so finite industry age keeps the distribution lognormal. Diffusion and drift decline with size. This is a direct counterexample in the proportional-growth class.

rows.system: Global ocean organisms, bacteria to whales (pre-industrial reconstruction)
rows.zeta_estimate: Abundance per log size slope -1.04 (95% CI -1.05 to -1.02), upper ~200 m (bioRxiv preprint), so zeta = 1.04 [1.02, 1.05]. Repo re-expression: d ln(biomass per log bin)/d ln m = -0.039 (90% interval -0.058 to -0.026), so zeta = 1.039 [1.026, 1.058]. About 1 Gt per decade for most classes; bacteria above, large mammals below.
rows.dynamics_class: Size-structured predation and trophic transfer with growth (energy-flow cascade)
rows.citation: Hatton, Heneghan, Bar-On & Galbraith (2021) The global ocean size spectrum from bacteria to whales. Science Advances 7(46):eabh3732; preprint bioRxiv 10.1101/2021.04.03.438320; repo results/independent.json (ocean_top200)
rows.known_constraint_explaining_deviation: Trophic theory gives biomass per log mass proportional to m^(log TE / log PPMR), so zeta = 1 - log TE/log PPMR (my rearrangement). TE = 0.1 and PPMR = 10^4 give 1.25. The observed 1.04 implies higher efficiency or subsidies. Whaling truncates the top. This is a model-assisted reconstruction, not a census.

rows.system: Aquatic size spectra, many studies (GLOSSAQUA normalized-biomass subset; repo analysis)
rows.zeta_estimate: Median NBSS slope -1.015 over 1,300 slopes from 16 studies, so zeta = 1 - slope - 1 + 1 = 1.015 (density alpha = 1 - NBSS slope). Study-block 95% CI for the slope [-1.100, -0.990] gives zeta in [0.99, 1.10]. Pooling all method labels gives a median of -1.371 (mixed conventions; flagged).
rows.citation: Repo results/independent.json (glossaqua.subsets.primary_NBSS); Sheldon, Prakash & Sutcliffe (1972) L&O 17:327-340 (from repo references); Trebilco et al. (2013) TREE 28(7):423-431
rows.known_constraint_explaining_deviation: Individual spectra are widely dispersed (e.g., Arranz lakes SD about 0.28). Conventions are mixed across studies, two studies contribute 78% of the slopes, and some range metadata are invalid. Transfer efficiency, PPMR and fishing all shift slopes.

rows.system: Trees in forest stands (worldwide plots; tropical ForestGEO plots)
rows.zeta_estimate: Enquist & Niklas: abundance proportional to D^-2. With M proportional to D^(8/3), the mass density is proportional to M^(-11/8) (stated by a 2008 Ecology Letters paper, as quoted), so zeta_mass = 0.375 (top-heavy). Muller-Landau et al. 2006 (14 plots, 473 ha, >2 million trees): data 'uniformly inconsistent' with the metabolic prediction. White et al. 2008: diameter exponents cluster near -2.
rows.dynamics_class: Demographic growth-mortality equilibrium with competition for light and space
rows.citation: Enquist, B. J. & Niklas, K. J. (2001) Nature 410:655-660, doi:10.1038/35070500; Muller-Landau et al. (2006) Ecology Letters 9:589-602
rows.known_constraint_explaining_deviation: Size-dependent growth and mortality plus asymmetric light competition. Biomass is concentrated in the largest trees, and maximum tree size gives an upper cutoff. Under energetic equivalence, metabolism per linear diameter bin is constant, not per log bin (my derivation).

rows.system: Stellar initial mass function (Galactic field and clusters)
rows.zeta_estimate: Salpeter 1955: alpha = 2.35 for 0.4-10 Msun, so zeta = 1.35. Kroupa 2001: alpha = 2.3 +/- 0.3 (0.5-1 Msun) and 2.3 +/- 0.7 (>1 Msun), so zeta = 1.3; alpha = 1.3 +/- 0.5 (0.08-0.5 Msun), so zeta = 0.3; alpha = 0.3 +/- 0.7 (brown dwarfs), so zeta about -0.7.
rows.citation: Salpeter, E. E. (1955) ApJ 121:161; Kroupa, P. (2001) On the variation of the initial mass function. MNRAS 322:231-246, arXiv astro-ph/0009005
rows.known_constraint_explaining_deviation: The thermal Jeans mass sets a turnover near about 0.2-0.5 Msun, so mass per log interval peaks there: bottom-heavy above (zeta = 1.3), top-heavy below. Not zeta = 1 on either side.

rows.system: Galaxy stellar mass function, z < 0.06 (GAMA)
rows.zeta_estimate: Double Schechter fit: alpha2 = -1.47 (low-mass term), alpha1 = -0.35, M* = 10^10.66 Msun. Below M*, the number density per linear mass is proportional to M^-1.47, so zeta = 0.47 over about 10^8-10^10 Msun, with an exponential cutoff above M*. Wright et al. 2017: alpha2 = -1.50 +/- 0.01 +/- 0.15, so zeta about 0.50.
rows.dynamics_class: Hierarchical merging with feedback-regulated star formation (accretion)
rows.citation: Baldry, I. K. et al. (2012) GAMA: the galaxy stellar mass function at z < 0.06. MNRAS 421:621-634, arXiv 1111.5707; Wright, A. H. et al. (2017), arXiv 1705.04074
rows.known_constraint_explaining_deviation: Supernova and AGN feedback make star-formation efficiency depend on halo mass. This is a top-heavy allocation (most stellar mass near M*) held in place by an exponential cutoff.

rows.system: Dark-matter subhalos in a Milky-Way-mass halo (Aquarius N-body simulations; simulation, not observation)
rows.zeta_estimate: dN/dM proportional to M^-1.9, so zeta = 0.9 over many decades. The field-halo mass function approaches slope -2 at small masses (Press-Schechter type), so zeta approaches 1.
rows.dynamics_class: Hierarchical gravitational aggregation with mass conservation, plus tidal stripping
rows.citation: Springel, V. et al. (2008) The Aquarius Project: the subhaloes of galactic haloes. MNRAS 391:1685, arXiv 0809.0898; low-mass -2 limit per arXiv 0705.1599
rows.known_constraint_explaining_deviation: The effective spectral index of the CDM power spectrum (n_eff > -3) makes the slope slightly shallower than -2 (Press-Schechter scaling; from memory). Tidal stripping removes mass from subhalos.

rows.system: Global lakes
rows.zeta_estimate: Corrected: tau = 2.14 (density) above 0.46 km^2, so zeta = 1.14. The original, retracted subset analysis gave tau = 1.97 above 8.5 km^2. The percolation prediction tau = 187/91 = 2.055 gives zeta = 96/91 = 1.055. A later review puts the lower limit of the power law anywhere from 0.001 to 1 km^2.
rows.citation: Cael, B. B. & Seekell, D. A. (2016) The size-distribution of Earth's lakes. Scientific Reports 6:29633 (PMC4937396), Corrigendum 2017 (PMC5304202); Cael, Biggs & Seekell (2022) Frontiers in Environmental Science 10:888735
rows.known_constraint_explaining_deviation: Percolation-hull geometry predicts zeta of about 1.055, not 1. The observed 1.14 is slightly bottom-heavy.

rows.system: Islands (Korcak law)
rows.zeta_estimate: N(A > a) proportional to a^-B, with B about 0.65 on average (from about 0.5 for African islands to about 0.75 for Indonesian islands), so zeta about 0.5-0.75. A recent 131,063-island compilation exists, but its exponent was not retrieved.
rows.dynamics_class: Level set of self-affine topography (geometric, percolation-like)
rows.citation: Korcak, J. (1938); Mandelbrot, B. (1982) The Fractal Geometry of Nature (values as quoted in arXiv 1303.1610); Self-Affine Scaling of Earth's Islands, arXiv 2512.16659
rows.known_constraint_explaining_deviation: Mandelbrot links B to half the coastline fractal dimension (disputed). Area is dominated by the largest landmasses (top-heavy), with continents as the cutoff.

rows.system: River networks (North American basins)
rows.extensive_variable: Total contributing drainage area at each network link
rows.zeta_estimate: P(A >= a) proportional to a^-beta, with beta about 0.43-0.45 (0.45 in the 1992 abstract; about 0.43 per La Barbera 1994), so tau about 1.43-1.45. Energy dissipation: beta about 0.90.
rows.citation: Rodriguez-Iturbe, I., Ijjasz-Vasquez, E., Bras, R. L., Tarboton, D. G. (1992) Power law distributions of discharge mass and energy in river basins. Water Resources Research 28(4), doi:10.1029/91WR03033; Maritan et al. (1996) arXiv cond-mat/9610004
rows.known_constraint_explaining_deviation: Not additive across objects: drainage areas are nested, so each point is counted at every downstream link. This should not be read as a resource allocation. An EGU 2023 abstract reports independent basin-area exponents of 1.2-2.5 (convention unclear).

rows.system: Hydrocarbon (oil and gas) field sizes
rows.zeta_estimate: Not established. Barton (1994) reports 'fractal dimension' D = 2.43-2.98 in N(V) = aV^-D. If D refers to linear size, zeta_V = D/3 = 0.81-0.99; taken literally, zeta = 2.4-3.0 (conversion ambiguous; my inference). Gulf of Mexico reserves are better fit by a stretched exponential (c about 0.35). Pareto and truncated Pareto are rejected for four Russian provinces (2020).
rows.dynamics_class: Geological accumulation (trap filling, migration), sampled under economic truncation
rows.citation: Barton/Scholz abstracts (AAPG Search and Discovery 1991, 1994); Laherrere, J. & Sornette, D. (1998) Stretched exponential distributions in nature and economy, arXiv cond-mat/9801293; Izvestiya TPU 331(6) (2020)
rows.known_constraint_explaining_deviation: Discovery is incomplete for small fields, field definitions are ambiguous, and economic truncation applies. The functional form itself is disputed.

rows.system: Gene/protein family sizes in complete genomes
rows.zeta_estimate: Density exponents of about 2-4 in Huynen & van Nimwegen (bacteria, archaea, yeast, viruses), so zeta = 1-3; later studies give 2-3, so zeta = 1-2. Distributions become flatter (zeta falls toward 1) as gene number increases.
rows.citation: Huynen, M. A. & van Nimwegen, E. (1998) The frequency distribution of gene family sizes in complete genomes. Molecular Biology and Evolution 15(5):583-589; range as reviewed in arXiv 1102.2331
rows.known_constraint_explaining_deviation: The exponent depends on the mean and variance of the log multiplication factor and on genome size, so it is not fixed at 1. Family definitions depend on the clustering threshold.

rows.system: Citations to scientific papers (ISI 1981; Physical Review)
rows.zeta_estimate: Redner 1998: N(x) proportional to x^-3, so zeta about 2 (Zipf slope about -1/2). Clauset 2009: alpha = 3.16 +/- 0.06, so zeta = 2.16. Golosovsky & Solomon 2012 (418,438 papers): gamma = 3.15, so zeta = 2.15, with an upward 'runaway' extreme tail.
rows.citation: Redner, S. (1998) EPJ B 4:131-134, arXiv cond-mat/9804163; Clauset et al. 2009 (value via search of arXiv 0706.1062); Golosovsky & Solomon (2012), arXiv 1206.1999
rows.known_constraint_explaining_deviation: FLAG: an in-degree (count of distinct citing papers), not a conserved resource held by the paper. Obsolescence and aging limit preferential growth, which gives zeta about 2.

rows.system: Web sites, users per site (AOL, December 1997)
rows.extensive_variable: Unique visitors (hits) per site per day
rows.zeta_estimate: Adamic & Huberman 2002: tau = 2.07 (binned density), so zeta = 1.07 (rank exponent about 1). Newman 2005: hits alpha = 2.40(1) at xmin = 1, so zeta = 1.40. Clauset 2009: power law rejected for web hits (alpha = 1.81 at xmin = 2, so zeta = 0.81; from memory, not verified).
rows.citation: Adamic, L. A. & Huberman, B. A. (2002) Zipf's law and the Internet. Glottometrics 3:143-150; Newman 2005; Clauset et al. 2009
rows.known_constraint_explaining_deviation: A one-day window (flux); the estimate depends on xmin and binning (0.81-1.40 across analyses of the same data).

rows.system: Web hyperlinks (1997 crawl, about 200 million pages)
rows.zeta_estimate: Clauset 2009: alpha about 2.336(9), so zeta about 1.34 (extracted table columns were misaligned, so tentative). Power law rejected (p = 0.00).
rows.citation: Clauset, Shalizi & Newman (2009) SIAM Review 51(4):661-703, arXiv 0706.1062
rows.known_constraint_explaining_deviation: FLAG: a degree, not a resource. A pure power law is statistically rejected.

rows.system: Biological network degrees (yeast protein interactions; E. coli metabolism)
rows.zeta_estimate: Protein interaction: alpha = 3.1 +/- 0.3, so zeta = 2.1 (Clauset 2009, contrasted with a previously reported 2.44). Metabolic: alpha = 2.80 +/- 0.10, so zeta = 1.8 (Clauset value as listed by Aschwanden & Scholkmann 2025; metabolic power law rejected in Clauset per memory).
rows.citation: Clauset et al. (2009) SIAM Review 51:661-703; Aschwanden & Scholkmann (2025) arXiv 2505.00748
rows.known_constraint_explaining_deviation: FLAG: degrees count distinct partners, not an additive held resource. No reason to expect zeta = 1.

rows.system: Communication network degrees (telephone calls received; Internet AS graph May 2006; email address books)
rows.extensive_variable: Calls received / AS degree / address-book size
rows.zeta_estimate: Telephone calls: Newman 2005 alpha = 2.22(1) at xmin = 10, so zeta = 1.22 (verified). Internet AS degree: Clauset alpha = 2.12(9), so zeta = 1.12 (not verified). Email address books: alpha = 3.5(6), so zeta = 2.5 (not verified).
rows.citation: Newman (2005) Contemporary Physics 46:323-351; Clauset et al. (2009)
rows.known_constraint_explaining_deviation: FLAG: degree and count variables. Address-book size is bounded by human capacity.

rows.system: Mammal species per genus
rows.zeta_estimate: Clauset 2009: alpha = 2.4(2), xmin = 4, so zeta = 1.4 (from memory, not verified).
rows.citation: Clauset et al. (2009) SIAM Review 51:661-703 (dataset confirmed: number of species per genus of mammals)
rows.known_constraint_explaining_deviation: FLAG: a count of distinct taxa that depends on taxonomic convention, not a resource. Yule-process exponents depend on the ratio of speciation to genus-origination rates.

rows.system: US bestselling books (1895-1965)
rows.zeta_estimate: Newman 2005: alpha = 3.51(16), xmin = 2,000,000, so zeta = 2.51. Clauset 2009: alpha = 3.7(3), so zeta = 2.7 (not verified).
rows.citation: Newman (2005) Table I; Clauset et al. (2009)
rows.known_constraint_explaining_deviation: Only bestsellers are sampled (top-selected), and sales are a flux over a period. The tail is far from 1.

rows.system: Papers authored per mathematician (MathSciNet)
rows.zeta_estimate: Clauset 2009: alpha = 4.3(1), xmin = 133, so zeta = 3.3 (from memory, not verified).
rows.citation: Clauset et al. (2009) (dataset confirmed: MathSciNet records compiled by J. Grossman)
rows.known_constraint_explaining_deviation: FLAG: a count of outputs, bounded by human lifetime and capacity, which steepens the tail.

rows.system: Religious followers
rows.zeta_estimate: Clauset 2009: alpha = 1.8(1), xmin = 3.85 million, so zeta = 0.8 (from memory, not verified).
rows.citation: Clauset et al. (2009) SIAM Review 51:661-703
rows.known_constraint_explaining_deviation: Very small tail sample; definitions of a religion vary.

rows.system: Bird species sightings (North American Breeding Bird Survey 2003)
rows.zeta_estimate: Clauset 2009: alpha = 2.1(2), xmin = 6,679, so zeta = 1.1 (from memory, not verified).
rows.citation: Clauset et al. (2009) (dataset confirmed in the paper's description)
rows.known_constraint_explaining_deviation: Only the extreme tail fits. Species abundance distributions are usually lognormal or log-series in the body.

rows.system: Earthquakes, rupture area (global; re-expressed from b and Kagan's beta)
rows.extensive_variable: Rupture area A (assuming self-similar M0 proportional to A^(3/2))
rows.zeta_estimate: zeta_A = b. Repo USGS 2010-2024, Mw >= 5.5: b = 0.998 [0.973, 1.024], so zeta_A = 1.00. From Kagan's moment exponent: zeta_A = 1.5 beta = 0.90-0.98 for beta = 0.60-0.65. Mid-ocean ridges (beta = 0.93) give zeta_A about 1.4.
rows.dynamics_class: SOC / branching rupture cascade on fault networks
rows.citation: Repo results/results.json (usgs); Kagan, Y. Y. (2002) Seismic moment distribution revisited I. GJI 148(3):520-541; Kagan (1997) JGR (regional beta, MOR beta = 0.93), as quoted; Schorlemmer, Wiemer & Wyss (2005) Nature 437:539-542, doi:10.1038/nature04094
rows.known_constraint_explaining_deviation: b depends on differential stress and faulting style: normal > strike-slip > thrust (Schorlemmer 2005). For Italy, reverse 0.75-0.81, normal 1.09, strike-slip 0.90-0.92 (Gulia & Wiemer 2010, as quoted). zeta_A = b holds only if M0 is proportional to A^(3/2), which breaks for large strike-slip ruptures. Choosing A as the 'resource' is post hoc.

rows.system: Earthquakes, seismic moment / radiated energy (global CMT; California)
rows.extensive_variable: Scalar seismic moment M0 (approximately proportional to radiated energy)
rows.zeta_estimate: zeta_M0 = beta = 0.60-0.65 (Kagan 2002, 'universal' for moderate events); 0.60 +/- 0.02 (Kagan 1999, declustered shallow); about 0.68 (CMT 1977-2008 slope, arXiv 0908.1207). Corner moment about 10^21 N m (mc about 8.0). Clauset 2009, California 1910-1992 maximum-amplitude 'intensity': alpha = 1.64 +/- 0.04, so zeta_amp = 0.64, power law rejected. Newman's alpha = 3.04(4) fits magnitude itself (a log variable), which is not interpretable as a resource.
rows.citation: Kagan (2002) GJI 148:520-541; Kagan (1999) Pure and Applied Geophysics (beta = 0.60 +/- 0.02), as quoted; Kagan, Earthquake size distribution: power-law with exponent beta = 1/2?, arXiv 0908.1207; Clauset et al. 2009 via arXiv 2505.00748
rows.known_constraint_explaining_deviation: Energy fails O_log (top-heavy). The total is dominated by the largest events and capped by a corner moment (tapered Gutenberg-Richter). Kagan argues theoretically for beta = 1/2.

rows.system: Solar flares, soft X-ray (GOES 1976-2000, about 50,000 flares; repo GOES 2022-2024)
rows.extensive_variable: Band-limited SXR fluence (energy per area, 1-8 Angstrom)
rows.zeta_estimate: Veronig et al. 2002: fluence alpha = 2.03 +/- 0.09, so zeta = 1.03; peak flux alpha = 2.11 +/- 0.13, so 1.11; duration 2.93. Reproduced by a 2006 refit: 2.01 (fluence), 2.16 (peak). Repo MLE on end fluence: alpha about 2.00-2.22 raw and 1.81-2.05 background-subtracted, so zeta about 0.8-1.2 (task context; not re-verified here).
rows.citation: Veronig, A., Temmer, M., Hanslmeier, A., Otruba, W., Messerotti, M. (2002) Temporal aspects and frequency distributions of solar soft X-ray flares. A&A 382:1070-1080, arXiv astro-ph/0207234
rows.known_constraint_explaining_deviation: Fluence in a narrow band is not total energy, and the band captures a temperature-dependent fraction. Background subtraction and catalogue thresholds shift alpha by about 0.2.

rows.system: Solar flares, hard X-ray (SMM/HXRBS, >12,000 flares)
rows.extensive_variable: Nonthermal electron energy (>25 keV); peak count rate
rows.zeta_estimate: Crosby et al. 1993: electron energy alpha = 1.53 +/- 0.02 (also 1.51 and 1.48 in other fits), so zeta about 0.5. Peak count rate about 1.73, so 0.73. Clauset 2009 (peak intensity, 1980-1989): alpha = 1.79 +/- 0.02, so zeta = 0.79 (power law with cutoff). Newman: 1.83(2), so 0.83. Fractal-diffusive SOC theory: alpha_E = 1.67 (zeta = 2/3), alpha_flux = 1.8 (zeta = 0.8).
rows.citation: Crosby, N. B., Aschwanden, M. J., Dennis, B. R. (1993) Solar Physics 143:275, doi:10.1007/BF00646488 (values via a 2022 comparison table, arXiv 2212.02678); Aschwanden & Scholkmann (2025) arXiv 2505.00748; Newman 2005; Clauset 2009
rows.known_constraint_explaining_deviation: Nonthermal energy depends on the assumed low-energy cutoff and the instrument threshold. SOC geometry predicts zeta = 2/3, not 1. Hudson (1991) noted that alpha < 2 means large flares dominate the energy budget.

rows.system: Stellar superflares on solar-type stars (Kepler)
rows.zeta_estimate: Shibayama et al. 2013 (1,547 flares on 279 G dwarfs, 500 days): alpha about 2, so zeta about 1. Wu et al. 2015 (4,944 flares, 77 stars): 2.04 +/- 0.17, so 1.04. Maehara et al., 1-min cadence: 1.5 +/- 0.1 for 4x10^33 to 1x10^36 erg, so zeta = 0.5. Solar flares 10^24 to 10^32 erg: alpha = 1.5-1.9, so zeta = 0.5-0.9.
rows.citation: Shibayama, T. et al. (2013) ApJS 209:5, doi:10.1088/0067-0049/209/1/5, arXiv 1308.1480; Maehara et al., arXiv 1504.00074; Wu et al. (2015) as quoted in arXiv 2212.10224
rows.known_constraint_explaining_deviation: Detection completeness depends on cadence (30-min vs 1-min), which moves alpha from 2 to 1.5. Pooling many stars mixes different distributions.

rows.system: Near-Earth-object impacts (satellite bolide detections, about 8.5 years); asteroid collisional cascade
rows.extensive_variable: Impact energy (approximately proportional to impactor mass); asteroid mass
rows.zeta_estimate: Brown et al. 2002: N(>E) = 3.7 E^-0.90 per year (E in kt, 0.1-10 kt, 300 events), so zeta_E = 0.90 (exponent via a secondary review). Dohnanyi 1969 equilibrium: dN proportional to m^(-11/6) dm, so zeta_m = 5/6 = 0.833 (cumulative D^-2.5).
rows.citation: Brown, P., Spalding, R. E., ReVelle, D. O., Tagliaferri, E., Worden, S. P. (2002) The flux of small near-Earth objects colliding with the Earth. Nature 420:294-296, doi:10.1038/nature01238; Dohnanyi, J. S. (1969) JGR 74:2531-2554
rows.known_constraint_explaining_deviation: Steady cascade mass flux gives 5/6, not 1. Size-dependent strength changes the slope (p = (7 + s/3)/(2 + s/3)), a small-size cutoff produces waves, and dynamical delivery affects NEOs. Velocity spread separates energy from mass.

rows.system: Rock fragmentation (crushers, impacts, comminution)
rows.zeta_estimate: Fragment-number dimension D (N(>r) proportional to r^-D): jaw crushers 2.18-2.32, cone 2.12-2.27, roll 2.30-2.43; granite about 1.95, quartz 2.09. With m proportional to r^3, zeta_m = D/3, about 0.65-0.81 (conversion assumes cumulative N; Turcotte notes the convention is not always stated). zeta = 1 would require D = 3.
rows.citation: Turcotte, D. L. (1986) Fractals and fragmentation. JGR 91(B2):1921, doi:10.1029/JB091iB02p01921; crusher D ranges as quoted from comminution studies (e.g., MATEC Web Conf. 25:02008, 2015)
rows.known_constraint_explaining_deviation: Mass conservation in breakup does not select D = 3. D measures fragility and the breakage mechanism. Most mass sits in large fragments (zeta < 1).

rows.system: Wildfires (USA, Australia)
rows.zeta_estimate: Malamud et al. 1998: density alpha about 1.3-1.5, so zeta = 0.3-0.5. Malamud et al. 2005 (88,916 fires, 18 ecoregions, 1970-2000): alpha = 1.3-1.75, so zeta = 0.3-0.75, with an east-west gradient. Clauset 2009 (US federal land 1986-1996, xmin about 6,324 acres): alpha = 2.2 +/- 0.3, so zeta = 1.2 (p about 0.05; cutoff preferred). Corral & Gonzalez 2019: truncated lognormal fits better; Hantson 2016: neither PL nor LN.
rows.dynamics_class: SOC-like / percolation of fuel driven by weather
rows.citation: Malamud, Morein & Turcotte (1998) Science 281:1840-1842; Malamud, Millington & Perry (2005) PNAS 102(13):4694-4699; Clauset et al. 2009 via arXiv 2505.00748; Corral & Gonzalez (2019) Earth and Space Science 6:673-697, doi:10.1029/2018EA000479
rows.known_constraint_explaining_deviation: Very strong xmin dependence (0.3 to 1.2). Fire suppression, landscape fragmentation, finite region size and scale-invariant weather (Boer et al. 2005) all matter.

rows.system: Landslides (event inventories: Italy, Guatemala, USA)
rows.zeta_estimate: Inverse-gamma fit with power tail exponent 2.40, so zeta = 1.40, and an exponential rollover at small areas. Central Italy: 2.5, so 1.5. Other inventory subsets: 2.2-3.3, so zeta = 1.2-2.3.
rows.citation: Malamud, B. D., Turcotte, D. L., Guzzetti, F., Reichenbach, P. (2004) Landslide inventories and their statistical properties. Earth Surface Processes and Landforms 29(6):687-711, doi:10.1002/esp.1064
rows.known_constraint_explaining_deviation: Hillslope length and cohesion limit large failures. Most area is in medium slides (bottom-heavy, zeta > 1). Inventory mapping resolution affects the tail.

rows.system: Tropical cyclones (4 ocean basins)
rows.extensive_variable: Power dissipation index per storm (integral of v^3 dt; energy-like)
rows.zeta_estimate: Density alpha = 1.19, 1.17, 0.98, 1.11 (+/- 0.07); overall range 0.95-1.25; NW Pacific about 0.96. With an upper cutoff, zeta is about 0-0.25 in the scaling range. The authors note that alpha = 1 means equal numbers per decade, so dissipated energy is concentrated in the largest storms.
rows.dynamics_class: Critical phenomenon / SOC-like (convective quasi-equilibrium) with a basin-size cutoff
rows.citation: Corral, A., Osso, A., Llebot, J. E. (2010) Scaling of tropical-cyclone dissipation. Nature Physics 6:693-696, doi:10.1038/nphys1725, arXiv 0910.0054
rows.known_constraint_explaining_deviation: Finite basin size and storm lifetime give a sharp upper cutoff, which allows zeta near 0. This is a strong counterexample to zeta = 1 for an energy-like event quantity.

rows.system: Rain events (precipitation)
rows.zeta_estimate: Baltic coast (Peters, Hertlein & Christensen 2002): alpha about 1.35-1.4, so zeta about 0.35-0.4. Multi-climate study (Peters et al. 2010): tau_s = 1.17(3), so zeta = 0.17. Corral & Gonzalez 2019: a truncated power-law regime.
rows.citation: Peters, O., Hertlein, C., Christensen, K. (2002) A complexity view of rainfall. PRL 88:018701, arXiv cond-mat/0201468; Peters et al. (2010) Universality of rain event size distributions, arXiv 1010.4201
rows.known_constraint_explaining_deviation: Moisture supply and storm size give an upper cutoff, so most rain falls in the largest events. Detection thresholds and time resolution shift the exponent.

rows.system: Neuronal avalanches (cortical slices and cultures, 60-electrode arrays)
rows.extensive_variable: Avalanche size (number of electrodes above threshold; LFP)
rows.zeta_estimate: alpha about 1.5 (-3/2), so zeta = 0.5, with a finite-array cutoff above about 35 electrodes. Spike-based avalanches: about 2.1, so 1.1.
rows.citation: Beggs, J. M. & Plenz, D. (2003) Neuronal avalanches in neocortical circuits. J. Neuroscience 23(35):11167-11177, doi:10.1523/JNEUROSCI.23-35-11167.2003 (values via arXiv cond-mat/0402538 and secondary sources)
rows.known_constraint_explaining_deviation: FLAG: size counts active sites, not a conserved resource. Branching-process criticality predicts zeta = 1/2, not 1.

rows.system: Interstate wars (Correlates of War, 1823-2003)
rows.zeta_estimate: Clauset 2018: alpha = 1.53 +/- 0.07 for x >= 7,061 (51 of 95 wars; p = 0.78), so zeta = 0.53. Clauset 2009 (intensity per 10,000 population, 1816-1980): 1.7 +/- 0.2, so 0.7. Newman 2005: 1.80(9), so 0.80. Cederman 2003 (draft): cumulative slope about 0.41.
rows.citation: Clauset, A. (2018) Trends and fluctuations in the severity of interstate wars. Science Advances 4:eaao3580 (values via arXiv 1901.05086); Clauset et al. 2009; Newman 2005; Cederman, L.-E. (2003) APSR 97(1):135-150
rows.known_constraint_explaining_deviation: Finite world population gives an upper cutoff. Total deaths are dominated by the largest wars (WWII); normalizing per population changes zeta (0.53 vs 0.7-0.8).

rows.system: Terrorist attacks worldwide (MIPT, 1968-2006, 9,101 events)
rows.zeta_estimate: Clauset 2009: xmin = 12 +/- 4, alpha = 2.4(2), n_tail = 547, p = 0.68, so zeta = 1.4. JCR preprint: alpha 'fluctuates about 2.5', so about 1.5. Lognormal and other alternatives are also plausible.
rows.citation: Clauset, Shalizi & Newman (2009) Table 6.1 (arXiv 0706.1062); Clauset, A., Young, M., Gleditsch, K. S. (2007) On the frequency of severe terrorist events. J. Conflict Resolution 51(1):58-87, doi:10.1177/0022002706296157
rows.known_constraint_explaining_deviation: Bottom-heavy (zeta > 1). The coalescence-fragmentation model predicts alpha = 2.5 (from memory). Weapon type and target economy matter less than expected.

rows.system: Electrical blackouts (USA, 1984-2002, NERC)
rows.zeta_estimate: Clauset 2009: alpha = 2.3 +/- 0.3, so zeta = 1.3 (p not verified). Carreras et al. 2004: several blackout-size measures have power tails (values not retrieved); other summaries give North American exponents of 1.3-2.0.
rows.citation: Clauset et al. 2009 via arXiv 2505.00748; Carreras, B. A., Newman, D. E., Dobson, I., Poole, A. B. (2004) IEEE Trans. Circuits and Systems I 51(9):1733-1740
rows.known_constraint_explaining_deviation: Operator and upgrade feedback, finite grid size, and incompleteness of the NERC list.

rows.system: Explosive volcanic eruptions (LaMEVE, Quaternary, M >= 4, 1,883 records)
rows.zeta_estimate: Counts per magnitude unit: 826 (M4), 591, 319, 119, 26 (M8). The ratios per decade of mass (0.72, 0.54, 0.37, 0.22) imply an apparent zeta_mass of about 0.14 to 0.66, increasing with size. This is my arithmetic on raw counts, uncorrected for strong under-recording of small eruptions. Deligne et al. 2010: the magnitude-frequency relation is robust only to M = 7.
rows.dynamics_class: Unknown (magma accumulation and release; threshold failure)
rows.citation: LaMEVE analysis, J. Applied Volcanology 3:5 (2014), doi:10.1186/2191-5040-3-5; Crosweller et al. (2012) J. Applied Volcanology 1:4; Deligne, Coles & Sparks (2010) JGR 115, doi:10.1029/2009JB006554
rows.known_constraint_explaining_deviation: Severe completeness bias and a magma-chamber volume cutoff. Not a clean power law, so no reliable zeta.

rows.system: HTTP transfer sizes (one research lab, 24 h, June 1996)
rows.zeta_estimate: Clauset 2009: alpha = 2.48(5), xmin = 36.25 kB, so zeta = 1.48 (from memory, not verified).
rows.dynamics_class: Unknown (file-size generation by human and software processes)
rows.citation: Clauset et al. (2009) (dataset confirmed: bytes received per HTTP request, June 1996)
rows.known_constraint_explaining_deviation: Designed and engineered objects with caching; not a natural allocation.

res.selection_notes:
How the systems were chosen. I started from the two standardized compilations to limit cherry-picking: Clauset, Shalizi & Newman (2009), with 24 datasets, and Newman (2005), with 12. I then added every system named in the task, plus systems I expected to be informative either way: European firms, natural cities, mutual funds, trees, the galaxy stellar mass function, dark-matter subhalos, tropical-cyclone PDI, rain, neuronal avalanches, bolides, rock fragmentation, superflares and volcanoes. Every contradicting system I found is kept.

Verification limits in this environment:
- WebFetch failed on DNS for every domain, and the outbound proxy allowed only GitHub and PyPI, so arXiv, publisher and PMC pages could not be opened directly.
- All verification therefore came from web-search result extracts. These often quote primary text (abstracts, figure captions, table fragments) and sometimes reliable secondary summaries.
- Clauset's Table 6.1 could not be retrieved whole. These rows were verified:
  - terrorism, directly;
  - citations 3.16 +/- 0.06 and protein interaction 3.1 +/- 0.3, directly;
  - wars, blackouts, cities, fires, flares, earthquakes and metabolic degree, through the comparison table in Aschwanden & Scholkmann (2025);
  - Moby Dick, through the poweRlaw documentation.
- These Clauset rows are from memory and marked verified=false: web links (tentative), Internet AS degree, email, species per genus, bird sightings, book sales, religions, surnames 2.5, net worth 2.3, papers authored, web hits 1.81, HTTP.
- Some rows mix verified and unverified numbers. In those, the unverified sub-values are labeled in the text, and the flag reflects the headline value.

Conversions:
- A density exponent alpha gives zeta = alpha - 1. A rank exponent r gives zeta = 1/r.
- For mass from linear size, zeta_m = D/3 (fragments) or 11/8 - 1 (trees, via M proportional to D^(8/3)).
- For rupture area, zeta_A = b, assuming M0 proportional to A^(3/2). For seismic moment, zeta_M0 = beta.
- For Schechter functions, zeta = -(alpha_Schechter + 1) below M*.
- For NBSS slope s, zeta = -s. For abundance per log bin slope s_N, zeta = -s_N.
- Ambiguous conventions are flagged: oil fields (D), islands, river basins, landslide subsets.

Known selection biases:
1. Selection on fame. Firms, cities, words and the Sheldon spectrum are studied because they are famous for Zipf or a slope of -1. Systems with exponential or lognormal tails are rarely written up as power laws, so publication favors heavy tails.
2. Top-tail-only samples. Forbes 400, top incomes, the top 135 metro areas, bestsellers and xmin-selected tails all are.
3. xmin and estimator dependence. The same data give 0.3-1.2 for fires, 0.95-1.20 for words, 1.09-1.49 for wealth, 0.5-1.0 for superflares and 0.81-1.40 for web hits. OLS rank regressions are biased.
4. Freedom to choose the variable. If q is proportional to k^d, then zeta_q = zeta_k/d, so any power-law variable can be rescaled to zeta = 1 by choosing its power after the fact. Earthquake rupture area (zeta about 1) versus moment or energy (zeta about 0.63) is the clearest case, including the repo's own re-expression. Only additive, conserved resources declared in advance should count.
5. Non-independence. Several city rows, and Clauset and Newman, reuse the same datasets.
6. Representative values. The summary uses one value per row, chosen by me, and the summary statistics are sensitive to those choices.
7. Non-resource variables. Degrees, counts of distinct things (species per genus, papers authored, active electrodes) and nested quantities (river drainage area) appear in the standard compilations and are flagged.

Omitted, and why:
- Bank sizes: no exponent retrieved. Janicki & Prescott find neither lognormal nor Pareto fits the whole range; Goddard et al. reject Zipf for the upper tail.
- Moon craters: diameter is not a held resource.
- Species-abundance distributions: lognormal or log-series, with no power-law exponent to report.
- Snow avalanches, stock-market capitalization, Kuiper-belt objects: not checked.
- Gabaix's formula zeta = 1/(1 - s_min/mean): taken from the task context and not verified in this session. The Blank & Solomon critique was verified through Malevergne et al. (2013).
res.pattern_summary:
Does zeta cluster at 1? Only partly, and much less than a law would require.

Distribution:
- Across 47 rows, using one representative value per row: median about 1.0, interquartile range about 0.65-1.36, range 0.1 to 3.3. Only about 30% of rows lie within +/-0.1 of 1 and about 40% within +/-0.25.
- Restricted to the 39 additive resource variables (stocks, fluxes and events): median 1.00, interquartile range about 0.65-1.30, 36% within +/-0.1.
- The least cherry-picked set, Clauset 2009's 24 datasets, does not center on 1. Converted values have a median of about 1.3, an interquartile range of about 1.0-1.7, and only 2-3 of 24 within +/-0.1. Newman 2005's resource-like rows have a median of about 1.2.

By class:
- Stocks (20 rows): cluster nearest 1. Median about 1.01, interquartile range about 0.90-1.13, about 45-50% within +/-0.1.
  - Stocks built by proportional growth with entry and exit come closest: US firms 1.06, European firms 0.89-1.00, US metro areas 1.005, natural cities about 1, word tokens 0.95-1.2, surnames 0.94. So do the ocean biomass spectrum (1.04) and aquatic size spectra (1.015).
  - But the same class also gives clear exceptions: administrative-city top tails 1.3-1.4 (zeta = 1 rejected), Forbes wealth 1.09-1.49, income 1.5-2.5 (a flux), gene families 1-3, and mutual funds with a lognormal tail and no power law at all.
  - Stocks from other mechanisms are often far from 1: trees 0.375, galaxy stellar mass 0.47, islands about 0.65, the stellar IMF 1.35 above the turnover and 0.3 below it, lakes 1.14 (percolation theory predicts 1.055), and simulated dark-matter subhalos 0.9.
- Events and cascades (16 rows): median about 0.8, and most lie below 1 (top-heavy), commonly 0.1-0.7.
  - Below 1: tropical-cyclone dissipation about 0-0.25, rain 0.17-0.4, wildfires 0.3-0.75, war deaths 0.53, hard X-ray flare energy about 0.5, seismic moment or energy 0.60-0.68, rock fragments 0.65-0.81, bolides 0.90.
  - Near 1: GOES soft X-ray fluence 1.03, Kepler superflares about 1 (or 0.5 at 1-min cadence), and earthquake rupture area 1.0. Rupture area is a re-expression of b about 1 and is not independent of the moment row.
  - Above 1: landslides 1.4, terrorism 1.4, blackouts 1.3.
  - Several event classes have theories that predict zeta not equal to 1: mean-field branching 1/2, fractal-diffusive SOC energy 2/3, Dohnanyi cascade 5/6, Kagan's argued beta = 1/2.
- Degree and count variables (8 rows) do not cluster at 1 (median about 1.4, range 0.43-3.3) and should be excluded from any test.

So yes, stocks with proportional growth cluster nearer 1 than events and cascades, but with large exceptions inside the favored class.

Theory checks (verified):
- Malevergne, Saichev & Sornette (2013) show that Gibrat growth gives zeta = 1 only under a balance condition: incumbent net growth, including exits, must equal growth of investment in entrants. Otherwise zeta differs from 1. They interpret zeta = 1 as the signature of maximum sustainable growth under a resource limit. That makes zeta = 1 a boundary case, not a generic attractor.
- Gabaix's limit (s_min/mean -> 0) was criticized by Blank & Solomon (2000) as incompatible with a finite number of units.
- Schwarzkopf & Farmer show relaxation to the Zipf steady state can be too slow to matter.

My synthesis (not a verified claim):
- The defensible mathematical statement is that zeta = 1 is the unique scale-free allocation in which resource per log-size decade is constant, so neither the lower nor the upper cutoff dominates the total.
- Every observed zeta < 1 system has an explicit upper cutoff: tropical-cyclone basin size, galaxy M*, the corner moment, finite world population for wars. Every zeta > 1 system has a lower cutoff.
- On this evidence, orthopolity in its log form works as a null or reference allocation: approximately realized by growth-driven stocks and by a few event classes, and violated by most cascades.
- 'Deviations are imposed by constraints' is testable only where the constraint predicts the deviation in advance, as in Dohnanyi's 5/6, percolation's 96/91, the trophic relation zeta = 1 - log TE/log PPMR, and Malevergne et al.'s balance condition. In those cases the predicted values are generally not 1.
- The compiled evidence does not support calling zeta = 1 a general natural law.

design.precise_statement:
Tags used in every field: [V] verified (in this task or marked verified in the dossier from a primary or reliable secondary source); [R] computed by the repository and read from its results JSON; [D] my own derivation, checked numerically in the scratchpad ([session scratchpad, not retained], front_check.py) but not found in the literature; [U] unverified (from memory, or the source was not seen).

STRONGEST DEFENSIBLE STATEMENT. It has three parts: a conditional transport identity, an exact theorem for one dynamical class, and a zero-parameter empirical law to be tested. It is not an unconditional empirical universal.

Setting
- Units i hold amounts S_i > 0 of an additive resource. Let u = ln(S/s_e), where s_e is the largest size at which new units enter.
- Coordinate = the resource itself (k = q). Reference measure = du, the Haar measure of dilations. No cost exponent d appears.
- O_log means the resource per unit u, B(u), is constant on a range. Equivalently P(S > s) ∝ s^-zeta with zeta = 1 on that range.

Part A. Transport identity (any system in which resource is carried through log-size)
- At stationarity, B(u) = F(u)/v(u), where F is the resource flux through u and v is the log-speed at which the resource moves.
- Hence zeta - 1 = -d ln B/du = -d ln F/du + d ln v/du, plus a diffusive correction given exactly in Part B.
- O_log holds on an interval iff two conditions hold there:
  - (i) the flux is conserved: no net local creation or loss, i.e. growth exactly balances attrition;
  - (ii) the log-speed is scale-invariant: rates are homogeneous of degree 0 in size, which is Gibrat's law.
- Condition (ii) is the precise content of "nature does not care about concentration" (multiplicative indifference). Condition (i) is the precise content of "conservation". Additive indifference gives an exponential instead (Dragulescu and Yakovenko 2000) [V].
- This is the standard Kolmogorov/Obukhov cascade closure: energy per ln k = epsilon/omega(k) ∝ k^(-2/3) [V]. Here it is applied to unit-held stocks [D].

Part B. Theorem for the Gibrat stock class
Assumptions:
- (A1) Incumbents follow dS = mu S dt + sigma S dW, with mu and sigma^2 independent of S. mu is measured relative to the growth of the entrant scale.
- (A2) Units exit at a size-independent hazard h.
- (A3) Units enter at sizes ≤ s_e, at a rate growing as e^(nu t).
- (A4) The system is stationary relative to the entrant scale.

Result: for every S > s_e, not only asymptotically,
B(u) = J_R / sqrt(m^2 + 2 sigma^2 phi) · exp[-(zeta - 1) u],
with
- m = mu + sigma^2/2,
- phi = h + nu - mu,
- J_R = resource entry flux,
- zeta - 1 = [sqrt(m^2 + 2 sigma^2 phi) - m]/sigma^2. Equivalently (zeta - 1)(mu + sigma^2 zeta/2) = phi, i.e. the positive root of (sigma^2/2) z^2 + (mu - sigma^2/2) z - (h + nu) = 0.

Provenance: the exponent equation is Reed (2001) Econ. Lett. 74:15-19 [V], Reed and Hughes (2002) PRE 66:067103 [V], and Saichev, Malevergne and Sornette (2010) [V]. The exact all-S profile and its normalization are [D]: Monte Carlo agrees to within 0.2% for u ≤ 3 at phi = 0 and phi = 0.01.

Corollaries:
- (B1) O_log ⟺ phi = 0 ⟺ each entry cohort's expected resource, measured relative to the entry flow, is conserved ⟺ expected resource per unit age is constant [D]. Conveyor picture: plateau height = J_R/m, i.e. resource flux divided by resource log-speed [D].
- (B2) Linear response: zeta - 1 = phi/m + O(phi^2) [D].
- (B3) Sign rule.
  - Balanced growth with net injection at the bottom (phi > 0) gives zeta > 1.
  - Incumbents outgrowing the entry flow (phi < 0) gives zeta < 1. The normalized mean then diverges (condensation; non-stationary relative to the total).
  - Reflecting-floor special case: zeta = 1/(1 - s_min/s̄) (Gabaix 1999) [V].
  - Kesten special case: zeta = 1 iff E[A] = 1 [V].
  - Simon special case: zeta = 1/(1 - alpha) [V].
- (B4) Finite-age front: a system of age T is flat only up to u ≈ mT. The half-height falls at u = 4.5, 9.5 and 19.5 for mT = 5, 10 and 20 [D].
- (B5) Size-dependent rates: zeta(S) solves the same equation with local coefficients plus gradient terms (Gabaix 1999; Ioannides and Overman 2003) [V/U for the exact printed form]. In the deterministic limit, zeta(S) = h(S)/g(S) + d ln g/d ln S, where g is the specific growth rate [D; it agrees with McKendrick-von Foerster/demographic equilibrium, Muller-Landau et al. 2006 [V]].

Part C. Empirical law to be tested (the substantive claim)
Across all real systems that pass preregistered gates for A1-A4:
- observed zeta = zeta_pred(mu, sigma^2, h, nu), with all four rates measured from unit-level panel data and no free parameters;
- O_log is observed exactly where measured phi ≈ 0.

"Orthopolity is general" is replaced by this: O_log is the zero-deviation fixed point of a stated transport class, and deviations are a measurable linear response.

Domain of validity
In domain:
- stocks of a unit-held additive resource;
- multiplicative, size-independent growth;
- entry at the bottom and size-independent exit;
- observed after relaxation (mT exceeds the fitted log-range), on s_e < S < (finite-age or physical cutoff).

Outside the domain, Part A predicts non-O_log values, which test the deviation calculus and not O_log:
- event catalogs: earthquakes, flares, fires, rain, wars. There is no incumbent-growth transport, and critical branching gives zeta = 1/2 [V];
- additive exchange, which gives an exponential [V];
- coagulation/fragmentation cascades and turbulence, where v is size-dependent: zeta = (1+nu_K)/2, 5/6, k^(-2/3) [V/D];
- size-structured food webs and forests, where v ∝ S^(n-1);
- systems that have not relaxed.

Explicitly NOT claimed:
- a universal natural or cosmological law;
- a maximum-entropy selection of zeta = 1 (Visser 2013 [V]: MaxEnt does not select 1);
- that observing zeta ≈ 1 identifies the mechanism (sample-space-reducing processes and latent-variable mixtures also give it [V]).
design.resource_selection_rule:
RULE R. Frozen and posted (OSF timestamp plus git commit hash) before any size distribution of a test system is examined. It is enforced in code, so that predictions are computed and hashed before the code that fits the held-out cross-section can run.

R1 Unit
- Defined by a published operational algorithm that does not use size statistics. Examples: GHSL urban-centre delineation, legal enterprise identifier, tagged tree stem.
- No post hoc merging or splitting.
- Alternative unit definitions are preregistered sensitivity analyses. They are reported, never selected. (Rozenfeld et al. 2011 [V] show the exponent depends on the unit definition.)

R2 Resource
- Must be additive, held by units, and have a system budget that can be closed term by term from the panel: dQ_tot/dt = incumbent growth + entry - exit ± measured transfers.
- Admissible examples: population, employment, total assets, aboveground carbon, members.
- Inadmissible as a primary resource:
  - any proxy obtained by converting another variable through an assumed scaling, such as magnitude→rupture area or peak flux→fluence. Diameter→biomass is allowed only through a preregistered allometry with propagated error;
  - degrees or counts of distinct partners;
  - nested quantities, such as drainage area;
  - instrument-band fractions of energy.

R3 Multiplicity
- If several resources are admissible (firms: employment, assets, revenue), each is analysed with its own measured rates and receives its own prediction. All count toward the falsification tally.
- This closes the main loophole: the claim is zeta_obs(q) = zeta_pred(q) for every admissible q, never "zeta_obs = 1 for some q".

R4 Coordinate and measure
- Size coordinate = the resource itself (k = q), with measure d ln q. No cost exponent d, no reparametrization.
- Reason: by the vacuity lemma, any density ∝ k^-alpha satisfies O_log for q ∝ k^(alpha-1). Fixing k = q removes this freedom.

R5 Fitting range, taken from the theory
- Lower bound s_e = the 95th percentile of entrant sizes observed in the panel. This is where Theorem B makes the profile exact.
- Upper bound = min(the finite-age front s_e·exp(mT - 2 sigma sqrt(T)), any physical cutoff named in advance).
- No KS-optimized xmin. The dossier shows xmin choice alone moves zeta by 0.3-0.9 for fires and wealth [V].
- Sensitivity runs at s_e ×0.5 and ×2 are preregistered.

R6 Class gates
- Computed from panel rates only, before zeta is computed:
  - Gibrat gate: |d ln sigma^2/d ln S| ≤ 0.15 and |d mu/d ln S| ≤ 0.1 m;
  - hazard gate: |d ln h/d ln S| ≤ 0.15;
  - relaxation gate: mT ≥ fitted log-range + 2 sigma sqrt(T).
- Thresholds must be justified by a preregistered power and bias simulation.
- Failing systems are scored only in a separate, preregistered local-formula (B5) analysis. They are counted and reported.

R7 Event catalogs
- The rule designates the budgeted released quantity: seismic moment, or radiated or magnetic energy.
- Catalogs are out-of-domain controls.

R8 Holdout
- Rates are estimated in an earlier window. The tested cross-section is a later epoch, a later data release, or a prospective collection.

What Rule R implies for the repository's existing cases
- Earthquakes: resource = seismic moment, giving zeta_M0 = 0.666 [0.649, 0.683] (USGS Mw ≥ 5.5, n = 6,639) [R]. This is not O_log. The rupture-area result zeta_A = b = 0.998 [0.973, 1.024] [R] is inadmissible: a proxy, without a budget, chosen post hoc. Aki's D = 2b relation [V] means it is also not new.
- Flares: resource = energy. GOES 1-8 Å end fluence (alpha = 2.125 [2.026, 2.219] raw; 1.899 [1.820, 1.986] crudely background-subtracted) [R] is an instrument-band proxy and inadmissible. Literature energy exponents are alpha_E ≈ 1.5-1.8, i.e. zeta ≈ 0.5-0.8 [V].
- Ocean: carbon biomass with coordinate = individual mass is admissible, but the system is outside the Gibrat class (Part A with v ∝ m^(n-1)).
design.theory_section:
PLANNED THEORY SECTION (main text about 4 pages, with derivations in the SI). Each item says whether it is known (K) or possibly new (N); N items require a full-text literature check before any priority claim.

T1. Accounting and measure. Keep from repo paper §2.1-2.2.
- O_mu(k) = q̄(k) dN/dmu. Linear and log allocation give different exponents.
- With k = q, O_log ⟺ zeta_q = 1.
- Known K: Sheldon 1972; Hudson 1991 alpha = 2 criterion [V]; Winslow et al. lake equal-share slopes 0.63/1/1.12 [V]; Newman 2005 top-share W = P^((alpha-2)/(alpha-1)) [V].

T2. Vacuity lemma and impossibility of static selection. K, repo §2.3.
- Any density ∝ k^-alpha is O_log for q ∝ k^(alpha-1). Any p_N is Haar-uniform for q = 1/(k p_N).
- Dilation symmetry gives only the power family nu_gamma = k^(-1-gamma) dk. O_log is the trivial character on the resource measure, which is an added postulate [D; the classical result is in Frank 2009/2016 and Pinkham 1961 [V]].
- MaxEnt with no constraint returns the reference measure (Jaynes 1957/1968 [V]). A log-moment constraint gives any exponent (Visser 2013 [V]).
- Conclusion stated as a theorem-level negative result: no static conservation, symmetry or entropy argument selects zeta = 1. Content must come from dynamics. This answers the authors' "nature doesn't care" intuition honestly.

T3. Log-size continuity (transport identity). K in pieces, N as a unifying statement [D].
- For resource density B(u), flux F and log-speed v: dB/dt + dF/du = (local creation - loss). At stationarity, B = F/v and zeta - 1 = -d ln F/du + d ln v/du.
- Recovers K results as measured deviations:
  - Kolmogorov: k E(k) = epsilon/omega(k) ∝ k^(-2/3) [V, standard flux closure].
  - Dohnanyi: lossless downward flux, with collisional lifetime ∝ D^(1/2) ∝ m^(1/6). So v ∝ m^(-1/6) and zeta_m - 1 = -1/6, giving 5/6 [V for 11/6; D for this reading].
  - Coagulation with source, kernel homogeneity nu_K: zeta = (1+nu_K)/2, so O_log iff nu_K = 1 (Connaughton, Rajesh and Zaboronski 2004, PRE 69:061114) [V].
  - O'Brien and Greenberg 2003: zeta_m = 5/(6+s), with s the strength-scaling exponent [V formula; D conversion].
  - Platt and Denman 1977: biomass per log class ∝ w^-0.22 [V].
  - Size spectra (Hartvig, Andersen and Beyer 2011): biomass/log w ∝ w^(n-q) [V].
- Message: O_log is the unique profile with conserved flux and scale-invariant log-speed. Every known non-1 exponent in the dossier is a measurable speed gradient or loss term.

T4. Main theorem (Gibrat stock class). Exponent K; exact profile N [D].
- Statement as in precise_statement Part B.
- Proof via the occupation density of Brownian motion with drift. For X_t = m t + sigma W_t, the integral ∫0^∞ e^(-phi t) p_t(u) dt equals exp[(m u - |u| sqrt(m^2 + 2 sigma^2 phi))/sigma^2]/sqrt(m^2 + 2 sigma^2 phi). Apply this under the size-biased (resource-weighted) measure, whose drift is m = mu + sigma^2/2.
- Entry spread below s_e convolves the result without changing the exponential form above s_e.
- Numerical checks:
  - [D] scratchpad profile_check.py, ratio simulation/exact = 1.000-1.002 for u ≤ 3;
  - [R] repo results/gibrat.json: the exact sampler gives zeta = 1.0019 ± 0.0022 at phi = 0 and 1.614 ± 0.005 against predicted 1.618 at phi = 0.05;
  - [R] the time-stepped run gives 0.988 ± 0.010 at phi = 0.
- Attribution:
  - Reed (2001) Econ. Lett. 74(1):15-19 [V]; Reed and Hughes (2002) PRE 66:067103 [V];
  - Saichev, Malevergne and Sornette (2010) LNEMS 632 [V]; Malevergne, Saichev and Sornette (2013) JEDC 37:1195-1212 [V], whose balance condition mu - h = d + c0 gives Zipf;
  - Luttmer (2007) QJE 122(3):1103-1144 [V]: tail index just above 1 when the entrant-incumbent growth gap is small;
  - Gabaix (1999) QJE 114:739-767 [V]; Levy and Solomon (1996) [V]; Malcai, Biham and Solomon (1999) [V]; Bouchaud and Mézard (2000) [V]; Simon (1955) [V]; Kesten (1973) and Goldie (1991) [V].

T5. Corollaries. Mostly N [D]; the sign rule is implicit in MSS 2013 (K).
- Cohort/age equivalence: phi = 0 ⟺ equal expected resource per unit age ⟺ flat B(u). This yields an age-profile test that needs no tail fit.
- Linear response zeta - 1 ≈ phi/m.
- Sign rule and condensation for phi < 0, linked to Bouchaud-Mézard condensation [V].
- Finite-age front at u ≈ mT [D: front_check.py gives half-height at 4.52/9.54/19.51 for mT = 5/10/20]. This connects to the slow-transition result of Gabaix, Lasry, Lions and Moll (2016) [V] and is K in spirit.
- Finite N and order of limits (Malcai et al. 1999 [V]): with zeta = 1 on [s_e, S_max], the expected top share scales as ln(S_max/S)/ln(S_max/s_e). Fluctuations of the largest unit must be stated.

T6. Local and deterministic generalization. K.
- zeta(S) = 1 - 2 mu(S)/sigma^2(S) + d ln sigma^2/d ln S in the reflected, zero-flux case (Gabaix 1999; Ioannides and Overman 2003) [V content; exact printed form U].
- Deterministic killed growth: zeta = h/g + d ln g/d ln S [D; it agrees with McKendrick-von Foerster, Zhou and Huntley 1997 [V], and Muller-Landau et al. 2006 Ecol. Lett. 9:589-602 [V]].
- Firms: sigma ∝ S^-0.2 (Stanley 1996; Amaral 1997) [V] gives a local shift of -2beta ≈ -0.4. This is a predicted curvature, not a fudge.

T7. Class map: where O_log is and is not predicted. Mostly K, compiled as a table.
- Gibrat stocks: phi = 0 fixed point.
- Additive exchange: exponential [V].
- Cascades and turbulence: speed gradients [V/D].
- Critical branching events: zeta = 1/2 (mean-field tau = 3/2; Kagan 2010; Fisher et al. 1997) [V].
- Percolation lakes: 96/91 [V].
- Press-Schechter halos: zeta = 1 - (n_eff+3)/6 [V].
- Possible remark, clearly labelled conjecture [D/U]: zeta = 1 for stocks and zeta = 1/2 for event sizes are both marginal power laws of martingale (conservation-in-expectation) dynamics. Stocks are observed at an exponential killing time; event sizes are time-integrals of a critical branching process.

T8. Estimation theory. K.
- Hill/MLE with SE ≈ zeta/sqrt(n_tail). Gabaix and Ibragimov (2011) JBES 29(1):24-39 rank-1/2 OLS with SE = b·sqrt(2/n) [V]. Clauset, Shalizi and Newman (2009) [V].
- Errors-in-variables calibration regression. Block bootstrap for dependence.
- Delta-method SE(zeta_pred) ≈ SE(phi)/m.

What the theory section must not contain:
- MaxEnt "derivation" of O_log;
- independent-inputs exponent addition (repo §2.3 counterexample);
- cosmology;
- the ensemble claims of repo §2.4. The cosh lemma may stay in the SI as a statistical caution.

deviation_predictions.constraint: Net injection share phi = h + nu - mu relative to the resource log-speed m = mu + sigma^2/2
deviation_predictions.predicted_deviation: zeta - 1 = [sqrt(m^2 + 2 sigma^2 phi) - m]/sigma^2 ≈ phi/m. The resource-per-log profile is exactly exponential above the entry scale s_e. Reed 2001 / SMS 2010 [V]; exact profile [D].
deviation_predictions.data_available: Unit-level panels (entry, exit, growth). Public options are listed in the empirical tests. Many firm and product panels are confidential.

deviation_predictions.system: Amazee online groups (Zhang & Sornette 2011, Physica A 390:4124)
deviation_predictions.constraint: Mean growth exceeds death rate (phi < 0, unbalanced growth)
deviation_predictions.predicted_deviation: zeta = 0.75 ± 0.05 predicted with no free parameters, matching the ML fit [V]. The sign rule predicts zeta < 1.
deviation_predictions.data_available: Published rates. Use only as pipeline validation (replicate with the repo's gibrat_zeta); it is not new evidence.

deviation_predictions.constraint: Measured growth, volatility, birth and hazard rates
deviation_predictions.predicted_deviation: Temporal and product variation in zeta is captured without adjustable parameters [V]
deviation_predictions.data_available: Proprietary point-of-sale data. Published results are used only as prior-art validation.

deviation_predictions.system: Gibrat stock with a reflecting floor, normalized by the total (Gabaix 1999)
deviation_predictions.predicted_deviation: zeta = 1/(1 - s_min/s̄) ≥ 1. For example 0.2 gives 1.25 [V mechanism; formula derived in dossier]. Repo simulation: 1.31-1.40 at 0.2, with a finite-N/time lag.
deviation_predictions.data_available: Only where a real floor exists. Definitional thresholds (e.g., ≥50k for urban centres) are NOT reflecting barriers and must not be used.

deviation_predictions.constraint: sigma ∝ S^-beta with beta = 0.18-0.20 (Stanley et al. 1996; Amaral et al. 1997) [V]
deviation_predictions.predicted_deviation: Local zeta(S) shifts by d ln sigma^2/d ln S = -2 beta ≈ -0.4 unless a compensating size-dependent drift exists. This predicts measurable curvature in B(u). The observed zeta is about 1.06-1.10 (Axtell 2001; SBA 2011) [V].
deviation_predictions.data_available: beta is published from Compustat-type data. All-firm microdata (LBD) are confidential. Public BDS gives size and age classes only.

deviation_predictions.system: Any Gibrat stock of finite age T
deviation_predictions.predicted_deviation: The plateau (or exponential profile) extends only to ln(S/s_e) ≈ (mu + sigma^2/2)T, with a front width of about sigma sqrt(T) [D, front_check.py]. Beyond it, B(u) collapses. Systems with mT smaller than the fitted range must not be expected to show the stationary zeta (cf. Gabaix-Lasry-Lions-Moll 2016; Schwarzkopf & Farmer 2010 mutual funds, lognormal) [V].
deviation_predictions.data_available: Requires system age plus panel rates. Online platforms and cities with known founding epochs.

deviation_predictions.constraint: Cohort resource conservation relative to the entry flow
deviation_predictions.predicted_deviation: Under Theorem B, employment per unit firm age ∝ e^(-phi a). A flat age profile ⟺ flat size profile [D]. A declining cohort employment share predicts zeta > 1.
deviation_predictions.data_available: Census BDS public tables by firm age and firm size [V that BDS publishes firm-age and firm-size statistics; exact cross-tabs and current year coverage U].

deviation_predictions.constraint: Size-dependent specific growth g(M) and mortality h(M) (deterministic local budget)
deviation_predictions.predicted_deviation: zeta(M) = h(M)/g(M) + d ln g/d ln M, plus diffusion terms [D; demographic-equilibrium prior art, Muller-Landau et al. 2006 [V]]. Predicted top-heavy (zeta < 1) wherever large-tree mortality is below specific growth. The Enquist-Niklas mass exponent implies zeta ≈ 0.375 [V].
deviation_predictions.data_available: Condit et al. 2019, Dryad doi:10.15146/5xcp-0d46: 8 censuses 1982-2015 [V]. Terms of use may request co-authorship [V].

deviation_predictions.constraint: Search-volume exponent q vs metabolic exponent n (physiology)
deviation_predictions.predicted_deviation: Biomass per log mass ∝ m^(n-q), giving about -0.05 for q = 0.8, n = 0.75 (Andersen & Beyer 2006; Hartvig et al. 2011) [V]. Observed: -0.039 [-0.058, -0.026] [R, repo re-expression of Hatton et al. 2021] and -0.04 [-0.05, -0.02] [V]. Consistent, but this is prior-art theory; orthopolity adds nothing beyond the Part A reading.

deviation_predictions.constraint: Collisional lifetime vs size (log-speed gradient). Strength scaling Q* ∝ D^s

With strength scaling, zeta_m = 5/(6+s): 0.89 (strength regime, s ≈ -0.4), 0.68 (gravity regime, s ≈ +1.3) [V formula, O'Brien & Greenberg 2003; conversion D]. O_log only if s = -1.

deviation_predictions.predicted_deviation: zeta = (1+nu_K)/2. O_log iff nu_K = 1. A constant kernel gives 1/2 (Connaughton et al. 2004) [V].
deviation_predictions.data_available: Aerosol and polymer systems with known kernels. Out of class.

deviation_predictions.predicted_deviation: Resource = seismic moment: zeta_M0 = 2b/3 = 0.666 [0.649, 0.683] [R]. GCMT beta = 0.60-0.65 (Kagan 2002) [V]. Scholz 2015 b = 1.23 - 0.0012 Δσ [V] gives zeta_M0 = 0.82 - 0.0008 Δσ, so O_log in moment (b = 1.5) is never reached for Δσ ≥ 0. Mean-field branching gives 1/2 (Kagan 2010) [V]. Illustration only: Hanks-Bakun width saturation moves the inadmissible area proxy to 4b/3, and repo Mw ≥ 6.7 gives 1.355 [1.286, 1.443] [R/V].
